nodes.statement: A topology on X is a family of subsets containing the empty set and X, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
nodes.mathText: A topology on X is a family of subsets containing the empty set and X, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.

nodes.statement: A subset C of X is closed exactly when its complement X ∖ C is open.
nodes.mathText: A subset C of X is closed exactly when its complement X ∖ C is open.

nodes.statement: A subset A of a topological space X inherits the topology consisting of all intersections U ∩ A, where U is open in X.
nodes.mathText: A subset A of a topological space X inherits the topology consisting of all intersections U ∩ A, where U is open in X.

nodes.statement: A map f : X → Y is continuous at x if every neighborhood V of f(x) contains f(U) for some neighborhood U of x. It is continuous if this holds at every x.
nodes.mathText: A map f : X → Y is continuous at x if every neighborhood V of f(x) contains f(U) for some neighborhood U of x. It is continuous if this holds at every x.

nodes.statement: A map f : X → Y is continuous exactly when the preimage of every closed subset of Y is closed in X. Only parts (1) and (3) are modeled here.

nodes.statement: A homeomorphism is a bijection f for which both f and its inverse function are continuous.
nodes.mathText: A homeomorphism is a bijection f for which both f and its inverse function are continuous.

nodes.en: A continuous bijection, not a homeomorphism
nodes.statement: With the usual subspace topologies, f : [0,1) → S¹ given by f(t) = (cos 2πt, sin 2πt) is a continuous bijection. Its inverse is discontinuous at (1,0).

nodes.statement: A map is closed if it sends every closed subset of its domain to a closed subset of its codomain. The source definition is unnumbered.
nodes.formula: C closed in X ⇒ f(C) closed in Y
nodes.mathText: A map is closed if it sends every closed subset of its domain to a closed subset of its codomain. The source definition is unnumbered.

nodes.statement: A space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods.
nodes.mathText: A space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods.

nodes.statement: Every metric space is Hausdorff: distinct points x and y have disjoint open balls of radius d(x,y)/2.
nodes.mathText: Every metric space is Hausdorff: distinct points x and y have disjoint open balls of radius d(x,y)/2.

nodes.statement: A space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. The same definition occurs again as Definition 6.56.
nodes.formula: Every open cover has a finite subcover
nodes.mathText: A space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. The same definition occurs again as Definition 6.56.

nodes.statement: For Y ⊆ X with the subspace topology, Y is compact exactly when every cover of Y by open sets of X has a finite subcover.
nodes.mathText: For Y ⊆ X with the subspace topology, Y is compact exactly when every cover of Y by open sets of X has a finite subcover.

nodes.statement: Every closed subset C of a compact space X is compact with its subspace topology.
nodes.formula: X compact ∧ C closed ⇒ C compact
nodes.mathText: Every closed subset C of a compact space X is compact with its subspace topology.

nodes.statement: Every compact subspace K of a Hausdorff space Y is closed in Y.
nodes.formula: K compact ∧ Y Hausdorff ⇒ K closed
nodes.mathText: Every compact subspace K of a Hausdorff space Y is closed in Y.

nodes.statement: For real a < b with the usual topology, the intervals (a,b] and [a,b) are not compact: they are not closed in the Hausdorff space ℝ.
nodes.mathText: For real a < b with the usual topology, the intervals (a,b] and [a,b) are not compact: they are not closed in the Hausdorff space ℝ.

nodes.statement: If f : X → Y is continuous and X is compact, the image f(X), with the subspace topology, is compact.
nodes.formula: f continuous ∧ X compact ⇒ f(X) compact
nodes.mathText: If f : X → Y is continuous and X is compact, the image f(X), with the subspace topology, is compact.

nodes.statement: Let X and Y be topological spaces. If f : X → Y is a continuous bijection, X is compact, and Y is Hausdorff, then f is a homeomorphism.
nodes.formula: Compact X ∧ Hausdorff Y ∧ continuous bijective f ⇒ homeomorphism f
nodes.mathText: Let X and Y be topological spaces. If f : X → Y is a continuous bijection, X is compact, and Y is Hausdorff, then f is a homeomorphism.

nodes.statement: The notes introduce the natural numbers, integers and real numbers as examples of sets.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.1. Some basic examples of sets include:
    • The natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, . . .}

    • The integers Z = {. . . , −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, . . .}
    • The real numbers R

Set calculus A set A is a subset of a set B if every element of A is also an
element of B. We write A ⊆ B to denote that A is a subset of B. If A is a
subset of B but not equal to B, we say that A is a proper subset of B and denote
it by A ⊊ B.
    We let P(A) denote the power set of A, which is the set of all subsets of A.
    We say two sets A and B are equal if they have the same elements, that is,
if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. We write A = B to denote that A and B are equal.
    We let A\B denote the set difference of A and B, which is the set of elements
in A that are not in B. Formally, A\B = {x ∈ A : x ∈    / B}. When B ⊆ A, we
say A\B is the complement of B in A.
    The empty set, denoted ∅, is a set that contains no elements. It is a subset
of every set.

nodes.statement: A family has sets as its elements. Its union collects elements in at least one member; its intersection collects elements in every member.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.2. A family of sets A is a set whose elements are sets. Usually,
we can write the family of sets as

                                      A = {Ai }i∈I

for some index set I.
    If A is a family of sets, we define the union of the family as
                            [
                                A := {x|∃A ∈ A, x ∈ A}.
                             A∈A

and the intersection as
                              \
                                   A := {x|∀A ∈ A, x ∈ A}.
                             A∈A

nodes.mathText:

nodes.statement: The putative collection of all sets leads to a contradiction when one asks whether the set of sets not containing themselves contains itself.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.4 (Russell’s paradox). Let P denote the set of all sets. Then, form
Q := {A ∈ P |A ∈
               / A}. Is Q ∈ Q?
   More axiomatic treatment of sets can be found in Zermelo-Fraenkel set the-
ory (ZF), which provides a formal foundation for set theory and avoids para-
doxes like Russell’s paradox by carefully restricting the kinds of sets that can
be formed. For example, under ZF axioms, the collection of all sets is not a set
but a proper class, because it violates one of the axioms requiring that a set
cannot contain itself as an element.

nodes.statement: A Cartesian product with an empty factor is empty.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 1.5. If one set is empty, then the Cartesian product is also empty:

                               A × ∅ = ∅ × B = ∅.

nodes.statement: A function assigns exactly one element of its codomain to each element of its domain, viewed as a subset of their Cartesian product.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.6. A function f : A → B is a subset of the Cartesian product
A × B such that for any a ∈ A, there exists a unique b ∈ B such that (a, b) ∈ f .

nodes.statement: The same formula x² + 1 defines different functions when the codomain is changed.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.7. f : R → R defined by x 7→ x2 + 1 is a function {(x, x2 + 1) ∈
R × R}.
   Formally, g : R → R+ defined by x 7→ x2 + 1 is a different function where
R+ := {x ∈ R|x > 0}.
    Of course, since each a ∈ A is associated with a unique b ∈ B, we often write
f (a) = b and then
                        f = {(a, f (a)) : a ∈ A} ⊆ A × B.
   For any C ⊆ A, we define the image of C under f as the set

                               f (C) = {f (a) : a ∈ C}.
We call f (A) the image of f .
  For any D ⊆ B, we define the preimage of D under f as the set

                         f −1 (D) = {a ∈ A : f (a) ∈ D}.

    If the image of f is equal to B, we say that f is onto or surjective. If for any
a1 ̸= a2 we have that f (a1 ) ̸= f (a2 ), we say that f is one-to-one or injective.
If a function is both injective and surjective, it is called a bijection. We usually
denote a bijection by f : A ∼= B.
    Let f : A → B and g : B → C be two functions. The composition of f and
g is the function g ◦ f : A → C defined by

                       (g ◦ f )(a) = g(f (a))   for all a ∈ A.

nodes.statement: The identity on a nonempty set is a bijection and leaves a function unchanged under the appropriate composition.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.8. For any nonempty set A, we define the identity function idA :
A → A by idA (a) = a for all a ∈ A. It is clear that idA is a bijection. Moreover,
for any function f : A → B, we have f ◦ idA = f and idB ◦ f = f .

Cartesian products of families of sets If {Ai }i∈I is a family of sets indexed
by a set I, the Cartesian product of the family is defined as

                  Ai = {f : I →     Ai : f (i) ∈ Ai for all i ∈ I}.

nodes.statement: A Cartesian product over a finite index set is identified with ordered tuples.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.9. If I = {1, 2, . . . , n} is a finite set, then i∈I Ai can be identified
with the set of ordered n-tuples (a1 , a2 , . . . , an ) where ai ∈ Ai for each i.

nodes.statement: A relation on S is a subset of S × S. Reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity and antisymmetry are stated separately.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.11. We say that R is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive,
symmetric, and transitive. An equivalence relation is usually denoted by ∼ and
if (a, b) ∈∼ we write a ∼ b.

nodes.statement: Integers are equivalent when their difference is even.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.12. The relation R on Z defined by aRb if and only if a − b is even
is an equivalence relation.

nodes.statement: A function determines an equivalence relation by equality of function values.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.13. Let f : A → B be any function. The relation R on A defined
by aRb if and only if f (a) = f (b) is an equivalence relation.

nodes.statement: Similarity gives an equivalence relation on triangles in the plane.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.14. Let T denote the set of all triangles in the plane. The relation
R on T defined by △1 R△2 if and only if △1 is similar to △2 is an equivalence
relation.

nodes.statement: The equivalence class of a consists of the elements equivalent to a.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.15. Let A be a non empty set. For any a ∈ A, we define the
equivalence class of a as
                                    [a] = { b ∈ A : a ∼ b }.

nodes.statement: Parity splits the integers into the even and odd equivalence classes.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.16. Consider the equivalence relation ∼ on Z defined by a ∼ b if
and only if a − b is even. Then, there are two equivalence classes: the even
integers and the odd integers. Specifically,
    [0] = {. . . − 4, −2, 0, 2, 4, 6, . . . },         [1] = {. . . − 5, −3, −1, 1, 3, 5, . . . }.

nodes.statement: A partition is a family of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is the whole nonempty set.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.17. Let A be a non empty set. A partition of A is a family of
nonempty subsets {Ai }i∈I such that:
   • A = i∈I Ai
         S

   • Ai ∩ Aj = ∅ for all i ̸= j
We sometimes will call each Ai a block of the partition.

nodes.statement: The displayed three blocks form a partition of a five-element set.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.18. Consider the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Then, {{1, 2}, {3}, {4, 5}}
is a partition of A.

nodes.statement: Singleton blocks give the discrete partition; one block containing the whole set gives the trivial partition.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.19. For any set A, we call {{a}}a∈A the discrete partition of A
and we call {A} the trivial partition of A.
    We denote by Part(A) the set of all partitions of A and by EqRel(A) the set
of all equivalence relations on A.

nodes.statement: On a nonempty set, grouping elements in the same block and taking equivalence classes are inverse constructions.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.20 (Partitions and equivalence relations). Let A be a nonempty set.
There is a one-to-one correspondence between partitions of A and equivalence
relations on A:
   • Define f : Part(A) → EqRel(A) by sending a partition {Ai }i∈I to the
     equivalence relation ∼ on A defined by a ∼ b if and only if ∃i ∈ I with
     a, b ∈ Ai .
   • Conversely, define g : EqRel(A) → Part(A) by sending an equivalence
     relation ∼ on A to the family of equivalence classes
                                                 {[a] : a ∈ A}
      which is a partition of A.
Then, f and g are bijections and they are inverse to each other, i.e.,
                        g ◦ f = idPart(A) ,            f ◦ g = idEqRel(A) .

nodes.statement: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; strict comparison excludes equality.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.21. A relation R on A is a partial order if it is reflexive, antisym-
metric, and transitive. A partial order is usually denoted by ≤. A set equipped
with a partial order is called a partially ordered set or poset, and is denoted by
(A, ≤). When a ≤ b and a ̸= b, we write a < b.

nodes.statement: The ordinary order of real numbers satisfies the three partial-order axioms.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.22. Consider the set of real numbers R with the usual order relation
≤. This is a partial order because it is reflexive (every number is less than or
equal to itself), antisymmetric (if a ≤ b and b ≤ a, then a = b), and transitive
(if a ≤ b and b ≤ c, then a ≤ c).
    Just a funny note: we humans know that 0.9 > 0.11 but somehow many
LLMs think 0.9 < 0.11. So be careful when using AIs in your studies :)

nodes.statement: Inclusion is a partial order on the subsets of a fixed nonempty set.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.23. Let A be a non empty set and consider its power set P(A),
the set of all subsets of A. Define, for B, C ∈ P(A),

                             B≤C        ⇐⇒       B ⊆ C.

Then (P(A), ≤) is a partial order.

nodes.statement: One partition is finer than another when every block of the first lies in a block of the second.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.24. Partitions of a fixed set A are partially ordered by refinement:
for partitions π, σ ∈ Part(A)

               π≤σ     if and only if    (∀B ∈ π)(∃C ∈ σ) B ⊆ C.

Thus π ≤ σ means “π is finer than σ” (equivalently, “σ is coarser than π”).

nodes.statement: The discrete partition of a three-element set refines the displayed two-block partition.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.25 (Refinement — simple illustration). Let A = {1, 2, 3}. Consider
the partitions

    π = {{1}, {2}, {3}}      (the discrete partition),          σ = {{1, 2}, {3}}.

We have π ≤ σ because each block of π is contained in a block of σ: {1} ⊆
{1, 2}, {2} ⊆ {1, 2}, {3} ⊆ {3}.

nodes.statement: For a finite poset, draw only covering pairs; place the larger element higher and suppress transitive edges.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.26. Hasse diagram. Let (A, ≤) be a finite poset. For x, y ∈ A,
say that y covers x if x < y and there is no z ∈ A with x < z < y. The Hasse
diagram of (A, ≤) is the directed acyclic graph with vertex set A and an edge
x → y precisely when x is covered by y. By convention it is drawn with y placed
higher than x and arrowheads omitted, and transitive edges are suppressed.

                                        {1, 2}



                       {1}                                {2}



                                          ∅

nodes.statement: A poset may contain two elements neither of which is below the other; the power-set diagram illustrates this.
Maximal and minimal exclude a strict comparison; largest and smallest compare with every element.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.28. Let (A, ≤) be a poset. A maximal element of A is an element
m ∈ A such that there is no x ∈ A with m < x. A minimal element of A is an
element n ∈ A such that there is no x ∈ A with x < n.
    The largest element of A, if it exists, is an element u ∈ A such that u ≥ x
for all x ∈ A. The smallest element of A, if it exists, is an element l ∈ A such
that l ≤ x for all x ∈ A.

nodes.statement: The source asks the reader to identify minimal, maximal, smallest and largest elements of the drawn poset.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.29. Consider the poset below. Indicate minimal/maximal and
smallest/largest elements.

                           b                      d


                                       c


                                       a

nodes.statement: The source gives a second poset exercise about extremal elements.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.30. Consider the poset below. Indicate minimal/maximal and
smallest/largest elements.

                            t                     u


                                       r


                           p                      q
    There is one case when the notion of maximal elements coincides with that
of largest elements: when the poset is totally ordered.

nodes.statement: A partial order is linear when every pair of elements is comparable.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.31 (Linear (total) order). A partial order ≤ on a set A is a linear
(or total) order if for all a, b ∈ A one has a ≤ b or b ≤ a (comparability).

nodes.statement: In a linearly ordered set, minimal means smallest and maximal means largest.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 1.32. A minimal element in a linear poset is also the smallest element.
Similarly, a maximal element is also the largest element.

nodes.statement: A linear order is a well-order when every nonempty subset has a minimal element.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.33 (Well-order). A linear poset (A, ≤) is well-ordered if every
nonempty subset B ⊆ A has a minimal element.

nodes.statement: The notes contrast the natural numbers with the usual real order and with [0,1].
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.34.      • The set of natural numbers N = {0, 1, 2, . . .} with the
    usual order ≤ is well-ordered. Be careful here and ask yourself why. This
    can be either taken as an axiom in Peano Axioms or proved under ZF.
   • The set of real numbers R with the usual order ≤ is not well-ordered. [0, 1]
     is not well-ordered as well.

nodes.statement: Finite powers of N are well-ordered lexicographically, while the displayed infinite sequence of sequences prevents the same conclusion for Nᴺ.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.35.         • We define the lexicographic order on N × N as follows:
    for (m1 , n1 ), (m2 , n2 ) ∈ N × N, we say that (m1 , n1 ) ≤ (m2 , n2 ) if either
    m1 < m2 or m1 = m2 and n1 ≤ n2 . Then, (N × N, ≤) is a well-ordered
    set.
   • We can similarly define the lexicographic order on Nk for any finite k ∈ N,
     which makes (Nk , ≤) a well-ordered set as well.
   • However, the lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered: consider the
      subset B = {(2, 1, 1, . . .) > (1, 2, 1, . . .) > . . .}. Then, B has no minimal
      element.
   The lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered. In fact, no one has found
an explicit well-order on NN so far. However, it turns out that in theory, one
can find a partial order on NN so that it is well-ordered.

nodes.statement: Every set admits a well-order; its relationship to choice is developed later in the notes.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.36 (Well-ordering theorem). Every set can be well-ordered.
    There is some caveat of this theorem though. We will mention a bit more
later on.

nodes.statement: The least element is denoted 0_A, and intervals are defined by order inequalities.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.37. Let A be a well-ordered poset. Then, A has a smallest element
which we denote by 0A . For any a, b ∈ A, we define the interval [a, b] as

                           [a, b] = {x ∈ A : a ≤ x ≤ b}.

We can similarly define [a, b), (a, b] and (a, b).

nodes.statement: An initial segment contains every element smaller than any one of its members.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.38. Let (A, ≤) be a well-ordered set. A subset S ⊂ A is called
an initial segment if for any x ∈ S and y ∈ A, y < x implies y ∈ S.

nodes.statement: Intervals starting at the least element are initial segments, and a nonempty initial segment is a union of such intervals.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.39. [0A , a) and [0A , a] are both
                                          S initial segments of A. Any nonempty
initial segment S of A can be written as s∈S [0A , s].
Order preserving maps An order preserving map between two posets (A, ≤A
) and (B, ≤B ) is a function f : A → B such that x ≤A y implies f (x) ≤B f (y).
An order isomorphism is a bijective order preserving map f : A → B such that
x ≤A y ⇐⇒ f (x) ≤B f (y).

nodes.statement: The map x ↦ ax + b is an order isomorphism of R when a > 0.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.40. f : R → R defined by x 7→ ax + b is an order isomorphism if
a > 0.
    There are infinitely many order isomorphisms f : R → R. But if we require
the poset to be well-ordered, then the situation changes. We start with the
following lemma.

nodes.statement: An order isomorphism of well-ordered sets preserves the least element and the indicated initial intervals.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 1.41. If f : A → B is an order isomorphism between two well-ordered
sets, Then
   1. f (0A ) = 0B ;
   2. for any a ∈ A, f ([0A , a]) = [0B , f (a)] and f ([0A , a)) = [0B , f (a)).

nodes.statement: Two order isomorphisms between the same well-ordered sets must agree.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 1.42. Let A, B be well-ordered sets. If f, g : A → B are order isomor-
phisms, then f = g.

nodes.statement: Order isomorphisms from one well-order onto initial segments of another are unique. The notes assign this strengthening as homework.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 1.43. Let A, B be well-ordered sets. If f, g are order isomorphisms
from A onto initial segments of B, then f = g.
   Now, we see an interesting result below saying that one can always somehow
“compare” two well-ordered sets.

sourceProofDisposition.quote: This can be strengthened as follows (this will be your homework)
sourceProofDisposition.note: Assigned as homework immediately before the lemma. No proof supplied.

nodes.statement: For two nonempty well-ordered sets, one is order-isomorphic to an initial segment of the other.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.44. Let A, B be two non empty well-ordered sets. Then, there
exists an order isomorphism from one of the sets to an initial segment of the
other.

nodes.statement: A choice function selects an element from each nonempty set in a family. The printed domain notation is retained for review.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.45. Let A = {Ai }i∈I Sbe a family of nonempty sets. A choice
function for A is a function f : A → i∈I Ai such that f (i) ∈ Ai for all i ∈ I.

nodes.statement: The disjoint-family Axiom of Choice yields a choice function for any family of nonempty sets.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 1.46. For any collection of nonempty sets, there exists a choice
function.

nodes.statement: A chain is a subset of a poset on which the inherited order is linear.
nodes.mathText: Definition 1.47. A chain is a totally (linearly) ordered subset of a poset.

nodes.statement: An upper bound of a subset is an element of the ambient poset above all of its members.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.48. Let A be a poset and B ⊆ A. Then, an upper bound of B in
A is an element u ∈ A such that b ≤ u for all b ∈ B.

nodes.statement: The displayed nested subsets form a chain under inclusion.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.49. Consider the set A = {1, 2, 3} and the subset {∅, {2}, {1, 2, 3}} ⊂
P (A) is a chain.

    (Maximum Principle) In a poset, every chain is contained in a maximal chain
(i.e., a chain that is not properly contained in any other chain).
    (Zorn’s Lemma) Let A be a poset. If every chain in A has an upper bound
in A, then A has a maximal element.

nodes.statement: A maximal chain and its upper bound yield a maximal element under Zorn’s hypotheses.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 1.50 (Maximum principle implies Zorn’s lemma). If we assume
the Maximal Principle is true for all posets, then Zorn’s Lemma is true for all
posets.

nodes.statement: The notes state equivalence of Choice, Zorn’s Lemma, the Maximum Principle and well-ordering, and give selected implications.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.51. The following statements are equivalent:
  1. (Axiom of Choice) If {Ai }i∈I is a family of nonempty pairwise disjoint
     sets, there is a set B ⊂ ∪Ai such that B ∩ Ai is exactly one element for
     all i ∈ I.
  2. (Zorn’s Lemma) If each chain (linearly ordered set) in a nonempty poset
     A has an upper bound, then A has a maximal element.
  3. (Maximal Principle) In a poset, every chain is contained in a maximal
     chain.

  4. (Zermelo’s Well-Ordering Theorem) Every set can be well-ordered.

nodes.statement: The empty set has cardinality at most that of any set.
nodes.mathText: Remark 1.52. By convention, we say the emptyset |∅| ≤ |A| for any set A.

nodes.statement: For nonempty A and B, an injection A → B exists exactly when a surjection B → A exists; the reverse construction uses choice.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 1.53. Consider two nonempty sets A and B. Then, |A| ≤ |B| if and
only if there exists a surjective function g : B → A.

nodes.statement: Cardinal comparison is reflexive and transitive; mutual comparison gives equality; any two cardinalities are comparable. Some proofs are deferred.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.54.        1. |A| ≤ |A|
  2. |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |C| imply |A| ≤ |C|
  3. If |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A|, then |A| = |B| (This is quite nontrivial! It is
     the Bernstein-Cantor-Schröder theorem.)

  4. For any two sets A, B, either |A| ≤ |B| or |B| ≤ |A|.

nodes.statement: A finite set is empty or bijective with a finite initial segment of N; other sets are infinite.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.55. A set A is said to be finite if there is a bijection f : A →
{1, 2, . . . , n} for some n ∈ N or A is empty. Otherwise, we say that A is infinite.
   We intuitively say that A has cardinality n or 0.
   Goal: Show that cardinality of a finite set is unique.

nodes.statement: Removing a distinguished element changes a finite enumeration of length n + 1 into one of length n, and conversely.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 1.56. Let A be finite and a0 ∈ A. Then, there exists a bijection
f : A → {1, . . . , n + 1} for some n ∈ N if and only if there exists a bijection
g : A \ {a0 } → {1, . . . , n} for some n ∈ N.

nodes.statement: A set bijective with {1,…,n} has no proper subset bijective with that same finite segment.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.57. Suppose f : A → {1, . . . , n} is a bijection and let B ⊊ A.
Then, there is no bijection g : B → {1, . . . , n}.

nodes.statement: A finite set cannot be bijective with a proper subset of itself.
nodes.mathText:
Corollary 1.58. If A is finite, then there is no bijection from A onto a proper
subset of itself.

nodes.statement: Two finite enumerations of the same set have the same length.
nodes.mathText:
Corollary 1.59 (Uniqueness of finite cardinality). If A is finite and there are
bijections f : A → {1, . . . , n} and g : A → {1, . . . , m}, then n = m.

nodes.statement: The shift n ↦ n + 1 bijects N with a proper subset, so N cannot be finite.
nodes.mathText: Corollary 1.60. The set N = {1, 2, 3, . . .} is infinite.

nodes.statement: The notes distinguish infinite, countably infinite, countable and uncountable sets.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 1.61. A set A is
   • infinite if it is not finite.
   • countably infinite if it is in bijection with N; in this case, we write |A| = ℵ0 .
   • countable if it is either finite or countably infinite.

   • uncountable if it is not countable.

nodes.statement: An alternating enumeration is used to compare Z with N; the printed indexing needs review.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.62. Now we try to compare N and Z. We define a function f : N →
Z as follows: we let f (1) = 0 and for n ≥ 0,

                           f (2n) = n,              f (2n + 1) = −n.

The enumeration is visualised below:

 N:      1     2       3        4           5            6       7            8   ···   2i   2i + 1

 Z:      0     1      −1        2      −2                3      −3            4   ···   i     −i

Hence f is a bijection, so |Z| = ℵ0 .

nodes.statement: A diagonal traversal of numerator–denominator pairs, skipping repetitions, enumerates the positive rationals.
nodes.mathText:
Example 1.63. The set of positive rational numbers Q+ is countably infinite.
We can enumerate it as follows: Represent each rational number as a pair
(m, n) ∈ N2 by the (not necessarily reduced) fraction m/n. Enumerate lattice
points by successive anti-diagonals in a zig-zag (Cantor) pattern:
                                1     2      3     4     5
                                5     5      5     5     5


                                1     2      3     4     5
                                4     4      4     4     4


                                1     2      3     4     5
                                3     3      3     3     3


                                1     2      3     4     5
                                2     2      2     2     2


                                1     2      3     4     5
                                1     1      1     1     1




Skipping repetitions (keep only reduced fractions) we obtain an enumeration of
Q+ , i.e., an bijection from Q+ to N. Therefore, |Q+ | = ℵ0 .
   Now let’s see some criteria for countability.

nodes.statement: Every infinite subset of N is countably infinite.
nodes.mathText: Lemma 1.64. Let C ⊂ N be infinite. Then C is countably infinite.

nodes.en: Every infinite set contains a countable set
nodes.statement: An infinite set has cardinality at least that of N.
nodes.mathText: Proposition 1.65. If A is infinite, then |A| ≥ ℵ0 .
nodes.shortLabel: Every infinite set contains a countable set
nodes.mobileLabel: Every infinite set contains a countable set

nodes.statement: For a nonempty set, countability is equivalent to being a surjective image of N and to admitting an injection into N.
A finite product of countable sets is countable. The source proves the N × N special case next.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.67. The product of finitely many countable sets is countable.
        Instead of proving the general theorem, we show a special case.

sourceProofDisposition.quote: Instead of proving the general theorem, we show a special case.
sourceProofDisposition.note: The full finite-product result is not proved here; Proposition 1.68 gives the stated special case.

nodes.statement: Encoding (m,n) by 2ᵐ3ⁿ gives an injection into N; the product is also infinite.
nodes.mathText: Proposition 1.68. |N × N| = ℵ0 .

nodes.statement: A countable union of countable sets is countable; the printed surjection construction leaves empty members implicit.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.69. Let An be a countable set for each n ∈ N. Then n An is
    countable.

nodes.statement: Flipping the nth bit of the nth listed sequence constructs a binary sequence absent from any purported enumeration.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.70. {0, 1}N is uncountable. So the countable product of countable
    sets need not be countable.

nodes.statement: Subsets of N correspond to binary sequences, so the power set is uncountable.
No set surjects onto its power set; in particular its power set has strictly larger cardinality.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.72 (Cantor’s Theorem). For any set S, there is no surjective func-
tion from S to its power set P(S). In particular, |S| < |P(S)|.

nodes.statement: The source compares [0,1) with binary sequences and concludes it is uncountable.
A finite modification of an infinite set preserves cardinality; the source also states the countable-modification version for an uncountable set.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 1.74. Let A be an infinite set and F a finite set. Then,
    • |A ∪ F | = |A|.
    • |A \ F | = |A|.
The conclusion still holds if A is uncountable and F is infinitely countable.

nodes.statement: The four standard bounded intervals have the same cardinality.

nodes.en: An interval and the real line
nodes.statement: The open unit interval and R have the same cardinality.
nodes.mathText: Proposition 1.76. |(0, 1)| = |R|.
nodes.shortLabel: An interval and the real line
nodes.mobileLabel: An interval and the real line

nodes.statement: Removing Q from R leaves a set with the same cardinality as R.
nodes.mathText: Corollary 1.77. |R \ Q| = |R|.

nodes.statement: Injections in both directions between A and B imply the existence of a bijection.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.78 (Cantor-Schröder-Bernstein). If there exist injections f : A →
B and g : B → A, then there exists a bijection h : A → B.

nodes.statement: A maximal matching gives an injection in one direction between any two sets.
nodes.mathText: Theorem 1.79. If A, B are sets then either |A| ≤ |B| or |B| ≤ |A|.

nodes.statement: A diagonal subset prevents a surjection from S to its power set and gives a strict hierarchy of power-set cardinalities.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 1.80 (Cantor’s Theorem). For any set S, there is no surjective func-
tion from S to its power set P(S). In particular, |S| < |P(S)|.

nodes.statement: A metric separates points, is symmetric, and satisfies the triangle inequality. A pseudometric weakens point separation to d(x,x)=0.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.1 (Metric Space). A metric space is a pair (X, d) consisting of a
set X and a function d : X × X → [0, ∞) called a metric such that
    1. d(x, y) = 0 if and only if x = y;
    2. d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x, y ∈ X (symmetry);
    3. d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all x, y, z ∈ X (triangle inequality).
The value d(x, y) is called the distance between points x and y in the metric
space.
   If (X, d) satisfies 2 and 3 and 1’ below, it is called a pseudometric space.
   1’. d(x, x) = 0 for all x ∈ X.
                                                            Pn              1/p

nodes.statement: The source gives ℓᵖ and maximum metrics, a pseudometric induced by a real function, and the restriction of a metric to a nonempty subset.
nodes.mathText:
Example 2.2.         1. X = Rn , dp (x, y) = ∥x − y∥p = ( i=1 |xi − yi |p )     for
      1 ≤ p < ∞ and d∞ (x, y) = ∥x − y∥∞ = max1≤i≤n |xi − yi | are metrics on
      Rn .
    2. Let X be any set and f : X → R be any function. Then, the following
       defines a pseudometric on X:

                                   d(x, y) = |f (x) − f (y)|.

    3. Let (X, d) be a metric space and A ⊂ X be a nonempty subset. Then,
       (A, d|A×A ) is a metric space, called a subspace of (X, d).

nodes.statement: An isometric embedding preserves all distances; a surjective one is an isometry.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.3. Let (X, dX ) and (Y, dY ) be metric spaces. A function f : X →
Y is called an isometric embedding if

                  dY (f (x), f (x′ )) = dX (x, x′ )   for all x, x′ ∈ X.

The function f is called an isometry if it is an isometric embedding that is also
surjective and we say that (X, dX ) and (Y, dY ) are isometric if there exists an
isometry between them.

nodes.en: Embedding a line in the plane
nodes.statement: The map t ↦ (t,0) preserves Euclidean distances but is not surjective; the notes also ask about x ↦ (x,x).
nodes.mathText:
Example 2.4 (Isometric embedding). Let f : R → R2 be given by f (t) = (t, 0).
For s, t ∈ R,                     p
                ∥f (s) − f (t)∥2 = (s − t)2 + 02 = |s − t|.
Thus f preserves distances (an isometric embedding). It is not surjective, so it
is not an isometry. Its image is the x-axis in R2 .
    Is the map g(x) := (x, x) an isometric embedding?
nodes.shortLabel: Embedding a line in the plane
nodes.mobileLabel: Embedding a line in the plane

nodes.statement: A map is Lipschitz when one nonnegative constant bounds every image distance by that constant times the original distance.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.5. Let (X, dX ) and (Y, dY ) be metric spaces. A function f : X →
Y is called Lipschitz continuous if there exists a constant L ≥ 0 such that

               dY (f (x), f (x′ )) ≤ L · dX (x, x′ )   for all x, x′ ∈ X.

nodes.statement: At each point, every positive output tolerance admits a positive input tolerance forcing the indicated distance inequality.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.6. Let (X, dX ) and (Y, dY ) be metric spaces. A function f : X →
Y is called continuous at a point x0 ∈ X if for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0
such that
                 dY (f (x), f (x0 )) < ε whenever dX (x, x0 ) < δ.
The function f is called continuous if it is continuous at every point x0 ∈ X.

nodes.statement: Lipschitz maps are continuous, and isometric embeddings are Lipschitz. The printed proof divides by L, requiring review when L=0.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 2.7. Any Lipschitz continuous function between metric spaces is
continuous. Any isometric embedding is also Lipschitz continuous.

nodes.statement: A sequence converges when it is eventually within every positive distance tolerance of the proposed limit.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.8. A sequence (xn )n∈N in a metric space (X, d) is said to converge
to a point x ∈ X if for every ϵ > 0, there exists N ∈ N such that d(xn , x) < ϵ
for all n ≥ N .
   One can characterize continuity using sequences:

nodes.statement: A map between metric spaces is continuous at x₀ exactly when it preserves the limit of every sequence converging to x₀.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 2.9. A function f : X → Y is continuous at a point x0 ∈ X
if and only if for every sequence (xn )n∈N in X converging to x0 , the sequence
(f (xn ))n∈N converges to f (x0 ).

nodes.statement: The radius-r open ball consists of the points at distance strictly less than r from its center.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.10. Let (X, d) be a metric space. For any x ∈ X and r > 0, the
open ball of radius r centered at x is defined as

                          Br (x) = {y ∈ X : d(x, y) < r}.

nodes.statement: Euclidean, taxicab and maximum metrics on R² produce disks, diamonds and squares, respectively.
nodes.mathText:
Example 2.11 (Shapes of balls for different metrics on R2 ). For r > 0 the
open unit balls (centered at the origin) for the standard metrics on R2 have the
following shapes:

    Br(2) (0) = {x ∈ R2 : ∥x∥2 < r}                     (Euclidean) — disk,
     Br(1) (0) = {x ∈ R2 : |x1 | + |x2 | < r}           (Taxicab / ℓ1 ) — diamond,
    Br(∞) (0) = {x ∈ R2 : max(|x1 |, |x2 |) < r}        (Maximum / ℓ∞ ) — square.

Below we draw the case r = 1.
   Then, we can rewrite the definition of continuity using open balls.

nodes.statement: Continuity at x₀ is equivalent to sending some ball about x₀ into every prescribed positive-radius ball about f(x₀).
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 2.12. A function f : X → Y between metric spaces (X, dX ) and
(Y, dY ) is continuous at a point x0 ∈ X if and only if for every r > 0, there
exists δ > 0 such that
                            f (Bδ (x0 )) ⊆ Br (f (x0 )).
        x2                              x2                            x2



                     x1                             x1                            x1




     ℓ2 (disk)                    ℓ1 (diamond)                   ℓ∞ (square)

             Figure 1: Unit balls B1 (0) in R2 for ℓ2 , ℓ1 , ℓ∞ metrics.


   The definition of open balls of course depends on the metric. Suppose you
want to generalize everything so far to the setting when you don’t have metric.
Then, let’s try to define some language where the notion of metric will be hidden.

nodes.en: Open subsets of a metric space
nodes.statement: A subset is open when every one of its points has an open ball contained in the subset.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.13. A subset U ⊆ X is called open if for every point x ∈ U there
exists a radius r > 0 such that the open ball Br (x) is contained in U .
nodes.shortLabel: Open subsets of a metric space
nodes.mobileLabel: Open subsets of a metric space

nodes.statement: A smaller ball about a point inside an open ball stays in the original ball.
nodes.mathText: Proposition 2.14. Any open ball Br (x) is open.

nodes.en: Open sets are unions of balls
nodes.statement: A subset of a metric space is open exactly when it is a union of open balls.
nodes.mathText:
Corollary 2.15. Let (X, d) be a metric space and U ⊆ X be a subset. Then,
U is open iff U is a union of open balls.
nodes.shortLabel: Open sets are unions of balls
nodes.mobileLabel: Open sets are unions of balls

nodes.statement: A map is continuous at x₀ exactly when every open set containing f(x₀) contains the image of some open set containing x₀.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 2.16. Let f : X → Y be a function between metric spaces (X, dX )
and (Y, dY ). Then f is continuous at a point x0 ∈ X if and only if for every
open set V ⊆ Y containing f (x0 ), there exists an open set U ⊆ X containing
x0 such that f (U ) ⊆ V .

nodes.statement: A map between metric spaces is continuous exactly when preimages of open sets are open. The source defers a proof to the topological setting.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 2.17. f is continuous if and only if for every open set V ⊆ Y , the
preimage f −1 (V ) is open in X.
   The above theorem reads ”preimage of open is open”.

sourceProofDisposition.quote: We will not give a proof here
sourceProofDisposition.note: Proof explicitly deferred to the topological setting.

nodes.statement: A subset is closed when its complement is open.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.18. A subset A ⊆ X is called closed if its complement X \ A is
open.

nodes.statement: The closure is the least closed set containing a set, equivalently the intersection of all closed supersets.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.19. For any set A ⊆ X, the closure of A, denoted A, is the
smallest closed set containing A. Equivalently, it is the intersection of all closed
sets containing A.

nodes.statement: The notes characterize continuity by sending closures into closures of images; the source formula’s bars require the original typesetting.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 2.20. Let f : X → Y be a function between metric spaces (X, dX )
and (Y, dY ). Then f is continuous if and only if f (A) ⊆ f (A)
   The theorem above reads ”image of closure is contained in closure of image”,
or more intuitively, ”points that are in touch with a set remains in touch after
the map”.
   Now we prove the theorem.

nodes.statement: In a metric space, a point belongs to the closure of A exactly when a sequence in A converges to that point.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 2.21. Let A ⊆ X be a set. Then,

      A = {x ∈ X : there exists a sequence (xn )n∈N in A converging to x}.

nodes.statement: An ultrametric strengthens the triangle inequality by replacing the sum with the maximum of the two distances.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 2.22 (Ultrametric space). A metric space (X, d) is an ultrametric
space if d satisfies the strong triangle inequality

              d(x, z) ≤ max{d(x, y), d(y, z)}     for all x, y, z ∈ X.

We would usually use u instead of d to denote an ultrametric.

nodes.statement: Nearby centers determine the same ball; two balls are nested or disjoint; each triangle has two equal largest sides.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 2.23. Let (X, u) be an ultrametric space. Then,
  1. If r > 0 and x, y ∈ X with u(x, y) < r, then Br (x) = Br (y).
  2. Any two open balls are either disjoint or one contains the other.
  3. Every triangle is isosceles, i.e., if x, y, z ∈ X, then at least two of the
     distances u(x, y), u(y, z), and u(z, x) are equal, and the third is less than
     or equal to the common value.

nodes.en: An ultrametric on the Cantor set
nodes.statement: The source constructs the Cantor set by deleted middle thirds and measures separation by the first stage distinguishing two points.
nodes.mathText:
Example 2.24. Recall the definition of the Cantor set C ⊆ [0, 1]: it is con-
structed by repeatedly removing the open middle third from each interval. More
precisely, set C0 = [0, 1], and for each k ≥ 1, let Ck be the union of 2k closed in-
tervals obtained by removing the open middle third from each interval in Ck−1 .
The Cantor set is defined as
                                          ∞
                                          \
                                     C=      Ck .
                                        k=0

Equivalently, C consists of all numbers in [0, 1] whose base-3 expansion contains
only the digits 0 and 2. We endow the Cantor set C ⊆ [0, 1] with the ultrametric
as follows:
            (
              0     if x = y,
dC (x, y) =
               −n
              3     if x ̸= y and n = min{k ≥ 0 : x and y lie in different segments in Ck }.

    It is perhaps difficult for you to understand what happens in the example
above. It turns out that one can always create a nice visualization of ultrametric
spaces using trees. We will use this to help us understand ultrametric spaces
better. Although the following definition is for finite sets, it can be generalized
to infinite sets as well.

nodes.statement: A dendrogram is an order preserving family of partitions, starting discrete, eventually trivial, with the source’s stated local constancy condition.
Three singleton blocks merge first into two blocks and then into one; endpoint conventions are part of the example.
nodes.mathText:
Example 2.26. Consider X = {a, b, c}. Define θ : [0, ∞) → P art(X) by
                       
                       {{a}, {b}, {c}} if 0 ≤ t < 1
                       
                 θ(t) = {{a, b}, {c}}      if 1 ≤ t < 2
                       
                         {{a, b, c}}       if t ≥ 2
                       

Notice that the strict inequalities cannot be replaced with non-strict inequalities,
as this would violate the last condition.

nodes.statement: On a finite set, merge times determine an ultrametric and threshold equivalence classes determine a dendrogram; the constructions are inverse.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 2.27 (Finite dendrograms and ultrametrics are equivalent). Let X
be a finite set. Let D(X) be the set of dendrograms on X and U(X) be the set
of ultrametrics on X. There are two maps between D(X) and U(X) as follows:
  1. (From dendrogram to ultrametric) Given a dendrogram θ on X, define

      u(x, y) := inf{t ≥ 0 : x, y belong to the same block in θ(t)}    (x, y ∈ X).

      Then u is an ultrametric on X.
  2. (From ultrametric to dendrogram) Given an ultrametric u on X set, we
     define an equivalence relation ∼t for t ≥ 0,

                                x ∼t y ⇐⇒ u(x, y) ≤ t.

      Then we define θ by θ(t) := {[x]t : x ∈ X} where [x]t is the equivalence
      class of x under ∼t . This gives a dendrogram on X.
The above two maps, denoted by D : D(X) → U (X) and U : U(X) → D(X)
respectively, are inverses of each other.

nodes.statement: The displayed three-point dendrogram gives distances 0, 1 and 2; threshold partitions recover it.
nodes.mathText:
Example 2.28. Consider the dendrogram θ on X = {a, b, c} defined in the
previous example. The corresponding ultrametric u is given by
                           
                           0 if x = y,
                           
                  u(x, y) = 1 if {x, y} = {a, b},
                           
                             2 if {x, y} = {a, c} or {b, c}.
                           

Conversely, starting from this ultrametric u, we can recover the original den-
drogram θ.

nodes.statement: The whole and empty sets are closed; finite unions and arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 3.3.         1. X and ∅ are closed.

    2. Any finite union of closed sets is closed.
    3. Any arbitrary intersection of closed sets is closed.

nodes.statement: One can equivalently specify a topology through its collection of closed sets.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.4. A topology, i.e., the collection of open sets, can be equivalently
described by the collection of closed sets.

topologies?

nodes.statement: Metric open sets form a topology. A space is metrizable when a metric induces its topology.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.6. Every metric space is a topological space with the open sets
defined previously.
    As a special example, for R, every open ball is a bounded open interval
(a, b). Hence, every open set in R is a union of disjoint open intervals (including
unbounded intervals).
    Let (X, τ ) be a topological space. If there exists a metric d on X such that
open sets for d coincide with τ , we say (X, τ ) is metrizable.

nodes.statement: All subsets are open in the discrete topology, which the displayed discrete metric induces.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.7. Let X be any set. Let τ := P (X). Then, τ is a topology on X
and it is called the discrete topology. This topology is induced by the discrete
metric d(x, y) = 1 if x ̸= y and d(x, x) = 0.

nodes.statement: Only the empty set and whole set are open; the source asks about metrizability.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.8. Let X be any set. Let τ := {∅, X}. This is the trivial topology.
Is this metrizable?

nodes.statement: Each one-point subset of a metric space is closed.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 3.9. For a metric space (X, d), any point x ∈ X forms a closed set,
i.e., {x} is closed.

nodes.statement: The empty set and complements of finite sets form a topology; the real-line illustration shows its open sets.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.10. Let X be any set. Let τ := {O ⊂ X | O = ∅ or X \O is finite}.
Then τ is a topology on X called the finite complement topology.
   If X = R, a nonempty open set is R with at most finitely many points
removed. For example:

                          Nonempty open set: R \ {x1 , . . . , xn }

nodes.statement: On a fixed set, inclusion of topologies defines the coarser/finer comparison.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.11 (Comparing topologies). Let τ and τ ′ be topologies on the
same set X. If τ ⊆ τ ′ we say τ is coarser (or weaker ) than τ ′ , and τ ′ is finer
(or stronger ) than τ .

nodes.statement: The discrete topology is finest and the trivial topology coarsest on a set.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.12. The discrete topology P (X) is the finest topology on X, while
the trivial topology {∅, X} is the coarsest.

nodes.statement: A basis covers the set and refines intersections locally; arbitrary unions of basis elements form its generated topology.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.13 (Basis). A basis B for a topology on a set X is a nonempty
family of subsets of X such that:
  1. For every x ∈ X, there exists some B ∈ B such that x ∈ B.

  2. If x ∈ B1 ∩ B2 with B1 , B2 ∈ B, then there exists B3 ∈ B with x ∈ B3 ⊆
     B1 ∩ B 2 .
The topology generated by B is: any U ⊂ X is open if for every x ∈ U , there
exists B ∈ B such that x ∈ B ⊆ U . Equivalently,

                If x ∈ B1 ∩ B2 there exists B3 ∈ B with x ∈ B3 ⊆ B1 ∩ B2 .

nodes.statement: The open balls of a metric space form a basis for its topology.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.14. Let X be a metric space. Then, the collection of open balls
forms a basis for the topology on X.

nodes.statement: Singletons form a basis for the discrete topology.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.15. The collection of one point sets {{x} : x ∈ X} is a basis for
the discrete topology on X.

nodes.en: A topology as its own basis
nodes.statement: Every topology is a basis for itself.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.16. Let τ be a topology on X. Then, B := τ is a basis for τ . This
is a rather trivial case.
nodes.shortLabel: A topology as its own basis
nodes.mobileLabel: A topology as its own basis

nodes.statement: The collection generated from a basis satisfies the topology axioms; the source checks the required operations.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 3.17. The topology generated by a basis is indeed a topology.
           • ∅ and X are in τB : ∅ = i∈∅ Bi and X = x∈X Bx where Bx ∈ B
                                    S                S

nodes.statement: A family of open sets is a basis when every point of every open set lies in a member contained in that open set.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 3.18. Let (X, τ ) be a topological space and let B ⊂ τ . Assume
that for any x ∈ U where U ∈ τ , there exists B ∈ B with x ∈ B ⊆ U . Then B
is a basis for τ .

nodes.statement: Inclusion of the generated topologies is equivalent to the stated pointwise refinement condition on their bases.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 3.19 (Comparing topologies via bases). Let B1 , B2 be bases on X
generating τ1 , τ2 . Then τ1 ⊆ τ2 iff for every x ∈ X and B1 ∈ B1 with x ∈ B1
there exists B2 ∈ B2 with x ∈ B2 ⊆ B1 .

nodes.statement: Open Euclidean balls and axis-aligned open rectangles generate the same topology on R².
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.20. Let X = R2 . Let B = {open balls in R2 } and let B ′ =
{axis-aligned open rectangles in R2 }. Then they generate the same topology.

nodes.statement: A covering family generates a topology by taking arbitrary unions of finite intersections of its members.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.21 (Subbasis). A subbasis S for a topology on X is a collection
of subsets whose union is X. The topology generated by S is the collection of
all unions of finite intersections of members of S:

nodes.statement: Two displayed subsets cover three points but require an additional intersection to produce a basis.
nodes.shortLabel: A subbasis that is not a basis
nodes.mobileLabel: A subbasis that is not a basis

nodes.statement: Finite intersections of a subbasis form a basis for its generated topology.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.23. τS is a topology on X with the family of all finite intersections
of members of S being a basis.

nodes.statement: The topology generated by a subbasis is the smallest topology containing that family.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.24. τS is the smallest topology containing S, i.e., any other topology
on X containing S must also contain τS .

nodes.statement: Bounded open intervals form a basis of R; open rays form a subbasis for the same topology.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.25. In R the open intervals (a, b) form a basis. The family {(−∞, a), (a, ∞) :
a ∈ R} is a subbasis generating the same topology.

nodes.statement: A closure operation preserves the empty set and finite unions, contains each set, and is idempotent.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.26 (Closure Operation). Let X be a set and let

                                · : P(X) → P(X)

be a map. It is called a closure operation if for all A, B ⊂ X:

  (i) ∅ = ∅,
 (ii) A ⊂ A,
(iii) If D = A, then D = D,
 (iv) A ∪ B = A ∪ B.

   We now show that the closure operation and the topology we defined pre-
viously give rise to equivalent structures on a set. To this end, we identify the
notion of a closed set in a topological space first.

nodes.statement: Intersecting closed supersets gives a closure operation.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 3.27. Given a topological space (X, τ ), define

then the sets

nodes.statement: The interior is the largest open subset of a set, equivalently the union of all its open subsets.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.29 (Interior). Let X be a topological space and let A ⊆ X. The
interior of A, denoted int(A) or Å, is the largest open set contained in A.
Equivalently, it is the union of all open sets contained in A:
                                    [
                          int(A) = {U ∈ τX : U ⊆ A}.

nodes.statement: Every set contains its interior and lies in its closure.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.30. For any subset A ⊂ X, we have that

                                int(A) ⊆ A ⊆ A.

nodes.en: Interior and closure of an interval
nodes.statement: In R the half-open interval (0,1] has interior (0,1) and closure [0,1].
nodes.mathText: Example 3.31. Let X = R. Then, int((0, 1]) = (0, 1) and (0, 1] = [0, 1].
nodes.shortLabel: Interior and closure of an interval
nodes.mobileLabel: Interior and closure of an interval

nodes.statement: An open set containing a point is an open neighborhood of that point.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.32. Let X be a topological space. For any x ∈ X, we say any
open set containing x is a (open) neighbourhood of x.

nodes.statement: A point lies in the closure exactly when every neighborhood meets the set; it lies in the interior exactly when one neighborhood is contained in the set.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.33. Let X be a topological space and let A ⊆ X. Then,
   • x ∈ A if and only if every neighbourhood of x intersects A.
   • x ∈ int(A) if and only if there exists a neighbourhood of x contained in A.

nodes.statement: The four interval conventions on a linearly ordered set are specified by strict or non-strict endpoint inequalities.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.34 (Linearly ordered set and intervals). Let (X, ≤) be a linearly
ordered (totally ordered) set. For a, b ∈ X with a < b define

            (a, b) = {x ∈ X : a < x < b},            [a, b) = {x ∈ X : a ≤ x < b},

               (a, b] = {x ∈ X : a < x ≤ b},         [a, b] = {x ∈ X : a ≤ x ≤ b}.

nodes.statement: On a linearly ordered set with at least two elements, open intervals and the indicated endpoint intervals generate the order topology.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.35 (Order topology). Let (X, ≤) be a linearly ordered set with
at least two elements. Let B be the family consisting of

   • all open intervals (a, b) with a < b,
   • all [a0 , b) when a0 is the least element of X and b > a0 ,
   • all (a, b0 ] when b0 is the greatest element of X and a < b0 .
The topology generated by B is called the order topology on X.

nodes.statement: The family used to define the order topology satisfies the basis conditions.
nodes.mathText: Proposition 3.36. The family B above is a basis.

nodes.statement: The order topology of the ordinary real order agrees with the usual metric topology.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.37 (Standard topology on R). With the usual order on R, the sets
(a, b) already form B, hence the order topology coincides with the usual metric
topology on R.

nodes.statement: The lexicographic order topology differs from the Euclidean topology; its displayed intervals fail the Euclidean open-ball test.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.38 (Lexicographic order on R × R). Define (x1 , y1 ) < (x2 , y2 ) iff
x1 < x2 , or x1 = x2 and y1 < y2 . The interval ((a, b), (c, d)) looks like the
following:
      x = a, y > b
                     a < x < c : all y
      (a, b)




                                            (c, d)
                                         x = c, y < d
    This is different from the standard topology on R2 . In fact, the set above in
the basis is not open in the standard topology. To see this, consider the point
(a, b + 1) in the set. Any open ball around it will contain points with x < a,
which are not in the set.

nodes.statement: Singletons are open in the order topology on N, including the least-element case.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.39 (Discrete order on the integers). On N with the usual order,
the order topology is discrete:

                          {n} = (n − 1, n + 1)     for n > 1;

and 1 is the least element then {1} = [1, 2). Hence every singleton is open.

nodes.statement: The order topology on {1,2} × N has a point (2,1) whose singleton is not open.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.40 (Order topology on {1, 2} × N (lexicographic) is not discrete).
Give X = {1, 2} × N the lexicographic order:

                (i, m) < (j, n)   iff i < j or (i = j and m < n).

Then (1, 1) is the least element. In the order topology, any basis element con-
taining (2, 1) is of the form (a, b) (or [ (1, 1), b)) with a < (2, 1) < b, and therefore
must contain some (1, n). Hence {(2, 1)} is not open, so the order topology on
X is not the discrete topology.

nodes.statement: Products of open sets form a basis on X × Y; these rectangles need not themselves form a topology.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.41. Let (X, τX ) and (Y, τY ) be topological spaces. The product
topology on the product space X × Y is the topology generated by the basis
consisting of all products of open sets:

                        BX×Y = {U × V : U ∈ τX , V ∈ τY }.

Check: B is a basis. Note X × Y ∈ B so every point (x, y) ∈ X × Y lies in some
basis element.
   For U1 × V1 , U2 × V2 ∈ B, we have U1 ∩ U2 ∈ τX and V1 ∩ V2 ∈ τY , so

               (U1 × V1 ) ∩ (U2 × V2 ) = (U1 ∩ U2 ) × (V1 ∩ V2 ) ∈ B.



   Question: is B a topology? No, the union of basis elements is not necessarily
a basis element.
   It turns out that smaller bases can also generate the product topology.

nodes.statement: Products of basis elements from the two factors form a basis for the product topology.
The product of the usual real topologies agrees with the Euclidean metric topology via open rectangles.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.43. Let X = Y = R with the standard topology. Then, B =
{(a, b) : a < b} is a basis for R. Hence, B × B = {(a, b) × (c, d) : a < b, c < d}
is a basis for the product topology on R2 . Note that (a, b) × (c, d) is an axis-
aligned open rectangle in R2 . Previously, we showed that this generates the same
topology as the one generated by open balls in R2 . So the product topology on
R2 is the same as the standard metric topology on R2 .
    We can inductively define the product topology on X1 × X2 × · · · × Xn for
any finite n. But things will be a bit different for infinite products. We will
discuss this later.

nodes.statement: The two projections from X × Y select the first and second coordinates, and their inverse images give open strips.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.44. Let π1 : X × Y → X be defined by π1 (x, y) = x and π2 :
X × Y → Y be defined by π2 (x, y) = y. The maps π1 and π2 are called the
projections of X × Y onto its first and second factors, respectively.
   Note that for any open set U ⊂ X, we have that π1−1 (U ) = U × Y and
π2−1 (V ) = X × Vfor any open set V ⊂ Y .

nodes.statement: Inverse images of open factor sets under the two projections form a subbasis for X × Y.
The interval (0.5,1] is open relative to [0,1], although it is not open in R.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.47. [0, 1] is a subspace of R. Note that (0.5, 1] is not open in R
but open in [0, 1] with the subspace topology as

                            (0.5, 1] = (0.5, 2) ∩ [0, 1]

nodes.en: An open subspace has ambient open sets
nodes.statement: If Y is open in X, every relatively open subset of Y is open in X.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 3.48. Let (X, τ ) be a topological space and Y ⊆ X. If Y ∈ τ and
U ∈ τY (i.e. U is open in the subspace Y ), then U ∈ τ .
nodes.shortLabel: An open subspace has ambient open sets
nodes.mobileLabel: An open subspace has ambient open sets

nodes.statement: Intersecting ambient basis elements with Y gives a basis for the subspace topology on Y.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 3.49. Let (X, τ ) be a topological space and let B be a basis for τ . If
Y ⊆ X then
                        BY := { B ∩ Y : B ∈ B }
is a basis for the subspace topology τY on Y .

nodes.statement: For A ⊆ X and B ⊆ Y, the product topology on A × B equals the topology inherited from X × Y.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.50. If A ⊆ X and B ⊆ Y , then the product topology on A × B is
the same as the subspace topology inherited from X × Y .

nodes.statement: The metric obtained by restriction to Y induces precisely the topology Y inherits as a subspace.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.51. Let (X, d) be a metric space and let Y ⊆ X. Consider the
sub metric space (Y, dY ). Then, the topology induced by dY is the same as the
subspace topology inherited from (X, d).

    Although the subspace topology and the metric topology are compatible,
the order topology and the subspace topology are not always compatible. We
will see when they agree.

nodes.statement: For Y = [0,1) ∪ {2}, the point 2 is isolated in the subspace topology but not in the inherited order topology.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.52. The order and subspace topologies on a subset of a linearly or-
dered set need not agree. For instance, let Y = [0, 1)∪{2} ⊂ R with the induced
order. In the subspace topology, {2} is open in Y since {2} = (2 − 12 , 2 + 12 ) ∩ Y .
But in the order topology on Y , any basis element containing 2 is of the form
(a, 2]Y = {y ∈ Y : a < y ≤ 2} where a ∈ Y (because 2 is the greatest element of
Y ), so it contains points of Y strictly less than 2; hence {2} is not open there.

nodes.statement: A subset of a linear order is convex when it contains every point lying strictly between two of its members.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.53 (Convex subset). Let (X, ≤) be a linearly ordered set. A
subset Y ⊂ X is convex if for all a, b ∈ Y with a < b one has (a, b)X ⊂ Y .

nodes.statement: For a convex subset of an ordered space, the induced order topology and subspace topology agree. The source refers to Munkres for a proof.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.54. Let X be a linearly ordered set with the order topology, and
let Y ⊂ X be convex (with the induced order). Then the order topology on Y
coincides with the subspace topology inherited from X.
   For a proof, see Munkres, Theorem 16.4.

sourceProofDisposition.quote: For a proof, see Munkres, Theorem 16.4.
sourceProofDisposition.note: External proof reference as printed; the cited book is not included or fetched.

nodes.statement: For metric spaces, the metric and topology-based definitions of continuity coincide.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.56. A function f : X → Y between two metric spaces is continuous
in the metric sense if and only if it is continuous in the topological sense.

nodes.statement: Continuity, open preimages, closed preimages and preservation of closure inclusion are equivalent for maps between topological spaces.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.57. Let X and Y be topological spaces and let f : X → Y be a
function. The following are equivalent:
  1. f is continuous.
  2. For all open sets H in Y , f −1 (H) is open in X.

  3. For all closed sets C in Y , f −1 (C) is closed in X.
  4. For all A ⊂ X, f (A) ⊆ f (A) (This can be thought of as the Kuratowski
     definition of continuity).

nodes.statement: It suffices to test open preimages of basis elements in the target.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.58. A function f : (X, τX ) → (Y, τY ) is continuous if and only if the
statement (2) holds for all basis elements of Y :

                        U = ∪Bα     f −1 (U ) = ∪f −1 (Bα )

nodes.statement: It suffices to test open preimages of subbasis elements in the target.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.59. A function f : (X, τX ) → (Y, τY ) is continuous if and only if the
statement (2) holds for all subbasis elements of Y :

                    B = S1 ∩ · · · ∩ Sn    f −1 (B) = ∩f −1 (Si )

nodes.statement: The source notes that some texts define continuity directly using the open-preimage criterion.
nodes.mathText: Remark 3.60. In some books, they take the (2) as the definition of continuity.

nodes.en: A continuous map need not be open
nodes.statement: A constant real map is continuous but sends a nonempty open interval to a singleton, which is not open in R.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.61. Let f : R → R be the constant map f (x) = 0. Then f is
continuous, but the image of the open set (0, 1) is
                                 f ((0, 1)) = {0},
which is not open in R. Thus a continuous map need not send open sets to open
sets.
nodes.shortLabel: A continuous map need not be open
nodes.mobileLabel: A continuous map need not be open

nodes.en: A continuous map need not be closed
nodes.statement: Projection sends the closed hyperbola xy = 1 to R without zero, which is not closed.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.62. Let π : R2 → R be the projection π(x, y) = x, which is
continuous. Consider
                     C = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : xy = 1},
the hyperbola. Since C is the zero set of the continuous function f : (x, y) 7→
xy − 1, it is closed in R2 (i.e., C = f −1 ({0})). But
                       π(C) = {x ∈ R : x ̸= 0} = R \ {0},
which is not closed in R. Thus a continuous map need not send closed sets to
closed sets.

nodes.mobileLabel: A continuous map need not be closed

nodes.statement: Product projections are continuous, and the product topology is the least topology making both continuous.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.63. Let X × Y be endowed with the product topology. Then,
πX : X × Y → X and πY : X × Y → Y are continuous.
                                            −1
   Note that for any open set U in X, πX       (U ) = U × Y is open in X × Y .
                                      −1
Similarly, for any open set V in Y , πY (V ) = X × V is open in X × Y .
   Note also that the product topology τX×Y is the smallest topology on X × Y
such that both πX and πY are continuous: any topology on X × Y that makes
both πX and πY continuous must contain a basis for τX×Y : sets of the form
U × Y and X × V for all open sets U in X and V in Y .

nodes.statement: The source gives seven constructions: constants, inclusions, composition, restrictions, range changes, open local gluing and finite closed pasting.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.64.       1. (Constant function) If f : X → Y maps all of X to a
    single point y0 ∈ Y , then f is continuous.
  2. (Inclusion) If A is a subspace of X, the inclusion map i : A → X defined
     by i(a) = a is continuous.
  3. (Composition) If f : X → Y and g : Y → Z are continuous, then the
     composition g ◦ f : X → Z is continuous.
  4. (Restricting the domain) If f : X → Y is continuous and A ⊆ X, then
     the restriction f |A : A → Y defined by f |A (a) = f (a) is continuous.
  5. (Restricting or expanding the range) Let f : X → Y be continuous. If
     f (X) ⊂ Z ⊂ Y , then the function g : X → Z obtained by restricting the
     range of f is continuous. If Y ⊂ W , then the function h : iY →W ◦ f :
     X → W is continuous.

  6. (Local formulation) f : X → Y is continuous if X = ∪Uα for a family of
     open sets Uα and each restriction f |Uα is continuous.
  7. (Pasting lemma) If X = A ∪ B with A, B closed, and f : A → Y , g : B →
     Y are continuous and agree on A ∩ B (i.e., f (x) = g(x) for all x ∈ A ∩ B),
     then the function h : X → Y defined by
                                     (
                                       f (x), x ∈ A
                              h(x) =
                                       g(x), x ∈ B

        is continuous.

nodes.statement: A subset E of A is relatively closed exactly when it is F ∩ A for some closed subset F of X.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 3.65. Let A ⊂ X and let E ⊂ A. Then, E is closed in A if and
      only if there exists a closed set F in X such that E = F ∩ A.

nodes.statement: The source claims a set closed in A is closed in X without assuming A closed. This wording is retained and flagged for review.
nodes.mathText:
Corollary 3.66. Let A ⊂ X and let E ⊂ A. If E is closed in A then E
      is closed in X.

nodes.statement: The source compares the open local formulation with finite closed pasting and assigns the infinite version as homework.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.67. 7 is the closed set and finite version of 6. See your homework for
the infinite version of 7.

nodes.statement: A map to X × Y is continuous exactly when its two component maps are continuous.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.68. Let f : A → X × Y be given by f (a) = (fX (a), fY (a)). Then
f is continuous if and only if fX and fY are continuous.

nodes.statement: A homeomorphism induces a bijection between the open subsets of its source and target.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.70. Let f : X → Y be a homeomorphism. Then, f induces a map
f∗ : τX → τY defined by f∗ (U ) = f (U ) for all U ∈ τX . Furthermore, f∗ is a
bijection.

nodes.statement: The source uses a cup and solid torus as an intuitive example of homeomorphism.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.71. Suppose you have a subspace in some ambient Euclidean space.
You can stretch and bend it without tearing or gluing. This is a homeomor-
phism. For example, a coffee cup is homeomorphic to a donut (solid torus).

nodes.statement: A circle and a trefoil are homeomorphic as spaces even though the given embeddings cannot be deformed into each other without cutting.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.72. The circle and the trefoil knot are homeomorphic. But we
can’t deform one to the other in 3D space without cutting.
                                                           x

nodes.mathText:
Example 3.73. The map f : (−1, 1) → R defined by f (x) = 1−x 2 is a home-

nodes.statement: The source asks whether (0,1) and [0,1) are homeomorphic.
nodes.mathText: Example 3.75. Is (0, 1) homeomorphic to [0, 1)?

nodes.statement: Deleting a point and its image from a homeomorphism leaves a homeomorphism between the complements.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 3.76. Let f : X → Y be a homeomorphism. Let x0 ∈ X. Then, the
map g : X \{x0 } → Y \{f (x0 )} defined by g(x) = f (x) is also a homeomorphism.

nodes.statement: A connected space cannot be partitioned into two disjoint nonempty open sets.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.77. Let X be a topological space. We say X is connected if it
cannot be represented as the union of two disjoint non-empty open sets.

nodes.statement: Homeomorphic spaces share connectedness because their open sets correspond.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.78. If X is connected and X is homeomorphic to Y , then Y is also
connected. This holds obviously as the homeomorphism gives rise to a bijection
between the topologies.
   Now we are ready to answer the previous question.

nodes.statement: Removing the endpoint of [0,1) and the corresponding interior point of (0,1) gives a contradiction in connectedness.
nodes.mathText: Theorem 3.79. (0, 1) is not homeomorphic to [0, 1).

nodes.statement: The source observes that point deletion and connectedness similarly distinguish R and R².
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.80. Similarly, we can prove that R and R2 are not homeomorphic.
    How about R2 vs R3 ? Need algebraic topology. We will have a taste of it
later in the course.

Example 3.82. Let X = RN = n≥1 R. Then, the “diagonal” map f : R → X
defined by f (t) = (t, t, t, . . .) is not continuous when X is endowed with the box
topology. Consider the open set (−1, 1)×(−1/2, 1/2)×(−1/3, 1/3)×· · · . Then,

Example 3.95. RN with the box topology is not metrizable. Let A = {(x1 , . . .)|xi >
0} and let 0 = (0, 0, . . .). Then, 0 ∈ A: for any basis element U = (a1 , b1 ) ×
(a2 , b2 ) × · · · containing 0, we have that ai < 0 < bi for all i. So pick any point
(x1 , x2 , . . .) with xi ∈ (0, bi ) for all i, then (x1 , x2 , . . .) ∈ A ∩ U . So, A ∩ U ̸= ∅.
    Assume that RN with the box topology is metrizable with a compatible
metric d. Let an = (x1n , x2n , . . .) be a sequence in A converging to 0. Then,
construct B = {(−x11 , x11 ) × (−x22 , x22 ) × · · · }. Then, 0 ∈ B but an ∈            / B for
all n ∈ N. So there exists a ball Br (0) ⊆ B for some r > 0 containing no point
in the sequence an . This is a contradiction. So RN with the box topology is not
metrizable.

nodes.mathText:
Example 3.96. One can obtain a torus and a sphere via gluing/equivalence
relations.




  Figure 2: A torus and a sphere, illustrating the concept of quotient spaces.


    How can we get a topology on X ∗ from the topology on X? Recall that
the product topology can be characterized via some continuous maps. Maybe
we can do something similar here. A very natural map is the quotient map
p : X → X ∗ sending each point to its equivalence class.
    We of course want p to be continuous. That means we want a set of open
sets on X ∗ so that the preimage of each open set is open in X. We want to
make this topology as coarse as possible.

quotient topology on Y is defined by

When endowed with the quotient topology, we call Y a quotient space of X and
q a quotient map.

nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.98. The quotient topology is the finest topology on Y making q con-
tinuous: if τ is any topology on Y with q continuous, then τ ⊆ τq .

nodes.statement: The equivalence classes of a topological space carry the topology induced by the natural class projection.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.99 (Quotient space). Let X be a topological space. Let ∼ be
an equivalence relation on X and let X ∗ := X/ ∼ be the set of equivalence
classes. The quotient space of X by ∼ is the set X ∗ endowed with the quotient
topology via the natural projection map p : X → X ∗ sending each point to its
equivalence class.

is open in R.
   • p−1 ({−1}) = (−∞, 0) and p−1 ({1}) = (0, ∞) are open ⇒ {−1}, {1} are

   • p−1 ({−1, 1}) = R \ {0} = (−∞, 0) ∪ (0, ∞) is open ⇒ {−1, 1} open.
   • p−1 ({−1, 0}) = (−∞, 0] and p−1 ({0, 1}) = [0, ∞) are not open.

nodes.statement: The pictured gluing maps induce quotient topologies; agreement with the Euclidean subspace topologies is posed for later justification.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.101 (Torus and Sphere). Consider the maps shown in the image
(Figure 3). We then can endow the torus and the sphere (viewed as subsets of
R3 ) with the quotient topologies via these maps. Of course, there is the question
whether these quotient topologies coincide with the subspace topologies from
R3 . We will answer this question later.
     Now let q : X → Y be surjective. What if we have another topology τ on
Y?

nodes.statement: A surjection between topological spaces is a quotient map when openness is equivalent to openness of the preimage.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.102. For two topological spaces X, Y and a surjective map q :
X → Y , we say q is a quotient map if

             a subset U ⊆ Y is open in Y iff q −1 (U ) is open in X.
   In other words, q is a quotient map if the topology on Y coincides with the
quotient topology via q.
   Whenever we have a quotient map q : X → Y , we can identify Y with
the quotient space X ∗ of X by the equivalence relation induced by q. More
precisely, we have the following proposition.

x ∼ x′ iff q(x) = q(x′ ) and let X ∗ := X/ ∼= {q −1 (y) : y ∈ Y } endowed with
the quotient topology. Then, q induces a homeomorphism φ : X ∗ → Y such that

or closed, then q is a quotient map.

S 1 = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : x2 + y 2 = 1} with the subspace topology from R2 . Define

                         p : X → Y,     p(t) = (cos t, sin t).

Then, p is surjective and continuous. p is not open unfortunately: [0, a) will not

the targets are endowed with subspace topologies. In fact, all maps are closed
which we can prove later when we learn about compactness. Right now, we can

nodes.statement: Projection of the hyperbola together with the origin has an open preimage of {0}, although {0} is not open in R.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.107. Consider the subspace

  X = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : xy = 1} ∪ {(0, 0)} ⊂ R2 ,           q : X −→ R, q(x, y) = x.

The map q is surjective: for x ̸= 0 choose y = 1/x, and q(0, 0) = 0. It is
continuous as the restriction of the projection π1 : R2 → R.
   However q is not a quotient map. Indeed {(0, 0)} = Bε (0, 0) ∩ X for small
ε > 0, so {(0, 0)} is open in X. Thus

                        q −1 ({0}) = {(0, 0)} is open in X,

but {0} is not open in R. Hence the “only if” direction fails and q is not a
quotient map.
   The following theorem is analogous to the universal property of product
topology.

space. Let g : X → Z be such that g is constant on each fiber q −1 ({y}). This
induces a function f : Y → Z such that f ◦ q = g. Then
  1. f is continuous iff g is continuous.
  2. f is a quotient map iff g is a quotient map.
