nodes.statement: The source returns to R versus R² and introduces homotopy as preparation for comparing R² and R³.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.109. R and R2 are not homeomorphic. How about R2 vs R3 ?
    We would like to answer this question to some extent. In the process of
answering this question, we will introduce a very important concept in topology,
called homotopy.

nodes.statement: A homotopy is a continuous map X × [0,1] → Y interpolating between the two specified continuous maps.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.110. Let f and g be continuous maps from a topological space
X to a topological space Y . We say that f and g are homotopic if there exists a
continuous map H : X ×[0, 1] → Y such that H(x, 0) = f (x) and H(x, 1) = g(x)
for all x ∈ X. H is called a homotopy between f and g. We write f ≃ g to
indicate that f and g are homotopic.

nodes.statement: Every continuous map is homotopic to itself by ignoring the interval coordinate.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.111. Any continuous map f : X → Y is homotopic to itself via the
constant homotopy H(x, t) = f (x).

nodes.statement: The homotopy (1−t)x joins the identity of Rⁿ to the constant map at zero.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.112. In Rn the identity map f (x) = x is homotopic to the constant
map g(x) = 0 via the straight–line homotopy

                               H(x, t) = (1 − t)x.

nodes.statement: For maps into a convex subset of Rⁿ, linear interpolation is a homotopy; the same formula may fail when the target is restricted.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.113. More generally, if Y is a convex subset of some Rn and
f, g : X → Y are continuous, then

                         H(x, t) = (1 − t)f (x) + tg(x)

defines a homotopy f ≃ g. Thus any two maps into a convex (in particular,
contractible) space are homotopic. The target matters: regarded as maps S 1 →
D2 the identity and any constant map are homotopic, but as maps S 1 → S 1
they need not be. This is in fact quite nontrivial and we will return to it later.

nodes.statement: Homotopy of continuous maps is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 3.114. Homotopy is an equivalence relation on C(X, Y ), the set
of continuous maps X → Y .

nodes.statement: Two pairs of homotopic maps give homotopic composites when their domains and codomains match.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 3.115 (Composites of homotopic maps are homotopic). If f1 , g1 : X →
Y and f2 , g2 : Y → Z with f1 ≃ g1 and f2 ≃ g2 , then f2 ◦ f1 ≃ g2 ◦ g1 .

nodes.statement: Spaces are homotopy equivalent when continuous maps in both directions compose to maps homotopic to the respective identities.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.116. Two spaces X and Y are homotopy equivalent if there exist
continuous maps f : X → Y and g : Y → X such that g◦f ≃ idX and f ◦g ≃ idY .
In this case f and g are homotopy inverses and we write X ≃ Y .

nodes.statement: Homotopy equivalence is an equivalence relation, and a homeomorphism supplies a homotopy equivalence; the converse need not hold.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 3.117. Homotopy equivalence is an equivalence relation on spaces. Any
homeomorphism is a homotopy equivalence (take g = f −1 ). The converse fails;
see the example below.
   One special case of homotopy equivalence is when one of the spaces is a
point.

nodes.statement: A space is contractible when its identity map is homotopic to a constant map through maps into the same space.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.118. A space X is contractible if the identity map idX is homo-
topic to a constant map cx0 : X → X sending every point to x0 . Equivalently,
there exists H : X × I → X with H(x, 0) = x and H(x, 1) = x0 for all x.

nodes.statement: A space is contractible exactly when it is homotopy equivalent to a one-point space.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.119. A space X is contractible iff it is homotopy equivalent to a
one–point space.

nodes.statement: Straight-line interpolation to a chosen point contracts a convex subset of Euclidean space.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.120. Every convex subset of Rn (in particular Rn and any disk
Dn ) is contractible via the straight–line homotopy H(x, t) = (1 − t)x + tx0 .

nodes.statement: Rⁿ is contractible but the source notes it is not homeomorphic to a point.
nodes.mathText: Example 3.121. Rn is contractible but Rn is not homeomorphic to a point.

nodes.statement: The source states noncontractibility of S¹ and defers its proof.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.122. S 1 is not contractible. We will prove this later.
   The contractible case is the trivial case of homotopy equivalence. More
generally, we can often find a smaller subspace which is homotopy equivalent to
the whole space. This is made precise by the following definitions.

nodes.statement: A retraction onto A fixes each point of A; composing it with the inclusion gives the identity of A.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.123. Let A ⊆ X. A map r : X → A is a retraction if r(a) = a
for all a ∈ A (equivalently r ◦ i = idA where i : A ,→ X is inclusion).

nodes.statement: A deformation retraction joins the identity to a retraction while fixing every point of the retract throughout.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.124. A subspace A ⊆ X is a deformation retract of X if there
is a retraction r : X → A such that there is a homotopy H : X × I → X with
H(x, 0) = x, H(x, 1) = r(x), and H(a, t) = a for all a ∈ A, t ∈ I. We call H a
deformation retraction.

nodes.statement: A retraction and inclusion are homotopy inverses when the subspace is a deformation retract.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 3.125. If A is a deformation retract of X then A ≃ X. Thus a
deformation retract gives a special homotopy equivalence (with inverse given by
the retraction).

nodes.statement: The source gives an annulus retracting to S¹ and punctured Rⁿ retracting to Sⁿ⁻¹ by radial normalization.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.126.    1. The circle S 1 is a deformation retract of any annulus
               2
    A = {x ∈ R : 1 ≤ ∥x∥ ≤ R} with the retraction r(x) = x/∥x∥ and the
    homotopy H(x, t) = (1 − t)x + tr(x).
  2. Rn \ {0} deformation retracts onto S n−1 : the retraction is r(x) = x/∥x∥
     and the homotopy is H(x, t) = (1 − t)x + tr(x).

nodes.en: Retraction is weaker than deformation retraction
nodes.statement: A constant retraction onto a point is a deformation retraction only in the contractible case.
nodes.mathText:
Example 3.127. Not every retraction is a deformation retraction. In fact, for
any X and x0 ∈ X, the constant map cx0 : X → {x0 } is a retraction if {x0 } is
a retract of X, but it is a deformation retraction only if X is contractible.

is homotopic to a constant map, than f lifts, i.e., there exists a continuous
f˜ : S 1 → R with p ◦ f˜ = f .

nodes.mathText:
Corollary 3.134 (Brouwer Fixed Point). For every n ≥ 1, any continuous
map F : Dn → Dn has a fixed point, i.e. there exists x ∈ Dn with F (x) = x.

nodes.statement: An embedding is a continuous map that is a homeomorphism onto its image with the subspace topology; it is therefore injective.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.135 (Embedding). A continuous map f : X → Y is an embedding
if it is a homeomorphism onto its image f (X) (with the subspace topology
inherited from Y ). In particular, f is injective.

nodes.statement: A subset of X ⊔ Y is open exactly when its intersection with each summand is open there.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.136. Let X and Y be two disjoint topological spaces. Then, the
disjoint union of X and Y is the topological space

                                      X ⊔Y

whose underlying set is the disjoint union of sets X and Y and whose topology
is given by

    U ⊆ X ⊔ Y is open ⇐⇒ U ∩ X is open in X and U ∩ Y is open in Y.

Equivalently, the topology is given by

                       τX⊔Y = {U ⊔ V | U ∈ τX , V ∈ τY }.

nodes.statement: The mapping cylinder identifies the top end of X × [0,1] with its image under f in Y, and includes canonical copies of both spaces.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 3.137 (Mapping cylinder). Given a continuous map f : X → Y ,
the mapping cylinder of f is
                                               
                          Mf = (X × [0, 1]) ⊔ Y ∼

where (x, 1) ∼ f (x) for all x ∈ X. Write [x, t] for the class of (x, t) and [y] for
y ∈ Y . There are canonical embeddings

    iX : X ,→ Mf ,       x 7→ [x, 0],    and      iY : Y ,→ Mf ,      y 7→ [y].

There is a deformation retraction H : Mf × I → Mf onto iY (Y ) given by
H([x, t], s) = [x, (1 − s)t + s] and H([y], s) = [y], so Mf deformation retracts
onto Y .

defined by H([x, t], s) := [x, (1 − s)t + s] and H([y], s) := [y] is a deformation
retraction of Mf onto iY (Y ).

nodes.statement: The source states that f is a homotopy equivalence exactly when the source copy is a deformation retract of its mapping cylinder.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 3.139. f : X → Y is a homotopy equivalence if and only if iX (X) is
a deformation retract of Mf .

nodes.statement: Two spaces are homotopy equivalent exactly when they embed as deformation retracts of one common space, as stated and argued in the source.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 3.140 (Common deformation–retract envelope). For topological spaces
X and Y , the following are equivalent:
  1. X and Y are homotopy equivalent.

  2. There exists a space Z and embeddings iX : X ,→ Z, iY : Y ,→ Z such
     that iX (X) and iY (Y ) are each deformation retracts of Z (possibly via
     two different homotopies).

nodes.statement: Metric convergence is equivalent to eventually lying in every positive-radius ball about the limit.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 4.1. A sequence (xn )n∈N in a metric space X converges to a point
x ∈ X if and only if for every ϵ > 0, there exists N ∈ N such that xn ∈ Bϵ (x)
for all n ≥ N .
    This motivates the following definition in general topological spaces:

nodes.statement: A sequence converges to x when it is eventually in every neighborhood of x.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 4.2. A sequence (xn )n∈N in a topological space X is said to converge
to a point x ∈ X if for every neighbourhood U of x, there exists N ∈ N such
that xn ∈ U for all n ≥ N .

nodes.statement: Problem 4.3 includes a proof that the two convergence definitions agree in a metric space.
nodes.mathText:
Problem 4.3. A sequence (xn ) in a metric space converges in the metric sense
if and only if it converges in the topological sense defined above.

nodes.statement: If a sequence from A converges to x in a topological space, then x belongs to the closure of A.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 4.4. Let X be a topological space. For A ⊆ X and x ∈ X, if there
is a sequence (an ) ⊆ A with an → x, then x ∈ A.

nodes.statement: In the countable-complement topology on R, convergent sequences are eventually their limit, although uncountable proper subsets have closure R.
nodes.mathText:
Example 4.5. Let X = R be endowed with the countable complement topology:
a set U ⊆ X is open iff X \ U is countable or U = ∅.
   • Any sequence (xn ) converging to x is eventually equal to x. Indeed, we
     let B = {xn : xn ̸= x} and hence U = X \ B is an open neighborhood of
     x. Then, there exists N such that xn ∈ U for all n ≥ N , i.e., xn ∈
                                                                       / B for
     all n ≥ N . This means that xn = x for all n ≥ N .
   • The closed sets are exactly the countable sets and X itself. Hence, if
     A ⊊ X is uncountable, then A = X.

   Thus [0, 1] = R, but there is no sequence in [0, 1] converging to 2.

   Let’s see another example.

nodes.statement: The all-zero function lies in the closure of the specified finite-zero-support family, but is not the limit of a sequence from it. The printed construction has a flagged typo.

nodes.en: Every point can be a limit
nodes.statement: In a trivial topology a constant sequence converges to every point.
nodes.mathText:
Example 4.7. Let X be endowed with the trivial topology τ = {∅, X}. Then
the constant sequence (xn ) with xn = a ∈ X for all n ∈ N converges to every
point in X.
nodes.shortLabel: Every point can be a limit
nodes.mobileLabel: Every point can be a limit

nodes.en: Two limits in a two-point space
nodes.statement: The constant a-sequence converges to both points for the displayed topology.
nodes.mathText:
Example 4.8. Let X = {a, b} with the topology τ = {∅, {a}, X}. Then the
constant sequence (xn ) with xn = a for all n ∈ N converges to a and b.

    In general, the limit of a convergent sequence may not be unique. We will
need to give some additional conditions on the topology to ensure uniqueness
of limits.
    Finally, let’s talk about continuity.
nodes.shortLabel: Two limits in a two-point space
nodes.mobileLabel: Two limits in a two-point space

nodes.statement: A map continuous at x sends any sequence converging to x to a sequence converging to f(x).
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 4.9. Let f : X → Y be continuous at x. Then, whenever xn → x
in X, we have f (xn ) → f (x) in Y .

nodes.statement: A sequence in a product converges exactly when all its coordinate sequences converge.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 4.10. Let X = ΠXα be a product of topological spaces Xα . A se-
quence (xn ) in X converges to x ∈ X if and only if for every α, the sequence
(πα (xn )) converges to πα (x) in Xα .

nodes.statement: The support-size map on {0,1}ᴿ preserves sequential convergence into the specified two-point space but is not continuous.

nodes.statement: A directed set is nonempty and carries a reflexive, transitive relation in which every two elements have a common upper bound.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 4.12. A set Λ is a directed set if it is a non-empty set with a relation
≤ such that
   • reflexive: for all λ ∈ Λ, λ ≤ λ,
   • transitive: for all λ1 , λ2 , λ3 ∈ Λ, if λ1 ≤ λ2 and λ2 ≤ λ3 , then λ1 ≤ λ3 ,

   • directed: for all λ1 , λ2 ∈ Λ, there exists µ ∈ Λ such that λ1 ≤ µ and
     λ2 ≤ µ.
   This relation ≤ is called a direction on Λ.

nodes.en: Directions need not be partial orders
nodes.statement: Antisymmetry is not required; the displayed two-point relation is directed but not a partial order.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 4.13. Note a direction may not be a partial order, i.e., it may not be
antisymmetric. For example, let Λ = {a, b} with a ≤ b and b ≤ a. This is a
directed set but not a poset because a ̸= b.
nodes.shortLabel: Directions need not be partial orders
nodes.mobileLabel: Directions need not be partial orders

nodes.statement: The natural numbers with their usual order form a directed set.
nodes.mathText:
Example 4.14. N with the standard order (which is obviously a direction) is
a directed set.

nodes.statement: A net is a function from a directed set into a topological space.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 4.15. A net in a topological space X is a function P : Λ → X where
Λ is a directed set. We often write P (λ) = xλ and write the net (xλ )λ∈Λ or
(xλ ).

nodes.statement: A net converges when it is eventually in every neighborhood of the proposed limit.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 4.16. We say that a net (xλ )λ∈Λ converges to a point x ∈ X if
for every neighbourhood U of x, there exists λ0 ∈ Λ such that xλ ∈ U for all
λ ≥ λ0 .

nodes.statement: Taking N with its usual order recovers ordinary sequence convergence.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 4.17. Note that if we take Λ = N with the standard order, then the
notion of convergence of nets reduces to the notion of convergence of sequences.

nodes.statement: Refinement directs finite interval partitions; their lower and upper sums form nets, whose common limit defines the integral as stated in the notes.
nodes.mathText:
Example 4.18. Let P denote the collection of all finite partitions of the closed
interval [a, b] into closed subintervals. In other words, each P ∈ P has the form
P = {[x0 , x1 ], [x1 , x2 ], . . . , [xn−1 , xn ]} where a = x0 < x1 < · · · < xn = b.
    This becomes a directed set if we define the direction by refinement: for two
partitions P1 , P2 ∈ P, we say that P1 ≤ P2 if P2 is a refinement of P1 (i.e., every
subinterval in P1 is a union of subintervals in P2 ).
    Now, consider a function f : [a, b] → R. Define a net (RL (P ))P ∈P as follows:
for each partition P = {[x0 , x1 ], [x1 , x2 ], . . . , [xn−1 , xn ]}, let

                                      x∈[xi−1 ,xi ]

This net is called the lower Riemann sum net of f .
   Similarly, we can define the upper Riemann sum net (RU (P ))P ∈P by
                                n
                                X
                    RU (P ) =             sup         f (x) · (xi − xi−1 ).
                                i=1 x∈[xi−1 ,xi ]

    If both nets converge to the same limit L, then we say that f is Riemann
integrable on [a, b] with integral L.

nodes.statement: Neighborhoods ordered by reverse inclusion form a directed set, and choosing a point from each produces a net converging to the central point.
nodes.mathText:
Example 4.19. One typical example of a net is the following: let X be a
topological space and x ∈ X. Let Λ be the set of all neighbourhoods of x
and define the direction on Λ by U ≤ V iff V ⊆ U (reverse inclusion). You
should check that this is indeed a directed set. Pick a point xU ∈ U for each
neighbourhood U of x. Then the net (xU )U ∈Λ converges to x. To see this, let
V be any neighbourhood of x, then for all U ≥ V , we have xU ∈ U ⊆ V . This
shows that xU → x.

nodes.statement: A point is in the closure of E exactly when some net entirely in E converges to it.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 4.20. If E ⊂ X, then x ∈ E iff there is a net (xλ )λ∈Λ in E such
that xλ → x.

nodes.statement: A map is continuous at x exactly when it preserves the limit of every net converging to x.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 4.21. Let f : X → Y . Then f is continuous at x ∈ X iff for every
net (xλ )λ∈Λ in X such that xλ → x, we have f (xλ ) → f (x).

nodes.statement: An open set containing x is an open neighborhood of x.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 5.1 (Neighbourhood). Let (X, T ) be a topological space and x ∈ X.
A set B ∈ T is a (open) neighbourhood of x if x ∈ B.

nodes.statement: A countable local basis refines every neighborhood of a point; a space is first countable when every point has one.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 5.2. A space X has a countable basis at a point x ∈ X if there is
a countable collection of neighbourhoods B = {Bn : n ∈ N} of x such that for
every neighbourhood V of x, there exists n with Bn ⊆ V .
   We call X a first countable space if it has a countable basis at each point.

nodes.statement: The singleton of a point is a one-element local basis in a discrete space.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.3. Let X be equipped with the discrete topology. Then X is first
countable: for each x ∈ X, the collection {{x}} is a countable basis at x.

nodes.statement: The balls of radii 1/n form a countable local basis at each metric-space point.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.4. A metric space (X, d) is first countable: for each x ∈ X, the
collection {B1/n (x) : n ∈ N} is a countable basis at x.

nodes.statement: Finite intersections turn a countable local basis into a decreasing one.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 5.5. For a general first countable space, we can always
                                                         Tn    assume that
Bn+1 ⊆ Bn for all n. This is because we can replace Bn by i=1 Bi .
    Let’s see some non-examples of first countable spaces.

nodes.en: Cofinite R is not first countable
nodes.statement: A countable proposed local basis omits only countably many points in total, allowing a neighborhood that none of its members refines.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.6. Let X = R. Then, the complement finite topology on X is not
first countable. To see this, suppose there is a countable basis of neighbourhoods
{Bn : n ∈ N} at some point x ∈ S    X. Since each Bn is open, we have X \ Bn
is finite for each n. Let E = x ∪ n∈N (X \ Bn ). Then, E is countable. Now,
pick any y ∈ R \ E and consider the open set U = X \ {y}. Note that U is a
neighbourhood of x. However, for any n, we have Bn ̸⊆ U since y ∈ Bn \ U .
This contradicts the assumption that {Bn : n ∈ N} is a basis at x. Hence, X is
not first countable.
nodes.shortLabel: Cofinite R is not first countable
nodes.mobileLabel: Cofinite R is not first countable

nodes.en: An uncountable product is not first countable
nodes.statement: For a metric X with at least two points, a countable local basis in Xᴿ could control only countably many coordinates, giving a contradiction.
nodes.mathText:

first countable with the product topology. To see this, let g ∈ X R and suppose
there is a countable basis {Bn : n ∈ N} at g. Each Bn contains a basic open
neighbourhood of the form

                 Vn = {f ∈ X R : f (tn,i ) ∈ Un,i for i = 1, . . . , kn }

union of finite sets. Now, pick t0 ∈ R \ E and create

nodes.shortLabel: An uncountable product is not first countable
nodes.mobileLabel: An uncountable product is not first countable

nodes.en: Sequential tests in first countable spaces
nodes.statement: First countability restores the converses of the closure and sequential-continuity tests. The notes prove only the closure converse, with a flagged choice-of-points omission.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 5.8. Let X be a topological space.

   1. For A ⊆ X and x ∈ X, if there is a sequence (an ) ⊆ A with an → x,
      then x ∈ A. If X is first countable, the converse holds: x ∈ A implies that
      there exists a sequence (an ) ⊆ A with an → x.
   2. If f : X → Y is continuous at x and xn → x in X, then f (xn ) → f (x) in
      Y . If X is first countable, the converse holds: xn → x ⇒ f (xn ) → f (x)
      for all sequences (xn ) in X implies that f is continuous at x.
nodes.shortLabel: Sequential tests in first countable spaces
nodes.mobileLabel: Sequential tests in first countable spaces

nodes.statement: A space is second countable when its topology has a countable basis.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 5.9. Let X be a topological space. We say that X is second count-
able if it has a countable basis.

nodes.statement: A second countable space is first countable, but an uncountable discrete space gives a converse counterexample and a metric non-second-countable example.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.10. Every second countable space is first countable. The converse
is not true. For example, consider an uncountable set X with the discrete
topology. Then X is first countable but not second countable. This also implies
that not every metric space is second countable.

nodes.en: Cofinite R is not second countable
nodes.statement: Failure of first countability also prevents second countability in this example.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.11. Let X = R be endowed with the complement finite topology.
Then, X is not second countable since X is not first countable.
nodes.shortLabel: Cofinite R is not second countable
nodes.mobileLabel: Cofinite R is not second countable

nodes.statement: R, Rⁿ and Rᴺ have countable product bases built from rational endpoints.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.12. The space R with the usual topology is second countable: the
collection {(a, b) : a, b ∈ Q, a < b} forms a countable basis.
     Similarly, Rn has a countable basis {(a1 , b1 ) × · · · × (an , bn ) : ai , bi ∈ Q, ai <
bi }.
     RN with the product topology also has a countable basis: {(a1 , b1 ) × · · · ×
(an , bn ) × R × R × · · · : ai , bi ∈ Q, ai < bi , n ∈ N}.

nodes.statement: Subspaces and countable products preserve first and second countability. The source proves the first-countable case and leaves a countable-index assumption implicit in the proof.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 5.13. Subspaces and countable products of first (resp. second) count-
able spaces are first (resp. second) countable.

nodes.statement: A subset is dense when its closure is the whole space; a space is separable when it has a countable dense subset.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 5.14. A subset A of a topological space X is dense if A = X. A
space X is separable if it contains a countable dense subset.

nodes.statement: Q is countable and dense in R, and Q² is dense in R².
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.15. R is separable: Q is a countable dense subset of R.
  Q2 is also a dense subset of R2 , so R2 is separable.

nodes.en: Second countability gives Lindelöf and separability
nodes.statement: A countable basis yields a countable subcover of every open cover and a countable dense subset.
nodes.shortLabel: Second countability gives Lindelöf and separability
nodes.mobileLabel: Second countability gives Lindelöf and separability

nodes.statement: The two-point example motivates stronger separation conditions.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.17. Let X = {a, b} with the topology τ = {∅, {a}, X}. Then the
constant sequence (xn ) with xn = a for all n ∈ N converges to a and b.
   Let’s see some different ways to separate points and sets in a topological
space and check if they can help us to avoid such pathological examples.

nodes.statement: Separating a fixed point from each other point makes its complement open.
nodes.mathText: Lemma 5.19. Let X be a Hausdorff space. Then, one-point sets are closed.

nodes.en: Trivial spaces need not be Hausdorff
nodes.statement: A trivial topology on more than one point cannot separate distinct points by disjoint open sets.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.20. The trivial topology on a set of more than one point is not
Hausdorff.
nodes.shortLabel: Trivial spaces need not be Hausdorff
nodes.mobileLabel: Trivial spaces need not be Hausdorff

nodes.statement: The displayed topology on {a,b} lacks disjoint neighborhoods of the two points.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.21. Consider the space X = {a, b} with the topology T = {∅, {a}, {a, b}}.
This space is also not Hausdorff.

nodes.statement: For R with finite- or countable-complement topology, any two nonempty open sets intersect.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.22. Let X = R. Then, complement finite and complement count-
able topologies on X are not Hausdorff. This is because any two non-empty
open sets intersect.

nodes.en: Uniqueness of limits: source hypothesis gap
nodes.statement: The printed statement asserts unique sequence limits in a topological space; its proof assumes Hausdorffness. The missing hypothesis is flagged without changing the claim.
nodes.mathText: Proposition 5.24. Every sequence has a unique limit in a topological space.
nodes.shortLabel: Uniqueness of limits: source hypothesis gap
nodes.mobileLabel: Uniqueness of limits: source hypothesis gap

nodes.en: Unique sequential limits need not separate points
nodes.statement: In cocountable R every convergent sequence is eventually its limit, yet the space is not Hausdorff.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.25. Let X = R be endowed with the countable complement topol-
ogy. We know that any sequence (xn ) converging to x is eventually equal to
x. Hence, every converging sequence has a unique limit. However, X is not
Hausdorff.
nodes.shortLabel: Unique sequential limits need not separate points
nodes.mobileLabel: Unique sequential limits need not separate points

nodes.statement: A first countable space in which convergent sequences have unique limits is Hausdorff. The notes assign this as homework.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 5.26. Suppose X is first countable. Assume that every convergent
sequence has a unique limit in X. Then, X is Hausdorff. (This is homework)
   In fact, metric spaces satisfy stronger separation axioms. We will introduce
some of them.

sourceProofDisposition.note: Assigned as homework. No proof is supplied.

nodes.statement: With closed singletons assumed, regularity separates a point from a disjoint closed set and normality separates disjoint closed sets.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 5.27. Let X be a topological space such that one-point sets are
closed. We say that X is:
  1. regular if for any point x and a disjoint closed set B, there exist disjoint
     open sets U and V such that x ∈ U and B ⊆ V .
  2. normal if for any two disjoint closed sets A and B, there exist disjoint
     open sets U and V such that A ⊆ U and B ⊆ V .

nodes.statement: Under the source conventions, normality implies regularity and regularity implies Hausdorffness.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 5.28. A regular space is Hausdorff. A normal space is regular (hence
Hausdorff).

nodes.statement: The topology generated by intervals and intervals with {1/n} removed is Hausdorff but not regular.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.29 (The K–topology on R). Let K = {1/n : n ∈ N} and let RK
be R with the topology generated by the basis {(a, b), (a, b) \ K : a < b}.

   • It is Hausdorff: for x ̸= y pick disjoint usual intervals around x and y.
   • K is closed (note K is not closed in the usual topology): if x ∈   / K and
     x ̸= 0, choose ε > 0 with (x − ε, x + ε) ∩ K = ∅; if x = 0, then (−ε, ε) \ K
     is an open neighbourhood of 0 disjoint from K. Hence R \ K is open.

   • It is not regular: 0 ∈
                          / K. Suppose there are disjoint open sets U, V with
     0 ∈ U and K ⊆ V . Choose a basis element (a, b) \ K ⊂ U containing 0.
     Pick n large enough so that 1/n ∈ (a, b) and let (c, d) be a basis element
                                                                      1
     with 1/n ∈ (c, d) ⊆ V . Finally, choose z so that z ∈ (max(c, n+1   ), 1/n).
     Then, z ∈ U ∩ V , contradicting the assumption that U and V are disjoint.
Consequently RK is Hausdorff but not regular.

   Now we have some other useful ways of stating these properties.

nodes.statement: With closed singletons, regularity and normality are equivalent to the corresponding neighborhood-closure shrinking conditions.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 5.30. Let X be a topological space with one-point sets closed. Then,
  1. X is regular iff for every neighbourhood U of a any point x, there exists a
     neighbourhood V of x such that x ∈ V ⊂ V ⊂ U .

  2. X is normal iff for every closed set A and any open set U such that
     A ⊂ U ⊆ X, there exists an open V with A ⊂ V ⊂ V ⊂ U .

nodes.statement: Subspaces and products preserve Hausdorffness and regularity. The source proves the regular case.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 5.31. Subspaces and products of Hausdorff (resp. regular) spaces are
Hausdorff (resp. regular).

nodes.statement: The source gives Rᴿ and its relationship to a compact Hausdorff product as a counterexample to general subspace inheritance of normality, with an external exercise reference.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.32. RR is not normal (See Munkres Chapter 4 section 32 problem
9.)
    Since R ∼

         R

nodes.en: The lower-limit line and its square
nodes.statement: The lower-limit line is normal, but its square is not; the antidiagonal is used in the source counterexample and an external exercise is cited.
nodes.mathText:
Example 5.33. Let Rℓ be R endowed with the so-called lower limit topology
which is generated by the basis {[a, b)}. You can check that this is finer than
the usual topology on R since every
                                  S∞ open interval (a, b) can be written as the
union of basis elements: (a, b) = n=1 [a + n1 , b).
   Then, Rℓ is normal: let A and B be disjoint closed sets in Rℓ . For each
a ∈ A, choose a basis element such that [a, xa ) ∩ B = ∅. Similarly, S for each
b ∈ B, choose
          S    a basis element  such that [b, y b ) ∩ A = ∅. Let U =  a∈A [a, xa )
and V = b∈B [b, yb ). Then, U and V are disjoint open sets separating A and
B.
   By the theorem above, we know that Rℓ ×Rℓ is regular. But it is not normal.
Indeed, L = {(x, −x) : x ∈ R} is closed in R2 and hence closed in Rℓ × Rℓ . Note
{(a, −a)} = L ∩ [a, a + 1) × [−a, −a + 1) and hence {(a, −a)} is open in L. So L
has the discrete topology. So every subset of L is closed in subspace topology
and hence closed in Rℓ × Rℓ .
   Now let A = {(x, −x) : x ∈ Q} and B = L \ A. Both are closed in Rℓ × Rℓ .
One can check that there are no disjoint open sets separating A and B (see
Munkres Chapter 4 section 31 problem 9). So Rℓ × Rℓ is not normal.
   There is still a positive result about subspaces of normal spaces.

Theorem 5.36. Every metric space (and hence every metrizable space) is nor-
mal.

nodes.statement: In a normal space, two disjoint closed sets can be separated by a continuous function into [0,1] taking the values 0 and 1 on them.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 5.37 (Urysohn’s lemma). Let X be a normal space. Then for every two
disjoint closed sets A and B, there exists a continuous function f : X → [0, 1]
such that f |A ≡ 0 and f |B ≡ 1.

nodes.statement: Every regular space with a countable basis is metrizable; the source embeds it into a countable product of intervals.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 5.38 (Urysohn’s metrization theorem). Every regular space with a
countable base is metrizable.
   We first prove the following lemma.

nodes.statement: For a regular space with a countable basis, the source constructs countably many continuous functions that are positive at a point and vanish off any prescribed neighborhood.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 5.39. Let X be a regular space with a countable basis. Then, there
exists a countable family of continuous functions fn : X → [0, 1] such that for
any x ∈ X and any neighborhood U of x, there exists n with fn (x) > 0 and
fn |U c ≡ 0.

nodes.statement: The introductory IVT states an interior preimage for values in a closed endpoint range. The endpoint mismatch is retained and flagged.
A continuous real function on [0,1] attains a maximum.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.2 (Maximum value theorem). Let f : [0, 1] → R be a continuous
function. Then there exists c ∈ [0, 1] such that f (c) ≥ f (x) for all x ∈ [0, 1].
    These are due to the fact that [0, 1] is “connected” and “compact”. We will
talk about these two notions for general topological spaces in this and the next
section.

nodes.statement: The integer-centered radius-one interval cover of R has no finite subcover.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.4. R is not compact: {(n − 1, n + 1)}n∈Z is an open cover of R with
no finite subcover.

nodes.statement: Choosing one covering open set for each point gives a finite subcover of a finite space.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.5. Every finite topological space X is compact (regardless of the
topology): given any open cover U, for each point x ∈ X choose Ux ∈ U such
that x ∈ Ux . Then, {Ux : x ∈ X} is a finite subcover.

nodes.en: A half-open interval is not compact

Example 6.6. (0, 1] is not compact: {(1/n, 1] : n ∈ N} is an open cover of
(0, 1] with no finite subcover.

nodes.statement: The source announces compactness of closed real intervals and the later closed-and-bounded criterion in Rⁿ.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.7. Any closed interval such as [0, 1] in real line is compact. This
is not trivial and we will prove it later. As a consequence, we will see X ⊂ Rn
is compact iff it is closed and bounded (Heine-Borel theorem).
   Although we have the result for Rn , not every closed and bounded subset of
a general metric space is compact. Let me show you two examples.

nodes.en: Closed and bounded can be noncompact
nodes.statement: The discrete topology on [0,1] gives a closed bounded space whose singleton cover has no finite subcover.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.8. Let X = [0, 1] with the discrete topology. Then, X is closed
and bounded as a subset of itself. However, it is not compact: {{x} : x ∈ [0, 1]}
is an open cover of X with no finite subcover.

nodes.en: A convergent sequence with its limit
nodes.statement: The set {1/n} is not compact, but adjoining zero makes every open cover reducible to finitely many sets.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.10. {1/n}n∈N ⊂ R is not compact: {{1/n}} is an open cover with
no finite subcover.
    However, {0} ∪ {1/n}n∈N ⊂ R is compact: given any open cover U , there
exists U ∈ U such that 0 ∈ U . Choose ε > 0 such that (−ε, ε) ⊂ U . Then,
only finitely many points of the set {1/n}n∈N are outside U . Choosing open
sets from U covering these finitely many points gives a finite subcover.

nodes.statement: Every subset of R with its finite-complement topology is compact, although the space is not Hausdorff.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.14. Let X = R be endowed with the finite complement topology.
Then, X is not Hausdorff as we have seen. However, any subset Y of X is
compact.

nodes.statement: Use compactness of closed subsets and finite point-to-set separations to separate two disjoint closed sets.
nodes.mathText: Theorem 6.15. Every compact Hausdorff space is normal.

nodes.statement: Every finite subcollection has nonempty intersection.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.16. A collection of sets {Cα } in X is said to have the finite
intersection
Tn            property if for any finite subcollection {Cα1 , . . . , Cαn }, we have
  i=1 C αi ̸

nodes.statement: Compactness is equivalent to a nonempty total intersection for every closed family with the finite intersection property.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.17. A topological space X is compact iff for any collection
                                                              T       of closed
sets {Cα } in X with the finite intersection property, we have α Cα ̸= ∅.

nodes.statement: The source claims a maximum for a continuous real-valued map without assuming compactness of X; its proof uses that missing condition.
nodes.mathText:
Corollary 6.19 (Maximum value theorem). Let f : X → R be a continuous
function. Then there exists c ∈ X such that f (c) ≥ f (x) for all x ∈ X.

nodes.statement: Functions preserve finiteness of sets, while continuous maps preserve compactness of sets.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 6.21. Any function sends a finite set to a finite set.
  Any continuous map sends a compact set to a compact set.

nodes.en: Extrema on finite and compact sets
nodes.statement: The source contrasts extrema of a real function on a finite set with extrema of a continuous real function on a compact space.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.22.      • Any finite function f : A → R obtains maximal and
    minimal values.
   • Any continuous function f : X → R from a compact space X obtains
     maximal and minimal values.

nodes.mobileLabel: Extrema on finite and compact sets

nodes.en: Subsequences in finite and compact metric spaces
nodes.statement: A sequence in a finite set has a constant subsequence; a sequence in a compact metric space has a convergent subsequence.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.23.      • Any sequence (xn ) taking value in a finite set A has a
    convergent subsequence (actually constant).
   • Any sequence (xn ) taking value in a compact metric space X has a con-
     vergent subsequence.

nodes.mobileLabel: Subsequences in finite and compact metric spaces

nodes.statement: The source asserts compactness of closed intervals in a linear order with the least-upper-bound property and gives an order-cover argument.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.24. Let X be a linear post. Assume that X has the least upper
bound property1 . Then, any closed interval [a, b] in X is compact under the order
topology (generated by (a, b) and [a0 , b) and (a, b0 ] if a0 is the least element and
b0 is the greatest element).

nodes.statement: The order-interval theorem specializes to [a,b] in R.
nodes.mathText:
Corollary 6.25. Any closed and bounded interval [a, b] in R is compact.
   We can now use this corollary to prove the Heine-Borel theorem.

nodes.statement: A subset of Rⁿ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.26 (Heine-Borel theorem). A subset K of Rn is compact if and
only if it is closed and bounded.

nodes.statement: A sequence is Cauchy when its tail terms are pairwise arbitrarily close; a metric space is complete when all its Cauchy sequences converge in it.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.27. Let (X, d) be a metric space. A sequence (xn ) is said to be
Cauchy if for every ϵ > 0, there exists N ∈ N such that d(xn , xm ) < ϵ for all
n, m ≥ N .
    The metric space (X, d) is said to be complete if every Cauchy sequence in
X converges to a point in X.

nodes.statement: Rⁿ is complete; removing zero gives an incomplete metric subspace.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.28. The Euclidean space Rn is a complete metric space. Rn \ {0}
is not complete.

nodes.statement: For every positive radius, finitely many balls of that radius cover the metric space.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.29. A metric space (X, d) is said to be totally bounded if for every
ϵ > 0, there exists a finite set F ⊂ X such that X is covered by the open balls
Bϵ (x) for x ∈ F .

nodes.statement: The source states this metric characterization and defers its proof to the later three-way equivalence.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.30. A metric space is compact iff it is complete and totally bounded.
   We will postpone the proof of this theorem until we have developed more
tools.
   We now prove one thing that we used previously in showing §1 is not con-
tractible.

nodes.statement: A single positive input tolerance must work for every pair of points for each positive output tolerance.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.31. A function f : (X, dX ) → (Y, dY ) between two metric spaces
is said to be uniformly continuous if for every ϵ > 0, there exists δ > 0 such
that for all x1 , x2 ∈ X, if dX (x1 , x2 ) < δ, then dY (f (x1 ), f (x2 )) < ϵ.

nodes.statement: A continuous map from a compact metric space into a metric space is uniformly continuous.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.32. Let f : (X, dX ) → (Y, dY ) be a continuous function between
two metric spaces. If X is compact, then f is uniformly continuous.

nodes.statement: Every sequence has a subsequence converging to a point in the space.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.33. A space X is said to be sequentially compact if every sequence
in X has a convergent subsequence.

nodes.statement: For a metric space, compactness, completeness plus total boundedness, and sequential compactness are equivalent; the source proves the three implications.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.34. Let X be a metric space. Then, the following are equivalent:
  1. X is compact.
  2. X is complete and totally bounded.
  3. X is sequentially compact.

nodes.statement: The binary cube {0,1}^[0,1] is compact by Tychonoff, but a diagonal digit construction rules out a convergent subsequence of the given sequence.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.35 (Compact but not sequentially compact). Let X = {0, 1}[0,1]
with the product topology. By Tychonoff, X is compact. For each n ∈ N
define fn ∈ X by fn (r) = the n-th binary digit of r (choose the expansion not
ending in all 1’s). Take any subsequence (fnk ). If it converges, we know that for
any r ∈ [0, 1], the sequence (fnk (r)) must converge in [0, 1]. Choose r ∈ [0, 1]
whose binary expansion has digit nk equal to 0 if k is odd and 1 if k is even
(this is possible since we prescribe digits only on the positions {nk }). Then
fnk (r) = 0, 1, 0, 1, . . . does not converge. Therefore (fnk ) cannot converge in the
product topology. Hence no subsequence of (fn ) converges; X is not sequentially
compact.

nodes.statement: The countable-support subspace of the binary cube is sequentially compact by diagonalization but not closed in the compact Hausdorff cube.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.36 (Sequentially compact but not compact). Let Y ⊂ {0, 1}[0,1]
be a subspace consisting of all functions f such that f (r) = 1 for at most
countably many r ∈ [0, 1]. We claim that Y is sequentially
                                                    S            compact but not
compact. Given any sequence (fn ) in Y , let A = n {r : fn (r) = 1}. Then, A
is countable. For each r ∈ A, the sequence (fn (r)) in {0, 1} has a convergent
subsequence. By a diagonal argument, we can find a subsequence (fnk ) such
that for each r ∈ A, the sequence (fnk (r)) converges in {0, 1}. For r ∈
                                                                       / A, define
f (r) = 0. Then, it is easy to see that f ∈ Y and fnk → f in the product
topology. Hence, Y is sequentially compact.
    To see that Y is not compact, we just need to show that Y is not closed.
Pick 1 ∈ X \ Y being the constant function with value 1. For any basic open
neighbourhood of 1 of the form

                                       \

where πri : X → {0, 1} is the projection map, we can find f ∈ Y such that
f (ri ) = 1 for all i = 1, 2, . . . , n (for example, let f (r) = 1 if r = ri for some
i and f (r) = 0 otherwise). This shows that every open neighbourhood of 1
intersects Y . Hence, 1 ∈ Y \ Y and Y is not closed, therefore not compact.
    In general topological spaces, compactness can be characterized using nets.
A net is a generalization of a sequence that allows for indexing by a directed
set.

nodes.statement: Every neighborhood meets the net arbitrarily far along the directed set; this is weaker than eventual membership.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.37. We say a net (xα )α∈A has a cluster point x ∈ X if for every
open neighbourhood U of x and every α0 ∈ A, there exists (not for all) α ≥ α0
such that xα ∈ U .
   One equivalent way to describe cluster points is via subnets.

nodes.statement: A subnet is obtained by composing a net with an increasing cofinal map from another directed set.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.38. A subnet of a net P : Λ → X is the composition P ◦ φ where
φ : Γ → Λ is an increasing function between directed sets Γ and Λ such that: For
every λ ∈ Λ, there exists γ ∈ Γ such that λ ≤ φ(γ). If we represent P as (xλ ),
then the subnet can be represented as (xλγ ) or (xφ(γ) ) (cf. the subsequence
notation (xnk )).

nodes.statement: The increasing index map k ↦ n_k realizes a subsequence as a subnet.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.39. Any subsequence (xnk ) of a sequence (xn ) is a subnet. Note
that here the map φ : N → N is defined by φ(k) = nk .

nodes.statement: A point is a cluster point of a net exactly when a subnet converges to it.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 6.40. A net (xα )α∈A has a cluster point x ∈ X iff there exists a
subnet of (xα )α∈A that converges to x.

nodes.statement: A space is compact exactly when every net has a cluster point, equivalently a convergent subnet.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.41. A topological space X is compact iff every net in X has a
cluster point and hence iff every net in X has a convergent subnet.

nodes.statement: For every subset, an ultranet is eventually in that subset or eventually in its complement.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.42. A net {xλ } in a set X is an ultranet if for any subset S ⊂ X,
the net is eventually in S or eventually in X \ S (there exists λ0 such that either
xλ ∈ S for all λ ≥ λ0 or xλ ∈ X \ S for all λ ≥ λ0 ).

nodes.statement: Constant and eventually constant nets are ultranets; an index set with a greatest element makes any indexed net eventually constant.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.43. Any constant net is an ultranet. Any eventually constant net
is an ultranet. If Λ has a greatest element λ0 , then any net indexed by Λ is an
ultranet as it is eventually constant at xλ0 .
   One immediate consequence of this definition is the following lemma.

nodes.statement: The complement alternative for a neighborhood is incompatible with being a cluster point, so the ultranet is eventually in each neighborhood.
nodes.mathText: Lemma 6.44. An ultranet converges to each of its cluster points.

nodes.statement: Every net has an ultranet subnet. The notes explicitly provide a sketch using maximal admissible families and defer full details.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 6.45. Every net has a subnet that is an ultranet.
    This is a nontrivial result and we will not give a full proof here. I’ll provide
a reference on Canvas if you are interested in the full proof.

nodes.statement: Every map sends an ultranet to an ultranet, by applying the source alternative to the preimage of each subset.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 6.46. If {xλ } is an ultranet in X and f : X → Y is a map, then
{f (xλ )} is an ultranet in Y .

nodes.statement: A nonempty product space is compact exactly when each factor is compact; the source proof uses ultranet subnets and coordinate convergence.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.47 (Tychonoff’s theorem). A nonempty product space is compact
iff each factor space is compact.
                                                  Q

nodes.statement: The displayed binary and interval products are compact examples of Tychonoff’s theorem.
nodes.mathText: Example 6.48. {0, 1}[0,1] is compact. [0, 1]R is compact.

nodes.statement: The source gives closed-and-bounded and product-space approaches; checking that the sequence metric induces the product topology is left as an exercise.
nodes.mathText:
Example T   6.49. The Cantor set C is compact as C is bounded and C is closed
since C = Cn where each Cn is closed.
    We can also see this using Tychonoff’s theorem. We know there is a bijection
between C and {0, 2}N : each x ∈ C can be written in base 3 using only digits
0 and 2, and this gives a bijection between C and {0, 2}N . It turns out that
this bijection is actually a homeomorphism. To see this, let’s actually give a
metric on {0, 2}N that induces the product topology. For any two sequences
(an ), (bn ) ∈ {0, 2}N , define
                                  (
                                    0    if an = bn for all n
                d((an ), (bn )) =      k
                                    1/3 where k = min{n : an ̸= bn }

We defined an ultrametric on C before. You can check that this metric on
{0, 2}N is actually the same as the ultrametric on C under the above bijection.
So the bijection is an isometry. The only thing left to check is that this metric
on {0, 2}N induces the product topology. This is left as an exercise. Therefore,
C is homeomorphic to {0, 2}N which is compact by Tychonoff’s theorem. Hence,
C is compact.

nodes.statement: Every point has an open neighborhood contained in a compact subset.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.50. A topological space X is said to be locally compact if for
every point x ∈ X, there exists an open neighbourhood U of x and a compact
set K such that U ⊆ K.

nodes.statement: A compact space itself supplies the compact set required at each point.
nodes.mathText: Example 6.51. Any compact space is locally compact.

nodes.statement: Bounded boxes around a point lie inside compact closed boxes.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.52. R is locally compact. For each x ∈ R, we pick the open
neighbourhood U = (x − 1, x + 1) and the compact set K = [x − 1, x + 1] such
that U ⊂ K.
   Similarly, Rn is locally compact. For each x ∈ Rn , we pick the open neigh-
bourhood U = (x1 − 1, x1 + 1) × · · · × (xn − 1, xn + 1) and the compact set
K = [x1 − 1, x1 + 1] × · · · × [xn − 1, xn + 1] such that U ⊂ K.

nodes.statement: An unrestricted coordinate projection would send any compact neighborhood container onto noncompact R.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.53. RN is not locally compact. For any x ∈ RN , pick any basic
open neighborhood U = U1 × U2 × · · · × Un × R × R × · · · . Suppose there
exists some compact set K such that U ⊂ K. Consider the projection map
πn+1 : RN → R defined by πn+1 ((xi )) = xn+1 . Then, πn+1 (U ) = R and hence
πn+1 (K) ⊃ πn+1 (U ) = R. However, the continuous image of a compact set is
compact and R is not compact. This is a contradiction. Therefore, there does
not exist any compact set K such that U ⊂ K and hence RN is not locally
compact.

nodes.statement: The source characterizes locally compact Hausdorff spaces by adjoining one point to obtain a compact Hausdorff space; uniqueness is stated with a final exercise.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.54. Let X be a topological space. Then, X is locally compact
Hausdorff iff there exists a compact Hausdorff space Y such that

   • X is a subspace of Y ;
   • Y \ X consists of a single point.
Such a space Y is called the one-point compactification of X and is unique up
to homeomorphism.

nodes.statement: The source illustrates the one-point compactification of an open interval, hence R, by S¹.
A collection refines another when each of its members is contained in a member of the other collection.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.57. Let A be a collection of subsets of a set X. A collection B
of subsets of X is said to be a refinement of A if for each B ∈ B, there exists
some A ∈ A such that B ⊂ A.

nodes.statement: A space is compact exactly when every open cover has a finite open refinement that still covers the space.
nodes.mathText:
Proposition 6.58. A space X is compact iff every open cover of X has a finite
open refinement that covers X.
   This can be generalized as follows.

nodes.statement: Every open cover must have a locally finite open refinement covering the space; local finiteness means each point has a neighborhood meeting finitely many members.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.59. A space X is said to be paracompact if every open cover A
of X has a locally finite open refinement B that covers X, i.e., for each x ∈ X,
there exists some open neighbourhood U of x such that U intersects only finitely
many elements of B.

nodes.statement: The source constructs annular refinements of open covers of Rⁿ; its boundedness and local-finiteness details remain part of source review.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.60. Rn is paracompact. Let A be an open cover of Rn . For each
k ∈ N, consider the closed ball Bk (0) of radius k centered at the origin. Since
Bk (0) is compact, there exists a finite subcover Ak = {Ak,1 , . . . , Ak,nk } of A that
                                           n                              n
covers Bk (0). Then, let Bk = {Ak,1 ∩(R  S \Bk−1 (0)), . . . , Ak,nk ∩(R \Bk−1 (0))}
(Here we let B0 (0) = ∅). Then, B = Bk is a locally finite open refinement of
A that covers Rn . This is first of all because Bk (0) is covered by B1 ∪ · · · ∪ Bk .

nodes.statement: A finite subcover is a locally finite open refinement.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.61. Every compact space is paracompact.
   One useful fact about locally finiteness is the following lemma.

nodes.en: Closure commutes with locally finite unions
nodes.statement: For a locally finite family, the closure of its union equals the union of its members’ closures.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 6.62. S     Let ASbe a locally finite collection of sets in a topological space
X. Then, A∈A A = A∈A A.
                                                                     S
nodes.shortLabel: Closure commutes with locally finite unions
nodes.mobileLabel: Closure commutes with locally finite unions

nodes.statement: Local finiteness and separation first yield regularity; the source describes normality by the analogous argument.
nodes.mathText: Theorem 6.63. Every paracompact Hausdorff space X is normal.

nodes.statement: In a regular space, the four stated open, countably locally finite, locally finite and closed refinement properties are equivalent.
The source uses a well-order of a cover and distance-separated refinements; its transition from levelwise local finiteness is flagged for review.
nodes.mathText: Theorem 6.65. Every metric space is paracompact.

nodes.statement: The preceding theorem includes Rⁿ and [0,1) among the paracompact examples.
nodes.mathText:
Example 6.66. This theorem gives us a bunch of examples of paracompact
spaces, e.g. Rn , [0, 1) etc.

Partition of Unity

nodes.statement: A subordinate family of continuous [0,1]-valued functions has supports inside the corresponding cover members, locally finite supports, and pointwise sum one.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 6.67. Let U = {Uα }α∈A be an open cover of a topological space X.
A partition of unity subordinated to U is a collection of continuous functions
{φα : X → [0, 1]}α∈A such that:
   • supp ϕα ⊂ Uα ; here the support of a function f : X → R is defined as
     supp f = {x ∈ X : f (x) ̸= 0}
   • {supp φα } is locally finite; and
   • For every x ∈ X, α∈A φα (x) = 1.
                        P

nodes.statement: A Hausdorff paracompact space admits the stated indexed open shrinking of any open cover; the proof also establishes local finiteness.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 6.68. Let X be Hausdorff and paracompact. Then, every open cover
U = {Uα }α∈J of X has a shrinking, i.e., an open refinement {Vα }α∈J covering
X such that Vα ⊂ Uα for each α.

nodes.statement: Every open cover of a Hausdorff paracompact space admits a subordinate partition of unity, constructed by two shrinkings, Urysohn functions, and normalization of their positive sum.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 6.69 (Partition of Unity). Let X be Hausdorff and paracompact.
Then, every open cover of X has a partition of unity subordinated to it.

nodes.statement: The motivating IVT repeats the endpoint-range/interior-point mismatch of Theorem 6.1, retained for review.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.1 (Intermediate Value Theorem). Let f : [0, 1] → R be a continuous
function. WLOG, we assume that f (0) < f (1). Then, for any r ∈ [f (0), f (1)],
there exists c ∈ (0, 1) such that f (c) = r.
    This is a consequence of the fact that [0, 1] is “connected”.

nodes.statement: A separation consists of two disjoint nonempty open sets covering the space; a space is connected when no such pair exists.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 7.2. Let X be a topological space. A separation of X is a pair
of disjoint nonempty open sets U, V ⊆ X with X = U ∪ V . The space X is
disconnected if it admits a separation; otherwise X is connected.

nodes.statement: Homeomorphisms preserve connectedness because it depends on open sets.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 7.3. This is a pure topological property: it depends only on the open
sets of X. In particular, connectedness is preserved by homeomorphisms.

nodes.statement: A space is connected exactly when its only simultaneously closed and open subsets are the empty set and the whole space.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 7.4. X is connected iff the only subsets that are both open and closed
(clopen) are ∅ and X.

nodes.statement: The indicated two disjoint half-open intervals form a disconnected subspace of R.
nodes.mathText: Example 7.5. [−1, 0) ∪ (0, 1] is disconnected.

nodes.statement: The two-point trivial topology is connected.
nodes.mathText: Example 7.6. {a, b} with the trivial topology {∅, {a, b}} is connected.

nodes.statement: An irrational cut separates the rational numbers into two nonempty relatively open pieces.
nodes.mathText:
Example 7.7. Q is disconnected: for r irrational, (−∞, r) ∩ Q and (r, ∞) ∩ Q
separate Q.
    How do we check if a space is connected?

nodes.statement: A separation of the image of a connected space would pull back to a separation of the source.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.8. If f : X → Y is continuous and X is connected, then f (X) is
connected.

nodes.en: A connected set stays on one side
nodes.statement: If U and V separate X, a connected subspace lies entirely in one of those sides.
nodes.mathText:
Lemma 7.9. If X has separation U, V and Y ⊆ X is connected, then Y ⊂ U
or Y ⊂ V .
nodes.shortLabel: A connected set stays on one side
nodes.mobileLabel: A connected set stays on one side

nodes.en: Sets between a connected set and its closure
nodes.statement: If A is connected and A ⊆ B ⊆ closure(A), then B is connected.
nodes.mathText: Theorem 7.10. If A ⊂ X is connected and A ⊆ B ⊆ A, then B is connected.
nodes.shortLabel: Sets between a connected set and its closure
nodes.mobileLabel: Sets between a connected set and its closure

nodes.en: Connected unions with a common point
nodes.statement: The union of connected subspaces sharing a point is connected.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.11. The union of a collection of connected subspaces of X that
have a point in common is connected.
                S

nodes.mobileLabel: Connected unions with a common point

nodes.statement: A finite product of connected spaces is connected; the source proves the two-factor case and uses induction.
nodes.mathText: Theorem 7.12. A finite product of connected spaces is connected.

nodes.statement: Finite products show Rⁿ is connected once connectedness of R has been established.
nodes.mathText:
Example 7.13. Rn is connected for all n ≥ 1 (if we assume the connectedness
of R which will be proved later).

nodes.statement: A linear continuum has more than one point, the least-upper-bound property, and a point strictly between each ordered pair of distinct points.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 7.16. A linear poset L having more than one element is called a
linear continuum if the following hold:
   1. L has the least upper bound property: every nonempty subset of L that
      is bounded above has a least upper bound. (sup exists)
   2. If x < y, then there exists z ∈ L such that x < z < y.

nodes.statement: A subset of a linear continuum is convex when it contains the closed interval between any two of its points.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 7.17. Y ⊂ L is called convex if for any a, b ∈ Y with a < b, we
have that [a, b] ⊆ Y .

nodes.en: Convex subsets of linear continua are connected
nodes.statement: The supremum of one side of a hypothetical separation yields a contradiction in an ordered convex subset.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.18. If L is a linear continuum with the order topology, then every
convex subset Y of L is connected.
nodes.shortLabel: Convex subsets of linear continua are connected
nodes.mobileLabel: Convex subsets of linear continua are connected

nodes.statement: A continuous function on [a,b] takes every value strictly between f(a) and f(b); the source also refers to an undefined X in this statement.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.19 (Intermediate Value Theorem). Let f : [a, b] → R be a contin-
uous function with X being connected. Assume that f (a) < f (b). Then, for any
r ∈ (f (a), f (b)), there exists c ∈ (a, b) such that f (c) = r.

nodes.en: Intermediate values from a connected space
nodes.statement: For a continuous f : X → R with X connected, every value strictly between two image values is attained.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.20 (Intermediate Value Theorem). Let f : X → R be a continuous
function with X being connected. Assume that a, b ∈ X and that f (a) < f (b).
Then, for any r ∈ (f (a), f (b)), there exists c ∈ X such that f (c) = r.

   That intervals in R are connected gives a sufficient condition for showing
that a space is connected.
nodes.shortLabel: Intermediate values from a connected space
nodes.mobileLabel: Intermediate values from a connected space

nodes.statement: Every pair of points can be joined by a continuous map from a real interval with the given endpoints.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 7.21. A space X is path connected if every x, y ∈ X can be joined
by a path, i.e., there exists a continuous f : [a, b] → X with f (a) = x and
f (b) = y.

nodes.statement: A path joining opposite sides of a hypothetical separation would have a connected image meeting both sides.
nodes.mathText: Lemma 7.22. A path connected space X is connected.

nodes.statement: Euclidean closed balls are connected, and Sⁿ⁻¹ is connected for n≥2, as stated in the source.
nodes.mathText:
Example 7.23. The ball Bn = {x ∈ Rn |∥x∥ ≤ 1} is connected.
  The sphere Sn−1 = {x ∈ Rn |∥x∥ = 1} is connected for n ≥ 2.

nodes.statement: Connected-subspace membership and path joinability define equivalence relations; their classes are components and path components.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 7.25. Let X be a topological space. We define an equivalence
relation on X by declaring x ∼ y iff there exists a connected subspace of X
containing both x and y. The equivalence classes of this relation are called the
components of X.
    We define another equivalence relation on X by declaring x ≈ y iff there
exists a path in X connecting x and y. The equivalence classes of this relation
are called the path components of X.
   Symmetry and relexivity are clear. For transitivity, if x, y lie in a connected
subspace A and y, z lie in a connected subspace B, then x, z lie in the connected
subspace A ∪ B (since y ∈ A ∩ B).

nodes.statement: Components are disjoint connected subspaces covering X, and each nonempty connected subspace lies in one component.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.26. The components of X are connected disjoint subspaces of X
whose union is X, such that each nonempty connected subspace of X intersects
only one of them.

nodes.statement: Path components have the analogous partition and maximal path-connectedness properties; the source says the proof is similar and does not write it out.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.27. The path components of X are path connected disjoint sub-
spaces of X whose union is X, such that each nonempty path connected subspace
of X intersects only one of them.
   The proof is similar to that of the previous theorem.

sourceProofDisposition.quote: The proof is similar to that of the previous theorem.
sourceProofDisposition.note: The source says the proof is similar, without spelling it out. No invented proof is modeled.

nodes.statement: The closure of a connected component is connected. With finitely many components they are also open; infinitely many need not be.
nodes.mathText:
Remark 7.28. Each component of X is closed as its closure is connected. If X
has only finitely many components, then each component is also open, since its
complement is a finite union of closed sets. This doesn’t hold in general for
infinitely many components.

nodes.statement: Each component of Q is a singleton, and none is open in Q.
nodes.mathText: Example 7.29. Each component of Q is a singleton which is not open.

nodes.statement: The sine-curve closure has one connected component but two path components: the graph and the added vertical segment.
nodes.mathText:
Example 7.30. For the topologist’s sine curve S, the components are S itself,
while the path components are S and V = {(0, y)|y ∈ [−1, 1]}. Note that S is
open but not closed in S, while V is closed but not open in S.
  Each path component is connected and hence contained in a component.
When do they coincide?

nodes.en: Local connectedness and local path connectedness
nodes.statement: Every neighborhood of each point contains a connected, respectively path connected, open neighborhood of that point.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 7.31. A space X is locally (path) connected iff for every x ∈ X
and every open neighborhood U of x, there exists a (path) connected open
neighborhood V of x with V ⊆ U .
nodes.shortLabel: Local connectedness and local path connectedness
nodes.mobileLabel: Local connectedness and local path connectedness

nodes.en: Local path connectedness implies local connectedness
nodes.statement: The path version of the local property implies the connected version.
nodes.mathText: Remark 7.32. locally path connected =⇒ locally connected.
nodes.shortLabel: Local path connectedness implies local connectedness
nodes.mobileLabel: Local path connectedness implies local connectedness

nodes.statement: Small balls provide path connected neighborhoods inside any prescribed open neighborhood.
nodes.mathText: Example 7.33. Every open subset of Rn is locally path connected.

locally connected. It is not locally path connected since the only path connected
subsets are singletons.

nodes.statement: A space is locally connected, respectively locally path connected, exactly when every component, respectively path component, of each open set is open.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.37. A space is locally (path) connected iff for any open U ⊂ X,
each (path) component P of U is open.

nodes.statement: In a locally path connected space, connected components coincide with path components.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.38. If X is locally path connected, then the components and path
components of X coincide.

nodes.statement: A connected and locally path connected space is path connected.
nodes.mathText: Corollary 7.39. A connected, locally path connected space X is path connected.

nodes.en: Connected Euclidean open sets are path connected
nodes.statement: An open connected subspace of Rⁿ is locally path connected and hence path connected.
nodes.mathText: Corollary 7.40. An open connected subset of Rn is path connected.

nodes.statement: A space is totally disconnected when all its connected components are singletons.
nodes.mathText:
Definition 7.41. A space X is totally disconnected iff the components of X
are singletons.

nodes.statement: Both Q and R without Q are totally disconnected in their usual subspace topologies.
nodes.mathText:
Example 7.42. The space Q of rational numbers (with the subspace topology
from R) is totally disconnected.
   Its complement R \ Q is also totally disconnected.

nodes.en: The Cantor set is totally disconnected
nodes.statement: The source relates this to its ultrametric description and later to a product of two-point spaces.
nodes.mathText:
Example 7.43. The Cantor set is totally disconnected.
    We are actually going to prove this in two ways.
    As we know that the Cantor set topology can be generated by an ultrametric,
it turns out that the above example is a special case of the following general
fact.
nodes.shortLabel: The Cantor set is totally disconnected
nodes.mobileLabel: The Cantor set is totally disconnected

nodes.statement: An ultrametric ball separates any two distinct points into complementary open sets, so no component contains both.
nodes.mathText: Theorem 7.44. Every ultrametric space is totally disconnected.

nodes.statement: A connected subset of a product projects to a singleton in each totally disconnected factor and is therefore a singleton; this also applies to the Cantor product model.
nodes.mathText:
Theorem 7.45. Every product of totally disconnected spaces is totally discon-
nected.

nodes.mathText:
Naive definition: A set is an aggregate of things, called elements of the set. We
usually use capital letters to denote sets, such as A, B, C, and lowercase letters
for elements, such as a, b, c. The notation a ∈ A means that a is an element of
the set A. We write a ∈ / A to mean that a is not an element of the set A.

nodes.statement: Read Unnumbered: Subsets, power sets and complements in full above. Subsets, power sets and complements is the atlas reading cue; the original wording and all displayed conditions are preserved in the source passage.
nodes.mathText:
Set calculus A set A is a subset of a set B if every element of A is also an
element of B. We write A ⊆ B to denote that A is a subset of B. If A is a
subset of B but not equal to B, we say that A is a proper subset of B and denote
it by A ⊊ B.
    We let P(A) denote the power set of A, which is the set of all subsets of A.
    We say two sets A and B are equal if they have the same elements, that is,
if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. We write A = B to denote that A and B are equal.
    We let A\B denote the set difference of A and B, which is the set of elements
in A that are not in B. Formally, A\B = {x ∈ A : x ∈    / B}. When B ⊆ A, we
say A\B is the complement of B in A.
    The empty set, denoted ∅, is a set that contains no elements. It is a subset
of every set.

Cartesian product The Cartesian product of two sets A and B, denoted
A × B, is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a ∈ A and b ∈ B:

                        A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}.

   Formally, an ordered pair can be defined as follows and define the cartesian
product as a set of sets:
                            (a, b) := {{a}, {a, b}}.

a1 ̸= a2 we have that f (a1 ) ̸= f (a2 ), we say that f is one-to-one or injective.
If a function is both injective and surjective, it is called a bijection. We usually

Order preserving maps An order preserving map between two posets (A, ≤A
) and (B, ≤B ) is a function f : A → B such that x ≤A y implies f (x) ≤B f (y).
An order isomorphism is a bijective order preserving map f : A → B such that

nodes.mathText:
(Axiom of Choice) If {Ai }i∈I is a family of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets,
there is a set B ⊂ ∪Ai such that B ∩ Ai is exactly one element for all i ∈ I.

nodes.mathText:
(Maximum Principle) In a poset, every chain is contained in a maximal chain
(i.e., a chain that is not properly contained in any other chain).

nodes.statement: Read Unnumbered: Zorn’s Lemma in full above. Zorn’s Lemma is the atlas reading cue; the original wording and all displayed conditions are preserved in the source passage.
nodes.mathText:
(Zorn’s Lemma) Let A be a poset. If every chain in A has an upper bound
in A, then A has a maximal element.

nodes.number: Unnumbered: Equality and comparison of cardinality
nodes.statement: Read Unnumbered: Equality and comparison of cardinality in full above. Equality and comparison of cardinality is the atlas reading cue; the original wording and all displayed conditions are preserved in the source passage.
nodes.mathText:
For any two sets A and B, we say they have the same cardinality if there exists
a bijection f : A → B. Intuitively, this means that the sets “have the same
number of elements”.
    Having the same cardinality is an equivalence relation on the class of all sets.
    We write |A| = |B| to denote that the sets A and B have the same cardinality.
    We say A has cardinality less than or equal to B (or B has cardinality greater
than or equal to A), denoted |A| ≤ |B| or |B| ≥ |A|, if there exists an injection
f : A → B.

nodes.statement: Read Unnumbered: Continuity of real functions in full above. Continuity of real functions is the atlas reading cue; the original wording and all displayed conditions are preserved in the source passage.
nodes.mathText:
For real functions f : R → R, we have the notion of continuity using ε-δ defini-
tion: a function f : R → R is continuous at a point x0 ∈ R if for every ε > 0
there exists δ > 0 such that

                    |f (x) − f (x0 )| < ε   whenever |x − x0 | < δ.

We also have the notion of continuity using sequences: a function f : R → R is
continuous at a point x0 ∈ R if for every sequence (xn ) in R converging to x0 ,
the sequence (f (xn )) converges to f (x0 ).

Example 1.4 (Russell’s paradox). Let P denote the set of all sets. Then, form
Q := {A ∈ P |A ∈
               / A}. Is Q ∈ Q?
   More axiomatic treatment of sets can be found in Zermelo-Fraenkel set the-
ory (ZF), which provides a formal foundation for set theory and avoids para-
doxes like Russell’s paradox by carefully restricting the kinds of sets that can
be formed. For example, under ZF axioms, the collection of all sets is not a set
but a proper class, because it violates one of the axioms requiring that a set
cannot contain itself as an element.

Theorem 1.20 (Partitions and equivalence relations). Let A be a nonempty set.
There is a one-to-one correspondence between partitions of A and equivalence
relations on A:
   • Define f : Part(A) → EqRel(A) by sending a partition {Ai }i∈I to the
     equivalence relation ∼ on A defined by a ∼ b if and only if ∃i ∈ I with
     a, b ∈ Ai .
   • Conversely, define g : EqRel(A) → Part(A) by sending an equivalence
     relation ∼ on A to the family of equivalence classes
                                                 {[a] : a ∈ A}
      which is a partition of A.
Then, f and g are bijections and they are inverse to each other, i.e.,
                        g ◦ f = idPart(A) ,            f ◦ g = idEqRel(A) .

Example 1.35.         • We define the lexicographic order on N × N as follows:
    for (m1 , n1 ), (m2 , n2 ) ∈ N × N, we say that (m1 , n1 ) ≤ (m2 , n2 ) if either
    m1 < m2 or m1 = m2 and n1 ≤ n2 . Then, (N × N, ≤) is a well-ordered
    set.
   • We can similarly define the lexicographic order on Nk for any finite k ∈ N,
     which makes (Nk , ≤) a well-ordered set as well.

      subset B = {(2, 1, 1, . . .) > (1, 2, 1, . . .) > . . .}. Then, B has no minimal
      element.
   The lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered. In fact, no one has found
an explicit well-order on NN so far. However, it turns out that in theory, one
can find a partial order on NN so that it is well-ordered.

Proposition 2.23. Let (X, u) be an ultrametric space. Then,
  1. If r > 0 and x, y ∈ X with u(x, y) < r, then Br (x) = Br (y).
  2. Any two open balls are either disjoint or one contains the other.
  3. Every triangle is isosceles, i.e., if x, y, z ∈ X, then at least two of the
     distances u(x, y), u(y, z), and u(z, x) are equal, and the third is less than
     or equal to the common value.

occurrences.quote:
Theorem 2.27 (Finite dendrograms and ultrametrics are equivalent). Let X
be a finite set. Let D(X) be the set of dendrograms on X and U(X) be the set
of ultrametrics on X. There are two maps between D(X) and U(X) as follows:
  1. (From dendrogram to ultrametric) Given a dendrogram θ on X, define

      u(x, y) := inf{t ≥ 0 : x, y belong to the same block in θ(t)}    (x, y ∈ X).

      Then u is an ultrametric on X.
  2. (From ultrametric to dendrogram) Given an ultrametric u on X set, we
     define an equivalence relation ∼t for t ≥ 0,

                                x ∼t y ⇐⇒ u(x, y) ≤ t.

      Then we define θ by θ(t) := {[x]t : x ∈ X} where [x]t is the equivalence
      class of x under ∼t . This gives a dendrogram on X.
The above two maps, denoted by D : D(X) → U (X) and U : U(X) → D(X)
respectively, are inverses of each other.

Definition 3.41. Let (X, τX ) and (Y, τY ) be topological spaces. The product
topology on the product space X × Y is the topology generated by the basis
consisting of all products of open sets:

                        BX×Y = {U × V : U ∈ τX , V ∈ τY }.

Check: B is a basis. Note X × Y ∈ B so every point (x, y) ∈ X × Y lies in some
basis element.
   For U1 × V1 , U2 × V2 ∈ B, we have U1 ∩ U2 ∈ τX and V1 ∩ V2 ∈ τY , so

               (U1 × V1 ) ∩ (U2 × V2 ) = (U1 ∩ U2 ) × (V1 ∩ V2 ) ∈ B.



   Question: is B a topology? No, the union of basis elements is not necessarily
a basis element.
   It turns out that smaller bases can also generate the product topology.

Example 3.74 (Continuous bijection not a homeomorphism). Let

                                     X = [0, 1)

with the usual topology from R, and

                      Y = S 1 = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : x2 + y 2 = 1}

with the subspace topology from R2 .
   Define

Then f is a continuous bijection. However, f −1 is not continuous: around
(1, 0) ∈ S 1 , neighborhoods correspond to t near 0 and near 1, which are far
apart in [0, 1), so f −1 fails continuity there.

domain is not compact.

Example 3.96. One can obtain a torus and a sphere via gluing/equivalence
relations.




  Figure 2: A torus and a sphere, illustrating the concept of quotient spaces.


    How can we get a topology on X ∗ from the topology on X? Recall that
the product topology can be characterized via some continuous maps. Maybe
we can do something similar here. A very natural map is the quotient map
p : X → X ∗ sending each point to its equivalence class.
    We of course want p to be continuous. That means we want a set of open
sets on X ∗ so that the preimage of each open set is open in X. We want to
make this topology as coarse as possible.

Definition 3.110. Let f and g be continuous maps from a topological space
X to a topological space Y . We say that f and g are homotopic if there exists a
continuous map H : X ×[0, 1] → Y such that H(x, 0) = f (x) and H(x, 1) = g(x)
for all x ∈ X. H is called a homotopy between f and g. We write f ≃ g to
indicate that f and g are homotopic.

Definition 4.12. A set Λ is a directed set if it is a non-empty set with a relation
≤ such that
   • reflexive: for all λ ∈ Λ, λ ≤ λ,
   • transitive: for all λ1 , λ2 , λ3 ∈ Λ, if λ1 ≤ λ2 and λ2 ≤ λ3 , then λ1 ≤ λ3 ,

shows that xU → x.

   1. For A ⊆ X and x ∈ X, if there is a sequence (an ) ⊆ A with an → x,

      for all sequences (xn ) in X implies that f is continuous at x.
