Example 6.35 (Compact but not sequentially compact). Let X = {0, 1}[0,1]
with the product topology. By Tychonoff, X is compact. For each n ∈ N
define fn ∈ X by fn (r) = the n-th binary digit of r (choose the expansion not
ending in all 1’s). Take any subsequence (fnk ). If it converges, we know that for
any r ∈ [0, 1], the sequence (fnk (r)) must converge in [0, 1]. Choose r ∈ [0, 1]
whose binary expansion has digit nk equal to 0 if k is odd and 1 if k is even
(this is possible since we prescribe digits only on the positions {nk }). Then
fnk (r) = 0, 1, 0, 1, . . . does not converge. Therefore (fnk ) cannot converge in the
product topology. Hence no subsequence of (fn ) converges; X is not sequentially
compact.

Example 6.53. RN is not locally compact. For any x ∈ RN , pick any basic
open neighborhood U = U1 × U2 × · · · × Un × R × R × · · · . Suppose there
exists some compact set K such that U ⊂ K. Consider the projection map
πn+1 : RN → R defined by πn+1 ((xi )) = xn+1 . Then, πn+1 (U ) = R and hence
πn+1 (K) ⊃ πn+1 (U ) = R. However, the continuous image of a compact set is
compact and R is not compact. This is a contradiction. Therefore, there does
not exist any compact set K such that U ⊂ K and hence RN is not locally
compact.

Definition 6.67. Let U = {Uα }α∈A be an open cover of a topological space X.
A partition of unity subordinated to U is a collection of continuous functions
{φα : X → [0, 1]}α∈A such that:
   • supp ϕα ⊂ Uα ; here the support of a function f : X → R is defined as
     supp f = {x ∈ X : f (x) ̸= 0}
   • {supp φα } is locally finite; and
   • For every x ∈ X, α∈A φα (x) = 1.

Definition 7.25. Let X be a topological space. We define an equivalence
relation on X by declaring x ∼ y iff there exists a connected subspace of X
containing both x and y. The equivalence classes of this relation are called the
components of X.
    We define another equivalence relation on X by declaring x ≈ y iff there
exists a path in X connecting x and y. The equivalence classes of this relation
are called the path components of X.
   Symmetry and relexivity are clear. For transitivity, if x, y lie in a connected
subspace A and y, z lie in a connected subspace B, then x, z lie in the connected
subspace A ∪ B (since y ∈ A ∩ B).

Set calculus A set A is a subset of a set B if every element of A is also an
element of B. We write A ⊆ B to denote that A is a subset of B. If A is a
subset of B but not equal to B, we say that A is a proper subset of B and denote
it by A ⊊ B.
    We let P(A) denote the power set of A, which is the set of all subsets of A.
    We say two sets A and B are equal if they have the same elements, that is,
if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. We write A = B to denote that A and B are equal.
    We let A\B denote the set difference of A and B, which is the set of elements
in A that are not in B. Formally, A\B = {x ∈ A : x ∈    / B}. When B ⊆ A, we
say A\B is the complement of B in A.
    The empty set, denoted ∅, is a set that contains no elements. It is a subset
of every set.

occurrences.originalNumber: Unnumbered: Equality and comparison of cardinality
occurrences.quote:
For any two sets A and B, we say they have the same cardinality if there exists
a bijection f : A → B. Intuitively, this means that the sets “have the same
number of elements”.
    Having the same cardinality is an equivalence relation on the class of all sets.
    We write |A| = |B| to denote that the sets A and B have the same cardinality.
    We say A has cardinality less than or equal to B (or B has cardinality greater
than or equal to A), denoted |A| ≤ |B| or |B| ≥ |A|, if there exists an injection
f : A → B.

occurrences.quote:
For real functions f : R → R, we have the notion of continuity using ε-δ defini-
tion: a function f : R → R is continuous at a point x0 ∈ R if for every ε > 0
there exists δ > 0 such that

                    |f (x) − f (x0 )| < ε   whenever |x − x0 | < δ.

We also have the notion of continuity using sequences: a function f : R → R is
continuous at a point x0 ∈ R if for every sequence (xn ) in R converging to x0 ,
the sequence (f (xn )) converges to f (x0 ).

(1) ⇒ (2) If A is countably finite, then there exists a bijection and hence surjection
          f : N → A. If A is finite, then the composition is what we need: N →
          {1, . . . , n} → A.

          g : A → N by g(a) = min{n ∈ N : f (n) = a} for all a ∈ A.
(3) ⇒ (1) If there exists an injection g : A → N, then we can decompose this as
          A → im(g) → N. If im(g) is finite, then A is finite. If im(g) is infinite,
          then by the lemma above, im(g) is countably infinite and hence so is A.

M = {M ⊆ A×B | each a ∈ A appears in at most one pair of M, and each b ∈ B appears in at most one}.
We partially order M by inclusion. If {Mi }i∈I is a chain in M, then

is again a matching, since no element of A or B can be matched to more than
one partner within a chain. Thus every chain has an upper bound.
    By Zorn’s Lemma, M has a maximal element M ∗ .
    Suppose there exist a ∈ A and b ∈ B both unmatched in M ∗ . Then
                               M ′ = M ∗ ∪ {(a, b)}
is a matching strictly larger than M ∗ , contradicting maximality. Therefore, at
least one side is fully matched: either every a ∈ A is matched, or every b ∈ B is
matched.
   • If every a ∈ A is matched, define f : A → B by f (a) = b whenever
     (a, b) ∈ M ∗ . This f is injective, so |A| ≤ |B|.
   • Otherwise, every b ∈ B is matched. Define g : B → A by g(b) = a
     whenever (a, b) ∈ M ∗ . Then g is injective, so |B| ≤ |A|.

   Thus, for any sets A and B, either |A| ≤ |B| or |B| ≤ |A|.

occurrences.quote:
Proof of Theorem 2.20. Suppose that f is continuous. Let x ∈ A. By the
lemma, there exists a sequence (xn ) in A converging to x. By continuity, (f (xn ))
converges to f (x). Since each f (xn ) ∈ f (A), by the lemma again, we have
f (x) ∈ f (A). Thus, f (A) ⊆ f (A).
    Conversely, suppose that f (A) ⊆ f (A) for every set A ⊆ X. Let x0 ∈ X
and let (xn ) be a sequence converging to x0 . Assume on the contrary that
(f (xn )) does not converge to f (x0 ). Then, there exists ε > 0 such that there is
a subsequence (f (xkn )) such that dY (f (xkn ), f (x0 )) ≥ ε for all n ∈ N.
    Now we let A = {xkn : n ∈ N}. Then, x0 ∈ A. Thus, f (x0 ) ∈ f (A) ⊆ f (A).
By the lemma, there exists a sequence (yn ) in f (A) converging to f (x0 ). But
this is not possible due to the ϵ constraint. Therefore, we conclude that (f (xn ))
must converge to f (x0 ).
    We now see that many intuitive properties of continuous real functions can
be generalized nicely to metric spaces. We will see that the open and closed
language still works well in the more general setting of topological spaces, while
the sequential language does not. In Willard’s book, a whole chapter is devoted
to the study of sequences in topological spaces.

   Now, for any set X with more than two elements, the trivial topology is not
metrizable since singletons are not closed.

Proof. Pick any U × V from the basis for the product topology. Now, for any
(x, y) ∈ U × V , we have that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Since B and B ′ are bases, there
exist Ux ∈ B and Vy ∈ B ′ such that x ∈ Ux ⊆ U and y ∈ Vy ⊆ V . Hence,
(x, y) ∈ Ux × Vy ⊆ U × V . This implies that the topology generated by B × B ′ is
finer than the product topology. On the other hand, since B × B ′ is a subset of
the basis for the product topology, the topology generated by B × B ′ is coarser
than the product topology. Therefore, they must be the same.

                           A \ E = A \ (F ∩ A) = A ∩ (X \ F ),
      where X \ F is open in X. Hence, A \ E is open in A, so E is closed in
      A.

connected. This is a contradiction.

Proof that p is closed. Let F ⊂ [0, 2π] be closed. We show p(F ) is closed in S 1 .
Since S 1 ⊂ R2 is a metric space, it suffices to use sequences.
   Take any sequence (yn ) ⊂ p(F ) with yn → y ∈ S 1 . For each n choose tn ∈ F
such that p(tn ) = yn . The sequence (tn ) lies in the bounded interval [0, 2π],
so by Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence tnk → t ∈ [0, 2π].
Because F is closed and each tnk ∈ F , we have t ∈ F . By continuity of p,

                                  p(tnk ) −→ p(t).

But p(tnk ) = ynk → y, hence y = p(t) ∈ p(F ). Thus every limit of a convergent
sequence in p(F ) lies in p(F ); so p(F ) is closed in S 1 .
    Therefore p sends closed subsets of [0, 2π] to closed subsets of S 1 , i.e. p is a
closed map. Since p is surjective and continuous, it is a quotient map.
   In this way, we can identify S 1 with the quotient space obtained by attaching
end points of an interval [0, 2π]/(0 ∼ 2π).

Proof. If X is contractible pick x0 ∈ X and set Y = {x0 }. Let j : Y ,→ X be
inclusion and c : X → Y the constant map. Then c◦j = idY and j ◦c = c ≃ idX ,

homotopy from idX to a constant map, so X is contractible.

d(xn , x) < ϵ for all n ≥ N . Hence, (xn ) converges to x in the metric sense.

Proof. Let B = {Bn : n ∈ N} be a countable basis of X.
   • Let U be an open cover of X. For each Bn , choose Un ∈ U such that
     Bn ⊆ Un if such Un exists (when exists, there could be multiple such Un ,
     and we just choose one). Then {Un : n ∈ N, Bn ⊆ Un } is a countable
     collection. We claim that it covers X. For any x ∈ X, there exists U ∈ U
     such that x ∈ U . Since B is a basis, there exists some Bm such that
     x ∈ Bm ⊆ U . By construction, there exists Um ∈ U such that Bm ⊆ Um .

   • For each Bn , choose xn ∈ Bn . Then A = {xn : n ∈ N, xn is chosen from Bn }

     any basis element Bn containing x, we have Bn ∩ A ̸= ∅. Hence x ∈ A.

Proof. When X is Hausdorff, suppose that a sequence (xn ) converges to both
x and y with x ̸= y. Since X is Hausdorff, there exist disjoint open sets U and
V such that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Since (xn ) → x, there exists N1 such that for all
n ≥ N1 , we have xn ∈ U . Similarly, since (xn ) → y, there exists N2 such that
for all n ≥ N2 , we have xn ∈ V . Let N = max{N1 , N2 }. Then, for all n ≥ N ,
we have xn ∈ U and xn ∈ V , contradicting the fact that U and V are disjoint.
Hence, the limit is unique.

Proof. We prove the regular case. The normal case is similar.
   Suppose X is regular. Let U be a neighbourhood of x. Then, X \ U is closed
and disjoint from {x}. By regularity, there exist disjoint open sets V and W
such that x ∈ V and X \ U ⊆ W . Since V ∩ W = ∅, we have that V ⊂ X \ W
which is closed. Then, V ⊆ X \ W ⊆ U . Hence, we have found a neighbourhood
V of x such that x ∈ V ⊆ V ⊆ U .
   Conversely, let U = X \ B, where B is a closed set disjoint from {x}. By
assumption, there exists a neighbourhood V of x such that x ∈ V ⊆ V ⊆ U .
So x ∈ V and X \ V ⊃ X \ U = B are disjoint open sets separating x and B.
Hence, X is regular.

Proof of Theorem 5.38. We reindex the functions in the lemma above as {fn :
n ∈ N}. Define a map F : X → [0, 1]N by F (x) = (f1 (x), f2 (x), . . .).
    Since each fn is continuous, F is continuous when [0, 1]N is equipped with
the product topology (cf. Theorem 3.91).
    We claim that F is an embedding. To see this, we first show that F is
injective. If x, y ∈ X with x ̸= y, then there exists a neighborhood U of x such
that y ∈/ U . By the lemma, there exists n such that fn (x) > 0 and fn |U c ≡ 0.
Hence, fn (y) = 0 ̸= fn (x), which shows that F (x) ̸= F (y).
    Next, we show that F is a homeomorphism onto its image. Since we already
showed that F is continuous and injective, it suffices to show that F (U ) is open
in F (X) for any open set U .
    Let x be any point in U and hence f (x) is an arbitrary point in F (U ). By
the construction of {fn }, there exists n such that fn (x) > 0 and fn |U c ≡ 0.
Let πn : [0, 1]N → [0, 1] be the projection onto the n-th coordinate. Then,
πn−1 ((fn (x)/2, 1]) ∩ F (X) is an open neighborhood of F (x) in F (X) and

   πn−1 ((fn (x)/2, 1]) ∩ F (X) = F ({y ∈ X : fn (y) > fn (x)/2 > 0}) ⊆ F (U ).

This shows that F (U ) is open in F (X).
   Now, we recall that [0, 1]N with the product topology is metrizable (Home-
work). Hence, F (X) is metrizable as a subspace of a metric space. Since F is
an embedding, X is metrizable.

Proof. Let U be an open cover of [a, b] where a < b. Define

        S = {x ∈ [a, b] : [a, x] can be covered by a finite subcover of U}.

It is clear that a ∈ S and if x ∈ S, then [a, x] ⊂ S. Since S is clearly upper-
bounded by b, we let c = sup S, i.e., the least upper bound of S. We will show
that c ∈ S and c = b.
     Clearly c ≤ b. If (a, c) is empty, then a = c ∈ S. Suppose (a, c) is nonempty.
Then, we have that [a, c) ⊂ S. Let Uc be an open set in U containing c. By the
definition of the order topology, there exists some (d, e) such that c ∈ (d, e) ⊆ Uc .
There must be some x ∈ (d, c) otherwise sup S ≤ d < c. Then, we know x ∈ S
and hence [a, x] can be covered by a finite subcover Ux of U. Note that Ux ∪{Uc }
is a finite subcover of [a, c]. This implies that c ∈ S.
     Suppose c < b. Now we consider the interval (c, b). Let T = {x ∈ [c, b] :
[c, x] = {c}} and let y = sup T . Note that y ≤ b. If y = c, then the open set
Uc containing c also contains some element z of (c, b), and hence [x, z] can be
covered by a finite subcover, which contradicts the definition of c. Therefore,
we must have y > c. But then the interval [a, y] can be covered by a finite
subcover of U by considering an open set around y, contradicting the definition
of c. Hence, we must have c = b.
     Therefore, we have shown that every open cover U of [a, b] has a finite sub-
cover. This completes the proof.

Proof. Given ϵ > 0, for each x ∈ X, by continuity of f at x, there exists
δx > 0 such that for all y ∈ X, if dX (x, y) < δx , then dY (f (x), f (y)) < ϵ/2.
Then, {Bδx /2 (x) : x ∈ X} is an open cover of X. By compactness of X, there
exists a finite subcover {Bδxi /2 (xi ) : i = 1, 2, . . . , n}. Let δ = min{δxi /2 : i =
1, 2, . . . , n}. We will show that this δ works. Given any x1 , x2 ∈ X such that
dX (x1 , x2 ) < δ, there exists some i such that x1 ∈ Bδxi /2 (xi ). This implies
that dX (x1 , xi ) < δxi /2 and hence dX (x2 , xi ) ≤ dX (x2 , x1 ) + dX (x1 , xi ) <
δxi /2 + δxi /2 = δxi . Therefore, we have

   dY (f (x1 ), f (x2 )) ≤ dY (f (x1 ), f (xi )) + dY (f (xi ), f (x2 )) < ϵ/2 + ϵ/2 = ϵ.

sequential compactness, there exists a convergent subsequence (xnk ) converging
to some x ∈ X. Since (xn ) is Cauchy, it must converge to the same limit x
(exercise). Hence, X is complete. For total boundedness, suppose not. Then,
there exists ϵ > 0 such that for any finite set F ⊂ X, there exists some x ∈ X
such that d(x, y) ≥ ϵ for all y ∈ F . In this way, we can construct a sequence (xn )
in X such that d(xn , xm ) ≥ ϵ for all n ̸= m. This sequence has no convergent
subsequence, contradicting the sequential compactness of X. Hence, X is totally
bounded.

open cover of X. Suppose there is no finite subcover.

We build inductively a sequence (xn ) with (i) xn ∈ Fn , (ii) no finite subfamily

a finite subcover. Induction: having chosen xn−1 , consider those y ∈ Fn with
B2−(n−1) (xn−1 ) ∩ B2−n (y) ̸= ∅. If each such ball had a finite subcover, finitely

    (1) ⇒ (3): Assume X is compact. Let (xn ) be any sequence in X. If
{xn : n ∈ N} is finite, then there exists some x ∈ X such that xn = x for
infinitely many n. Hence, the constant subsequence converges to x. Now assume
that {xn : n ∈ N} is infinite. Let A = {xn : n ∈ N}. Suppose that (xn ) has
no convergent subsequence. Then, for any x ∈ X \ A, there exists an open
neighbourhood Ux of x such that Ux ∩ A = ∅. This implies that A is closed
and hence compact. For any a ∈ A, since no subsequence of (xn ) converges to
a, there exists an open neighbourhood Va of a such that Va ∩ A = {a}. Then,
{Va } is an infinite open cover of A with no finite subcover, contradicting the
compactness of A. Therefore, (xn ) has a convergent subsequence.

in X \ U . Hence, it is eventually in U . Therefore, {xλ } converges to x.

Sketch of proof. Let (xλ ) be a net in a set X. We call Q ⊂ P (X) a admissible
family if

   • for any A1 , A2 ∈ Q, we have ∅ ̸= A1 ∩ A2 ∈ Q;
   • for any A ∈ Q, the net (xλ ) is frequently in A (for any λ0 , there exists
     some λ ≥ λ0 such that xλ ∈ A).
Let Q denote the collection of all admissible families and we partially order Q
by inclusion. Using Zorn’s lemma, we can show that Q has a maximal element
Qmax . You can show that if A ⊂ X, then either A ∈ Qmax or X \ A ∈ Qmax .
Now, we define a directed set Γ = {(λ, A) : λ ∈ Λ, A ∈ Qmax , s.t. xλ ∈ A} with
the order defined by (λ1 , A1 ) ≤ (λ2 , A2 ) if λ1 ≤ λ2 and A2 ⊆ A1 . Then, let
φ : Γ → Λ be defined by (λ, A) 7→ λ. This defines a subnet and you can check
that this subnet is indeed an ultranet.

Proof. Assume that Y has a separation A, B. Pick a ∈ A and b ∈ B with a < b.
Then, [a, b] ⊂ Y . Let A0 = A ∩ [a, b] and B0 = B ∩ [a, b]. Then, A0 , B0 are open
in [a, b] w.r.t. the subspace topology which is the same as the order topology
on [a, b]. So A0 , B0 form a separation of [a, b].
     Let c = sup A0 . We show that c ∈    / A0 and c ∈  / B0 , contradicting that
[a, b] = A0 ∪ B0 .
     Suppose c ∈ B0 . Then, c ̸= a, so c = b or a < c < b. Since B0 is open, in
either case, there exists d such that (d, c] ⊂ B0 . If c = b, then d is an upper
bound of A0 less than c, contradicting that c = sup A0 . If a < c < b, then since
c is an upper bound, (c, b] ∩ A0 = ∅. Hence, (d, b] = (d, c] ∪ (c, b] ∩ A0 = ∅ which
makes d an upper bound of A0 less than c, again a contradiction. Thus, c ∈     / B0 .
     Now suppose c ∈ A0 . Then, c ̸= b, and so c = a or a < c < b. Since A0 is
open, in either case, there exists e such that [c, e) ⊂ A0 . But then any z such
that c < z < e is in A0 , contradicting that c = sup A0 (z exists because of (2)).
Thus, c ∈ / A0 .
   Now we can prove the intermediate value theorem.

that the components of X are singletons. Let x, y ∈ X be distinct points. Let
r = u(x, y) > 0. Then, Br (x) is an open neighborhood of x. I claim that
X \ Br (x) is an open neighborhood of y. Indeed, for any point z ∈ X \ Br (x),
we have u(x, z) ≥ r > 0. Pick r0 ∈ (0, r). Then, for any z ′ ∈ Br0 (z), we have
that u(x, z ′ ) = u(x, z) ≥ r. Hence z ′ ∈
                                         / Br (x) and thus Br0 (z) ⊆ X \ Br (x).
This shows that X \ Br (x) is open and hence an open neighborhood of y. This
implies that x and y lie in different components. Since x, y ∈ X are arbitrary,
we conclude that the components of X are singletons.

Example 4.5. Let X = R be endowed with the countable complement topology:
a set U ⊆ X is open iff X \ U is countable or U = ∅.
   • Any sequence (xn ) converging to x is eventually equal to x. Indeed, we
     let B = {xn : xn ̸= x} and hence U = X \ B is an open neighborhood of
     x. Then, there exists N such that xn ∈ U for all n ≥ N , i.e., xn ∈
                                                                       / B for
     all n ≥ N . This means that xn = x for all n ≥ N .
   • The closed sets are exactly the countable sets and X itself. Hence, if
     A ⊊ X is uncountable, then A = X.

   Thus [0, 1] = R, but there is no sequence in [0, 1] converging to 2.

   Let’s see another example.

By the theorem above, we know that Rℓ ×Rℓ is regular. But it is not normal.
Indeed, L = {(x, −x) : x ∈ R} is closed in R2 and hence closed in Rℓ × Rℓ . Note
{(a, −a)} = L ∩ [a, a + 1) × [−a, −a + 1) and hence {(a, −a)} is open in L. So L
has the discrete topology. So every subset of L is closed in subspace topology
and hence closed in Rℓ × Rℓ .
   Now let A = {(x, −x) : x ∈ Q} and B = L \ A. Both are closed in Rℓ × Rℓ .
One can check that there are no disjoint open sets separating A and B (see
Munkres Chapter 4 section 31 problem 9). So Rℓ × Rℓ is not normal.
   There is still a positive result about subspaces of normal spaces.

Example 6.35 (Compact but not sequentially compact). Let X = {0, 1}[0,1]
with the product topology. By Tychonoff, X is compact. For each n ∈ N
define fn ∈ X by fn (r) = the n-th binary digit of r (choose the expansion not
ending in all 1’s). Take any subsequence (fnk ). If it converges, we know that for
any r ∈ [0, 1], the sequence (fnk (r)) must converge in [0, 1]. Choose r ∈ [0, 1]
whose binary expansion has digit nk equal to 0 if k is odd and 1 if k is even
(this is possible since we prescribe digits only on the positions {nk }). Then
fnk (r) = 0, 1, 0, 1, . . . does not converge. Therefore (fnk ) cannot converge in the
product topology. Hence no subsequence of (fn ) converges; X is not sequentially
compact.

Theorem 1.20 (Partitions and equivalence relations). Let A be a nonempty set.
There is a one-to-one correspondence between partitions of A and equivalence
relations on A:
   • Define f : Part(A) → EqRel(A) by sending a partition {Ai }i∈I to the
     equivalence relation ∼ on A defined by a ∼ b if and only if ∃i ∈ I with
     a, b ∈ Ai .
   • Conversely, define g : EqRel(A) → Part(A) by sending an equivalence
     relation ∼ on A to the family of equivalence classes
                                                 {[a] : a ∈ A}
      which is a partition of A.
Then, f and g are bijections and they are inverse to each other, i.e.,
                        g ◦ f = idPart(A) ,            f ◦ g = idEqRel(A) .

Definition 1.21. A relation R on A is a partial order if it is reflexive, antisym-
metric, and transitive. A partial order is usually denoted by ≤. A set equipped
with a partial order is called a partially ordered set or poset, and is denoted by
(A, ≤). When a ≤ b and a ̸= b, we write a < b.

edges.note: The printed passage uses “relation”. Mapping that term to Definition 1.10 is an editorial definition-use reading, pending teacher review.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Example 1.22. Consider the set of real numbers R with the usual order relation
≤. This is a partial order because it is reflexive (every number is less than or
equal to itself), antisymmetric (if a ≤ b and b ≤ a, then a = b), and transitive
(if a ≤ b and b ≤ c, then a ≤ c).
    Just a funny note: we humans know that 0.9 > 0.11 but somehow many
LLMs think 0.9 < 0.11. So be careful when using AIs in your studies :)

Example 1.35.         • We define the lexicographic order on N × N as follows:
    for (m1 , n1 ), (m2 , n2 ) ∈ N × N, we say that (m1 , n1 ) ≤ (m2 , n2 ) if either
    m1 < m2 or m1 = m2 and n1 ≤ n2 . Then, (N × N, ≤) is a well-ordered
    set.
   • We can similarly define the lexicographic order on Nk for any finite k ∈ N,
     which makes (Nk , ≤) a well-ordered set as well.
   • However, the lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered: consider the
      subset B = {(2, 1, 1, . . .) > (1, 2, 1, . . .) > . . .}. Then, B has no minimal
      element.
   The lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered. In fact, no one has found
an explicit well-order on NN so far. However, it turns out that in theory, one
can find a partial order on NN so that it is well-ordered.

Definition 2.1 (Metric Space). A metric space is a pair (X, d) consisting of a
set X and a function d : X × X → [0, ∞) called a metric such that
    1. d(x, y) = 0 if and only if x = y;
    2. d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x, y ∈ X (symmetry);
    3. d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all x, y, z ∈ X (triangle inequality).
The value d(x, y) is called the distance between points x and y in the metric
space.
   If (X, d) satisfies 2 and 3 and 1’ below, it is called a pseudometric space.
   1’. d(x, x) = 0 for all x ∈ X.

Theorem 2.27 (Finite dendrograms and ultrametrics are equivalent). Let X
be a finite set. Let D(X) be the set of dendrograms on X and U(X) be the set
of ultrametrics on X. There are two maps between D(X) and U(X) as follows:
  1. (From dendrogram to ultrametric) Given a dendrogram θ on X, define

      u(x, y) := inf{t ≥ 0 : x, y belong to the same block in θ(t)}    (x, y ∈ X).

      Then u is an ultrametric on X.
  2. (From ultrametric to dendrogram) Given an ultrametric u on X set, we
     define an equivalence relation ∼t for t ≥ 0,

                                x ∼t y ⇐⇒ u(x, y) ≤ t.

      Then we define θ by θ(t) := {[x]t : x ∈ X} where [x]t is the equivalence
      class of x under ∼t . This gives a dendrogram on X.
The above two maps, denoted by D : D(X) → U (X) and U : U(X) → D(X)
respectively, are inverses of each other.

Definition 3.26 (Closure Operation). Let X be a set and let

                                · : P(X) → P(X)

be a map. It is called a closure operation if for all A, B ⊂ X:

  (i) ∅ = ∅,
 (ii) A ⊂ A,
(iii) If D = A, then D = D,
 (iv) A ∪ B = A ∪ B.

   We now show that the closure operation and the topology we defined pre-
viously give rise to equivalent structures on a set. To this end, we identify the
notion of a closed set in a topological space first.

Definition 3.41. Let (X, τX ) and (Y, τY ) be topological spaces. The product
topology on the product space X × Y is the topology generated by the basis
consisting of all products of open sets:

                        BX×Y = {U × V : U ∈ τX , V ∈ τY }.

Check: B is a basis. Note X × Y ∈ B so every point (x, y) ∈ X × Y lies in some
basis element.
   For U1 × V1 , U2 × V2 ∈ B, we have U1 ∩ U2 ∈ τX and V1 ∩ V2 ∈ τY , so

               (U1 × V1 ) ∩ (U2 × V2 ) = (U1 ∩ U2 ) × (V1 ∩ V2 ) ∈ B.



   Question: is B a topology? No, the union of basis elements is not necessarily
a basis element.
   It turns out that smaller bases can also generate the product topology.

Example 3.43. Let X = Y = R with the standard topology. Then, B =
{(a, b) : a < b} is a basis for R. Hence, B × B = {(a, b) × (c, d) : a < b, c < d}
is a basis for the product topology on R2 . Note that (a, b) × (c, d) is an axis-
aligned open rectangle in R2 . Previously, we showed that this generates the same
topology as the one generated by open balls in R2 . So the product topology on
R2 is the same as the standard metric topology on R2 .

any finite n. But things will be a bit different for infinite products. We will
discuss this later.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Remark 3.52. The order and subspace topologies on a subset of a linearly or-
dered set need not agree. For instance, let Y = [0, 1)∪{2} ⊂ R with the induced
order. In the subspace topology, {2} is open in Y since {2} = (2 − 12 , 2 + 12 ) ∩ Y .
But in the order topology on Y , any basis element containing 2 is of the form
(a, 2]Y = {y ∈ Y : a < y ≤ 2} where a ∈ Y (because 2 is the greatest element of
Y ), so it contains points of Y strictly less than 2; hence {2} is not open there.

Definition 3.55. A function f : (X, τX ) → (Y, τY ) between topological spaces
is called continuous at a given point x ∈ X if for every neighbourhood V of
f (x) in Y , there exists a neighbourhood U of x in X such that f (U ) ⊆ V . We
say that f is continuous if it is continuous at every point x ∈ X.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Theorem 3.57. Let X and Y be topological spaces and let f : X → Y be a
function. The following are equivalent:
  1. f is continuous.
  2. For all open sets H in Y , f −1 (H) is open in X.

  3. For all closed sets C in Y , f −1 (C) is closed in X.
  4. For all A ⊂ X, f (A) ⊆ f (A) (This can be thought of as the Kuratowski
     definition of continuity).

Example 3.63. Let X × Y be endowed with the product topology. Then,
πX : X × Y → X and πY : X × Y → Y are continuous.
                                            −1
   Note that for any open set U in X, πX       (U ) = U × Y is open in X × Y .
                                      −1
Similarly, for any open set V in Y , πY (V ) = X × V is open in X × Y .
   Note also that the product topology τX×Y is the smallest topology on X × Y
such that both πX and πY are continuous: any topology on X × Y that makes
both πX and πY continuous must contain a basis for τX×Y : sets of the form
U × Y and X × V for all open sets U in X and V in Y .

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Theorem 3.64.       1. (Constant function) If f : X → Y maps all of X to a
    single point y0 ∈ Y , then f is continuous.
  2. (Inclusion) If A is a subspace of X, the inclusion map i : A → X defined
     by i(a) = a is continuous.
  3. (Composition) If f : X → Y and g : Y → Z are continuous, then the
     composition g ◦ f : X → Z is continuous.
  4. (Restricting the domain) If f : X → Y is continuous and A ⊆ X, then
     the restriction f |A : A → Y defined by f |A (a) = f (a) is continuous.
  5. (Restricting or expanding the range) Let f : X → Y be continuous. If
     f (X) ⊂ Z ⊂ Y , then the function g : X → Z obtained by restricting the
     range of f is continuous. If Y ⊂ W , then the function h : iY →W ◦ f :
     X → W is continuous.

  6. (Local formulation) f : X → Y is continuous if X = ∪Uα for a family of
     open sets Uα and each restriction f |Uα is continuous.
  7. (Pasting lemma) If X = A ∪ B with A, B closed, and f : A → Y , g : B →
     Y are continuous and agree on A ∩ B (i.e., f (x) = g(x) for all x ∈ A ∩ B),
     then the function h : X → Y defined by
                                     (
                                       f (x), x ∈ A
                              h(x) =
                                       g(x), x ∈ B

        is continuous.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Example 3.74 (Continuous bijection not a homeomorphism). Let

                                     X = [0, 1)

with the usual topology from R, and

                      Y = S 1 = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : x2 + y 2 = 1}

with the subspace topology from R2 .
   Define
                    f : X → Y, f (t) = (cos 2πt, sin 2πt).
Then f is a continuous bijection. However, f −1 is not continuous: around
(1, 0) ∈ S 1 , neighborhoods correspond to t near 0 and near 1, which are far
apart in [0, 1), so f −1 fails continuity there.
This shows that a continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism when the
domain is not compact.

Example 3.82. Let X = RN = n≥1 R. Then, the “diagonal” map f : R → X
defined by f (t) = (t, t, t, . . .) is not continuous when X is endowed with the box
topology. Consider the open set (−1, 1)×(−1/2, 1/2)×(−1/3, 1/3)×· · · . Then,

          f −1 ((−1, 1) × (−1/2, 1/2) × (−1/3, 1/3) × · · · )
           = f −1 ((−1, 1) × R × · · · ∩ R × (−1/2, 1/2) × R × · · · ∩ · · · )
             \
           =      f −1 (R × · · · × (−1/n, 1/n) × · · · )
               n≥1
               \
           =       (−1/n, 1/n) = {0}.
               n≥1


Then f −1 ((−1, 1) × (−1/2, 1/2) × (−1/3, 1/3) × · · · ) is not open in R. Hence,
f is not continuous.
    This example actually gives us a hint how we can make things right. The
problem above is that when considering the arbitrary intersection of open sets,
we don’t get an open set. SO, we want things to be finite in some sense. This
leads to the following definition.

(a2 , b2 ) × · · · containing 0, we have that ai < 0 < bi for all i. So pick any point
(x1 , x2 , . . .) with xi ∈ (0, bi ) for all i, then (x1 , x2 , . . .) ∈ A ∩ U . So, A ∩ U ̸= ∅.

metric d. Let an = (x1n , x2n , . . .) be a sequence in A converging to 0. Then,
construct B = {(−x11 , x11 ) × (−x22 , x22 ) × · · · }. Then, 0 ∈ B but an ∈            / B for
all n ∈ N. So there exists a ball Br (0) ⊆ B for some r > 0 containing no point
in the sequence an . This is a contradiction. So RN with the box topology is not
metrizable.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Example 3.96. One can obtain a torus and a sphere via gluing/equivalence
relations.




  Figure 2: A torus and a sphere, illustrating the concept of quotient spaces.


    How can we get a topology on X ∗ from the topology on X? Recall that
the product topology can be characterized via some continuous maps. Maybe
we can do something similar here. A very natural map is the quotient map
p : X → X ∗ sending each point to its equivalence class.
    We of course want p to be continuous. That means we want a set of open
sets on X ∗ so that the preimage of each open set is open in X. We want to
make this topology as coarse as possible.

Example 3.107. Consider the subspace

  X = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : xy = 1} ∪ {(0, 0)} ⊂ R2 ,           q : X −→ R, q(x, y) = x.

The map q is surjective: for x ̸= 0 choose y = 1/x, and q(0, 0) = 0. It is
continuous as the restriction of the projection π1 : R2 → R.
   However q is not a quotient map. Indeed {(0, 0)} = Bε (0, 0) ∩ X for small
ε > 0, so {(0, 0)} is open in X. Thus

                        q −1 ({0}) = {(0, 0)} is open in X,

but {0} is not open in R. Hence the “only if” direction fails and q is not a
quotient map.
   The following theorem is analogous to the universal property of product
topology.

Definition 3.110. Let f and g be continuous maps from a topological space
X to a topological space Y . We say that f and g are homotopic if there exists a
continuous map H : X ×[0, 1] → Y such that H(x, 0) = f (x) and H(x, 1) = g(x)
for all x ∈ X. H is called a homotopy between f and g. We write f ≃ g to
indicate that f and g are homotopic.

Example 3.113. More generally, if Y is a convex subset of some Rn and
f, g : X → Y are continuous, then

                         H(x, t) = (1 − t)f (x) + tg(x)

defines a homotopy f ≃ g. Thus any two maps into a convex (in particular,
contractible) space are homotopic. The target matters: regarded as maps S 1 →
D2 the identity and any constant map are homotopic, but as maps S 1 → S 1
they need not be. This is in fact quite nontrivial and we will return to it later.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Definition 4.12. A set Λ is a directed set if it is a non-empty set with a relation
≤ such that
   • reflexive: for all λ ∈ Λ, λ ≤ λ,
   • transitive: for all λ1 , λ2 , λ3 ∈ Λ, if λ1 ≤ λ2 and λ2 ≤ λ3 , then λ1 ≤ λ3 ,

   • directed: for all λ1 , λ2 ∈ Λ, there exists µ ∈ Λ such that λ1 ≤ µ and
     λ2 ≤ µ.
   This relation ≤ is called a direction on Λ.

edges.note: The printed passage uses “poset”. Mapping that term to Definition 1.21 is an editorial definition-use reading, pending teacher review.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Remark 4.13. Note a direction may not be a partial order, i.e., it may not be
antisymmetric. For example, let Λ = {a, b} with a ≤ b and b ≤ a. This is a
directed set but not a poset because a ̸= b.

Example 4.18. Let P denote the collection of all finite partitions of the closed
interval [a, b] into closed subintervals. In other words, each P ∈ P has the form
P = {[x0 , x1 ], [x1 , x2 ], . . . , [xn−1 , xn ]} where a = x0 < x1 < · · · < xn = b.
    This becomes a directed set if we define the direction by refinement: for two
partitions P1 , P2 ∈ P, we say that P1 ≤ P2 if P2 is a refinement of P1 (i.e., every
subinterval in P1 is a union of subintervals in P2 ).
    Now, consider a function f : [a, b] → R. Define a net (RL (P ))P ∈P as follows:
for each partition P = {[x0 , x1 ], [x1 , x2 ], . . . , [xn−1 , xn ]}, let
                                n
                                X
                    RL (P ) =             inf         f (x) · (xi − xi−1 ).
                                      x∈[xi−1 ,xi ]
                                i=1

This net is called the lower Riemann sum net of f .
   Similarly, we can define the upper Riemann sum net (RU (P ))P ∈P by
                                n
                                X
                    RU (P ) =             sup         f (x) · (xi − xi−1 ).
                                i=1 x∈[xi−1 ,xi ]

    If both nets converge to the same limit L, then we say that f is Riemann
integrable on [a, b] with integral L.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Example 4.19. One typical example of a net is the following: let X be a
topological space and x ∈ X. Let Λ be the set of all neighbourhoods of x
and define the direction on Λ by U ≤ V iff V ⊆ U (reverse inclusion). You
should check that this is indeed a directed set. Pick a point xU ∈ U for each
neighbourhood U of x. Then the net (xU )U ∈Λ converges to x. To see this, let
V be any neighbourhood of x, then for all U ≥ V , we have xU ∈ U ⊆ V . This
shows that xU → x.

Example 5.6. Let X = R. Then, the complement finite topology on X is not
first countable. To see this, suppose there is a countable basis of neighbourhoods
{Bn : n ∈ N} at some point x ∈ S    X. Since each Bn is open, we have X \ Bn
is finite for each n. Let E = x ∪ n∈N (X \ Bn ). Then, E is countable. Now,
pick any y ∈ R \ E and consider the open set U = X \ {y}. Note that U is a
neighbourhood of x. However, for any n, we have Bn ̸⊆ U since y ∈ Bn \ U .
This contradicts the assumption that {Bn : n ∈ N} is a basis at x. Hence, X is
not first countable.

Theorem 5.8. Let X be a topological space.

   1. For A ⊆ X and x ∈ X, if there is a sequence (an ) ⊆ A with an → x,
      then x ∈ A. If X is first countable, the converse holds: x ∈ A implies that
      there exists a sequence (an ) ⊆ A with an → x.
   2. If f : X → Y is continuous at x and xn → x in X, then f (xn ) → f (x) in
      Y . If X is first countable, the converse holds: xn → x ⇒ f (xn ) → f (x)
      for all sequences (xn ) in X implies that f is continuous at x.

     x ̸= 0, choose ε > 0 with (x − ε, x + ε) ∩ K = ∅; if x = 0, then (−ε, ε) \ K
     is an open neighbourhood of 0 disjoint from K. Hence R \ K is open.

   • It is not regular: 0 ∈
                          / K. Suppose there are disjoint open sets U, V with
     0 ∈ U and K ⊆ V . Choose a basis element (a, b) \ K ⊂ U containing 0.

                                                                      1
     with 1/n ∈ (c, d) ⊆ V . Finally, choose z so that z ∈ (max(c, n+1   ), 1/n).

Example 6.10. {1/n}n∈N ⊂ R is not compact: {{1/n}} is an open cover with
no finite subcover.
    However, {0} ∪ {1/n}n∈N ⊂ R is compact: given any open cover U , there
exists U ∈ U such that 0 ∈ U . Choose ε > 0 such that (−ε, ε) ⊂ U . Then,
only finitely many points of the set {1/n}n∈N are outside U . Choosing open
sets from U covering these finitely many points gives a finite subcover.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Example 6.35 (Compact but not sequentially compact). Let X = {0, 1}[0,1]
with the product topology. By Tychonoff, X is compact. For each n ∈ N
define fn ∈ X by fn (r) = the n-th binary digit of r (choose the expansion not
ending in all 1’s). Take any subsequence (fnk ). If it converges, we know that for
any r ∈ [0, 1], the sequence (fnk (r)) must converge in [0, 1]. Choose r ∈ [0, 1]
whose binary expansion has digit nk equal to 0 if k is odd and 1 if k is even
(this is possible since we prescribe digits only on the positions {nk }). Then
fnk (r) = 0, 1, 0, 1, . . . does not converge. Therefore (fnk ) cannot converge in the
product topology. Hence no subsequence of (fn ) converges; X is not sequentially
compact.

Example 6.36 (Sequentially compact but not compact). Let Y ⊂ {0, 1}[0,1]
be a subspace consisting of all functions f such that f (r) = 1 for at most
countably many r ∈ [0, 1]. We claim that Y is sequentially
                                                    S            compact but not

open neighbourhood U of x and every α0 ∈ A, there exists (not for all) α ≥ α0
such that xα ∈ U .
   One equivalent way to describe cluster points is via subnets.

Definition 6.38. A subnet of a net P : Λ → X is the composition P ◦ φ where
φ : Γ → Λ is an increasing function between directed sets Γ and Λ such that: For
every λ ∈ Λ, there exists γ ∈ Γ such that λ ≤ φ(γ). If we represent P as (xλ ),
then the subnet can be represented as (xλγ ) or (xφ(γ) ) (cf. the subsequence
notation (xnk )).

Definition 6.42. A net {xλ } in a set X is an ultranet if for any subset S ⊂ X,
the net is eventually in S or eventually in X \ S (there exists λ0 such that either
xλ ∈ S for all λ ≥ λ0 or xλ ∈ X \ S for all λ ≥ λ0 ).

Example T   6.49. The Cantor set C is compact as C is bounded and C is closed
since C = Cn where each Cn is closed.
    We can also see this using Tychonoff’s theorem. We know there is a bijection
between C and {0, 2}N : each x ∈ C can be written in base 3 using only digits
0 and 2, and this gives a bijection between C and {0, 2}N . It turns out that
this bijection is actually a homeomorphism. To see this, let’s actually give a
metric on {0, 2}N that induces the product topology. For any two sequences
(an ), (bn ) ∈ {0, 2}N , define
                                  (
                                    0    if an = bn for all n
                d((an ), (bn )) =      k
                                    1/3 where k = min{n : an ̸= bn }

We defined an ultrametric on C before. You can check that this metric on
{0, 2}N is actually the same as the ultrametric on C under the above bijection.
So the bijection is an isometry. The only thing left to check is that this metric
on {0, 2}N induces the product topology. This is left as an exercise. Therefore,
C is homeomorphic to {0, 2}N which is compact by Tychonoff’s theorem. Hence,
C is compact.

Example 6.52. R is locally compact. For each x ∈ R, we pick the open
neighbourhood U = (x − 1, x + 1) and the compact set K = [x − 1, x + 1] such
that U ⊂ K.
   Similarly, Rn is locally compact. For each x ∈ Rn , we pick the open neigh-
bourhood U = (x1 − 1, x1 + 1) × · · · × (xn − 1, xn + 1) and the compact set
K = [x1 − 1, x1 + 1] × · · · × [xn − 1, xn + 1] such that U ⊂ K.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Example 6.53. RN is not locally compact. For any x ∈ RN , pick any basic
open neighborhood U = U1 × U2 × · · · × Un × R × R × · · · . Suppose there
exists some compact set K such that U ⊂ K. Consider the projection map
πn+1 : RN → R defined by πn+1 ((xi )) = xn+1 . Then, πn+1 (U ) = R and hence
πn+1 (K) ⊃ πn+1 (U ) = R. However, the continuous image of a compact set is
compact and R is not compact. This is a contradiction. Therefore, there does
not exist any compact set K such that U ⊂ K and hence RN is not locally
compact.

Theorem 6.54. Let X be a topological space. Then, X is locally compact
Hausdorff iff there exists a compact Hausdorff space Y such that

   • X is a subspace of Y ;
   • Y \ X consists of a single point.
Such a space Y is called the one-point compactification of X and is unique up
to homeomorphism.

Definition 6.67. Let U = {Uα }α∈A be an open cover of a topological space X.
A partition of unity subordinated to U is a collection of continuous functions
{φα : X → [0, 1]}α∈A such that:
   • supp ϕα ⊂ Uα ; here the support of a function f : X → R is defined as
     supp f = {x ∈ X : f (x) ̸= 0}
   • {supp φα } is locally finite; and
   • For every x ∈ X, α∈A φα (x) = 1.
                        P

in R2 :                                          
                                    1
                     S=      x, sin     |x ∈ (0, 1]
                                    x
Note that
                            S = S ∪ {(0, y)|y ∈ [−1, 1]}.
This space is connected but not path connected.
     To see that it is connected, note that S is path connected (hence connected)
and hence S is connected.
     To see that it is not path connected, suppose there exists a path f : [a, b] → S
with f (a) = (0, 0) and f (b) = (1, sin 1). Consider A = f −1 (0 × [−1, 1]) ⊂
[a, b] which is the preimage of a closed set, hence closed. Let c = sup A ∈ A.
c ̸= b since f (b) = (1, sin 1). Then, f ((c, b]) ⊂ S. Replace [c, b] by [0, 1] for
convenience. We write f (t) = (x(t), y(t)). Then, x(0) = 0 and x(t) > 0 for all
                                                                           1
t ∈ (0, 1]. Since x is continuous, there exists tn → 0 with x(tn ) = nπ/2       for all
n ≥ 1 (intermediate value theorem). Then, y(tn ) = sin(nπ/2) = (−1)n does not
converge as n → ∞, contradicting the continuity of y at 0.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Definition 7.25. Let X be a topological space. We define an equivalence
relation on X by declaring x ∼ y iff there exists a connected subspace of X
containing both x and y. The equivalence classes of this relation are called the
components of X.
    We define another equivalence relation on X by declaring x ≈ y iff there
exists a path in X connecting x and y. The equivalence classes of this relation
are called the path components of X.
   Symmetry and relexivity are clear. For transitivity, if x, y lie in a connected
subspace A and y, z lie in a connected subspace B, then x, z lie in the connected
subspace A ∪ B (since y ∈ A ∩ B).

                    |f (x) − f (x0 )| < ε   whenever |x − x0 | < δ.

continuous at a point x0 ∈ R if for every sequence (xn ) in R converging to x0 ,
the sequence (f (xn )) converges to f (x0 ).

    f is injective: for m < n, f (n) ∈ C \ {f (1), . . . , f (n − 1)}, but f (m) is not
in the set. So, f (n) ̸= f (m).
    f is surjective: for any c ∈ C, there exists n ∈ N such that f (n) ≥ c. Let

c ∈

that f (m) = c.

edges.note: This is a proof or sketch printed for Theorem 1.66.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof. We prove the implications as follows:
(1) ⇒ (2) If A is countably finite, then there exists a bijection and hence surjection
          f : N → A. If A is finite, then the composition is what we need: N →
          {1, . . . , n} → A.
(2) ⇒ (3) If there exists a surjection f : N → A, then we can define an injection
          g : A → N by g(a) = min{n ∈ N : f (n) = a} for all a ∈ A.
(3) ⇒ (1) If there exists an injection g : A → N, then we can decompose this as
          A → im(g) → N. If im(g) is finite, then A is finite. If im(g) is infinite,
          then by the lemma above, im(g) is countably infinite and hence so is A.

is again a matching, since no element of A or B can be matched to more than
one partner within a chain. Thus every chain has an upper bound.

is a matching strictly larger than M ∗ , contradicting maximality. Therefore, at

and let (xn ) be a sequence converging to x0 . Assume on the contrary that

a subsequence (f (xkn )) such that dY (f (xkn ), f (x0 )) ≥ ε for all n ∈ N.

this is not possible due to the ϵ constraint. Therefore, we conclude that (f (xn ))
must converge to f (x0 ).

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof. Pick any U × V from the basis for the product topology. Now, for any
(x, y) ∈ U × V , we have that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Since B and B ′ are bases, there
exist Ux ∈ B and Vy ∈ B ′ such that x ∈ Ux ⊆ U and y ∈ Vy ⊆ V . Hence,
(x, y) ∈ Ux × Vy ⊆ U × V . This implies that the topology generated by B × B ′ is
finer than the product topology. On the other hand, since B × B ′ is a subset of
the basis for the product topology, the topology generated by B × B ′ is coarser
than the product topology. Therefore, they must be the same.

{U ×V : U ∈ BX , V ∈ BY } is a basis for the product topology on X ×Y . Hence,
the subspace topology of A × B has a basis

               BA×B = {(U × V ) ∩ (A × B) : U ∈ BX , V ∈ BY }.

   Then,

         BA×B = {(U ∩ A) × (V ∩ B) : U ∈ BX , V ∈ BY } = BA × BB .

This finishes the proof.

      A.

Proof. Suppose there exists a homeomorphism f : [0, 1) → (0, 1). Pick any
x0 = 0 and consider the map g : (0, 1) → (0, 1)\{f (x0 )} defined by g(x) = f (x).
By the previous lemma, g is a homeomorphism. Note that (0, 1) \ {f (x0 )} is
not connected regardless the value of f (x0 ). However, (0, 1) = [0, 1) \ {x0 } is
connected. This is a contradiction.

Proof that p is closed. Let F ⊂ [0, 2π] be closed. We show p(F ) is closed in S 1 .
Since S 1 ⊂ R2 is a metric space, it suffices to use sequences.
   Take any sequence (yn ) ⊂ p(F ) with yn → y ∈ S 1 . For each n choose tn ∈ F
such that p(tn ) = yn . The sequence (tn ) lies in the bounded interval [0, 2π],
so by Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence tnk → t ∈ [0, 2π].
Because F is closed and each tnk ∈ F , we have t ∈ F . By continuity of p,

                                  p(tnk ) −→ p(t).

But p(tnk ) = ynk → y, hence y = p(t) ∈ p(F ). Thus every limit of a convergent
sequence in p(F ) lies in p(F ); so p(F ) is closed in S 1 .
    Therefore p sends closed subsets of [0, 2π] to closed subsets of S 1 , i.e. p is a
closed map. Since p is surjective and continuous, it is a quotient map.
   In this way, we can identify S 1 with the quotient space obtained by attaching
end points of an interval [0, 2π]/(0 ∼ 2π).

the first lemma.

in the metric sense. For every neighborhood U of x, there exists ϵ > 0 such
that Bϵ (x) ⊆ U . Then, there exists N such that d(xn , x) < ϵ for all n ≥ N . In
particular, xn ∈ Bϵ (x) ⊂ U for all n ≥ N . So we have xn → x in the topological
sense.
    (⇐) Let (xn ) be a sequence in a metric space (X, d) converging to x ∈ X in
the topological sense. For every ϵ > 0, the open ball Bϵ (x) is a neighbourhood
of x, so there exists N such that xn ∈ Bϵ (x) for all n ≥ N . This means that
d(xn , x) < ϵ for all n ≥ N . Hence, (xn ) converges to x in the metric sense.

in the metric sense. For every neighborhood U of x, there exists ϵ > 0 such
that Bϵ (x) ⊆ U . Then, there exists N such that d(xn , x) < ϵ for all n ≥ N . In
particular, xn ∈ Bϵ (x) ⊂ U for all n ≥ N . So we have xn → x in the topological
sense.
    (⇐) Let (xn ) be a sequence in a metric space (X, d) converging to x ∈ X in
the topological sense. For every ϵ > 0, the open ball Bϵ (x) is a neighbourhood
of x, so there exists N such that xn ∈ Bϵ (x) for all n ≥ N . This means that
d(xn , x) < ϵ for all n ≥ N . Hence, (xn ) converges to x in the metric sense.

E ∩U for each neighbourhood U of x. Then the net (xU )U ∈Λ is a net converging

edges.note: This is a proof or sketch printed for Theorem 5.16.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof. Let B = {Bn : n ∈ N} be a countable basis of X.
   • Let U be an open cover of X. For each Bn , choose Un ∈ U such that
     Bn ⊆ Un if such Un exists (when exists, there could be multiple such Un ,
     and we just choose one). Then {Un : n ∈ N, Bn ⊆ Un } is a countable
     collection. We claim that it covers X. For any x ∈ X, there exists U ∈ U
     such that x ∈ U . Since B is a basis, there exists some Bm such that
     x ∈ Bm ⊆ U . By construction, there exists Um ∈ U such that Bm ⊆ Um .
     Hence, x ∈ Um . This shows that {Un : n ∈ N, Bn ⊆ Un } covers X.
   • For each Bn , choose xn ∈ Bn . Then A = {xn : n ∈ N, xn is chosen from Bn }
     is a countable dense subset of X. To see this, pick any x ∈ X. Then, for
     any basis element Bn containing x, we have Bn ∩ A ̸= ∅. Hence x ∈ A.

edges.note: This is a proof or sketch printed for Lemma 5.19.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof. Let x ∈ X. To show that {x} is closed, we show that its complement
X \ {x} is open. For any y ∈ X \ {x}, since X is Hausdorff, there exist disjoint
open sets U and V such that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Then V ⊆ X \ {x}. Hence for
each point in X \ {x}, we can find an open neighbourhood contained in X \ {x}.
This shows that X \ {x} is open.

edges.note: This is a proof or sketch printed for Proposition 5.24.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof. When X is Hausdorff, suppose that a sequence (xn ) converges to both
x and y with x ̸= y. Since X is Hausdorff, there exist disjoint open sets U and
V such that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Since (xn ) → x, there exists N1 such that for all
n ≥ N1 , we have xn ∈ U . Similarly, since (xn ) → y, there exists N2 such that
for all n ≥ N2 , we have xn ∈ V . Let N = max{N1 , N2 }. Then, for all n ≥ N ,
we have xn ∈ U and xn ∈ V , contradicting the fact that U and V are disjoint.
Hence, the limit is unique.

edges.note: This is a proof or sketch printed for Lemma 5.30.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof. We prove the regular case. The normal case is similar.
   Suppose X is regular. Let U be a neighbourhood of x. Then, X \ U is closed
and disjoint from {x}. By regularity, there exist disjoint open sets V and W
such that x ∈ V and X \ U ⊆ W . Since V ∩ W = ∅, we have that V ⊂ X \ W
which is closed. Then, V ⊆ X \ W ⊆ U . Hence, we have found a neighbourhood
V of x such that x ∈ V ⊆ V ⊆ U .
   Conversely, let U = X \ B, where B is a closed set disjoint from {x}. By
assumption, there exists a neighbourhood V of x such that x ∈ V ⊆ V ⊆ U .
So x ∈ V and X \ V ⊃ X \ U = B are disjoint open sets separating x and B.
Hence, X is regular.
   Let me state some important results about these separation axioms.

                                                                         c ≡ 0.

edges.note: This is a proof or sketch printed for Theorem 5.38.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof of Theorem 5.38. We reindex the functions in the lemma above as {fn :
n ∈ N}. Define a map F : X → [0, 1]N by F (x) = (f1 (x), f2 (x), . . .).
    Since each fn is continuous, F is continuous when [0, 1]N is equipped with
the product topology (cf. Theorem 3.91).
    We claim that F is an embedding. To see this, we first show that F is
injective. If x, y ∈ X with x ̸= y, then there exists a neighborhood U of x such
that y ∈/ U . By the lemma, there exists n such that fn (x) > 0 and fn |U c ≡ 0.
Hence, fn (y) = 0 ̸= fn (x), which shows that F (x) ̸= F (y).
    Next, we show that F is a homeomorphism onto its image. Since we already
showed that F is continuous and injective, it suffices to show that F (U ) is open
in F (X) for any open set U .
    Let x be any point in U and hence f (x) is an arbitrary point in F (U ). By
the construction of {fn }, there exists n such that fn (x) > 0 and fn |U c ≡ 0.
Let πn : [0, 1]N → [0, 1] be the projection onto the n-th coordinate. Then,
πn−1 ((fn (x)/2, 1]) ∩ F (X) is an open neighborhood of F (x) in F (X) and

   πn−1 ((fn (x)/2, 1]) ∩ F (X) = F ({y ∈ X : fn (y) > fn (x)/2 > 0}) ⊆ F (U ).

This shows that F (U ) is open in F (X).
   Now, we recall that [0, 1]N with the product topology is metrizable (Home-
work). Hence, F (X) is metrizable as a subspace of a metric space. Since F is
an embedding, X is metrizable.

y ∈ Y choose disjoint open sets Uy and Vy such that x ∈ Uy and y ∈ Vy . Then,
{Vy : y ∈ Y } is an open cover of Y . By compactness
                                             Tn         of Y , there exists a finite
subcover {Vy1 , . . . , Vyn } of Y . Let U = i=1 Uyi . Then, U is disjoint from
Vy1 ∪ · · · ∪ Vyn and hence is an open neighbourhood of x disjoint from Y . Hence,
X \ Y is open.
   In fact, the proof above shows that for any x ∈ X \ Y , there exist disjoint
open sets U and V such that x ∈ U and Y ⊆ V .

edges.note: This is a proof or sketch printed for Theorem 6.24.
edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof. Let U be an open cover of [a, b] where a < b. Define

        S = {x ∈ [a, b] : [a, x] can be covered by a finite subcover of U}.

It is clear that a ∈ S and if x ∈ S, then [a, x] ⊂ S. Since S is clearly upper-
bounded by b, we let c = sup S, i.e., the least upper bound of S. We will show
that c ∈ S and c = b.
     Clearly c ≤ b. If (a, c) is empty, then a = c ∈ S. Suppose (a, c) is nonempty.
Then, we have that [a, c) ⊂ S. Let Uc be an open set in U containing c. By the
definition of the order topology, there exists some (d, e) such that c ∈ (d, e) ⊆ Uc .
There must be some x ∈ (d, c) otherwise sup S ≤ d < c. Then, we know x ∈ S
and hence [a, x] can be covered by a finite subcover Ux of U. Note that Ux ∪{Uc }
is a finite subcover of [a, c]. This implies that c ∈ S.
     Suppose c < b. Now we consider the interval (c, b). Let T = {x ∈ [c, b] :
[c, x] = {c}} and let y = sup T . Note that y ≤ b. If y = c, then the open set
Uc containing c also contains some element z of (c, b), and hence [x, z] can be
covered by a finite subcover, which contradicts the definition of c. Therefore,
we must have y > c. But then the interval [a, y] can be covered by a finite
subcover of U by considering an open set around y, contradicting the definition
of c. Hence, we must have c = b.
     Therefore, we have shown that every open cover U of [a, b] has a finite sub-
cover. This completes the proof.


   As a corollary, we have the following result.

Proof. Given ϵ > 0, for each x ∈ X, by continuity of f at x, there exists
δx > 0 such that for all y ∈ X, if dX (x, y) < δx , then dY (f (x), f (y)) < ϵ/2.
Then, {Bδx /2 (x) : x ∈ X} is an open cover of X. By compactness of X, there
exists a finite subcover {Bδxi /2 (xi ) : i = 1, 2, . . . , n}. Let δ = min{δxi /2 : i =
1, 2, . . . , n}. We will show that this δ works. Given any x1 , x2 ∈ X such that
dX (x1 , x2 ) < δ, there exists some i such that x1 ∈ Bδxi /2 (xi ). This implies
that dX (x1 , xi ) < δxi /2 and hence dX (x2 , xi ) ≤ dX (x2 , x1 ) + dX (x1 , xi ) <
δxi /2 + δxi /2 = δxi . Therefore, we have

   dY (f (x1 ), f (x2 )) ≤ dY (f (x1 ), f (xi )) + dY (f (xi ), f (x2 )) < ϵ/2 + ϵ/2 = ϵ.

Proof. (3) ⇒ (2): For completeness, let (xn ) be a Cauchy sequence in X. By
sequential compactness, there exists a convergent subsequence (xnk ) converging
to some x ∈ X. Since (xn ) is Cauchy, it must converge to the same limit x
(exercise). Hence, X is complete. For total boundedness, suppose not. Then,
there exists ϵ > 0 such that for any finite set F ⊂ X, there exists some x ∈ X
such that d(x, y) ≥ ϵ for all y ∈ F . In this way, we can construct a sequence (xn )
in X such that d(xn , xm ) ≥ ϵ for all n ̸= m. This sequence has no convergent
subsequence, contradicting the sequential compactness of X. Hence, X is totally
bounded.

{xn : n ∈ N} is finite, then there exists some x ∈ X such that xn = x for
infinitely many n. Hence, the constant subsequence converges to x. Now assume
that {xn : n ∈ N} is infinite. Let A = {xn : n ∈ N}. Suppose that (xn ) has
no convergent subsequence. Then, for any x ∈ X \ A, there exists an open
neighbourhood Ux of x such that Ux ∩ A = ∅. This implies that A is closed
and hence compact. For any a ∈ A, since no subsequence of (xn ) converges to
a, there exists an open neighbourhood Va of a such that Va ∩ A = {a}. Then,
{Va } is an infinite open cover of A with no finite subcover, contradicting the
compactness of A. Therefore, (xn ) has a convergent subsequence.

Proof. (⇒) Assume x is a cluster point of the net (xα )α∈A . Define the directed
set
          Γ = {(α, U ) : α ∈ A, U is an open neighbourhood of xα }
with the order (α1 , U1 ) ≤ (α2 , U2 ) if and only if α1 ≤ α2 and U2 ⊆ U1 . Define
the map φ : Γ → A by (α, U ) 7→ α. Then, the subnet (xφ(γ) )γ∈Γ converges to
x. (Note that the map φ is not injective, so a subnet is quite different from a
subsequence.)
   (⇐) Assume there exists a subnet (xφ(γ) )γ∈Γ that converges to x. Given
any open neighbourhood U of x and any α0 ∈ A, by the definition of subnet,
there exists some γ0 ∈ Γ such that for all γ ≥ γ0 , we have φ(γ) ≥ α0 . Since the
subnet converges to x, there exists some γ1 ≥ γ0 such that for all γ ≥ γ1 , we have
xφ(γ) ∈ U . In particular, for this choice of γ1 , we have some β = φ(γ1 ) ≥ α0
such that xβ = xφ(γ1 ) ∈ U . Therefore, x is a cluster point of the net.

Proof. Let {xλ } be an ultranet in X and let x ∈ X be a cluster point of the net.
Given any open neighbourhood U of x, since {xλ } is an ultranet, it is eventually
in U or eventually in X \ U . Since x is a cluster point, it cannot be eventually
in X \ U . Hence, it is eventually in U . Therefore, {xλ } converges to x.

Sketch of proof. Let (xλ ) be a net in a set X. We call Q ⊂ P (X) a admissible
family if

   • for any A1 , A2 ∈ Q, we have ∅ ̸= A1 ∩ A2 ∈ Q;
   • for any A ∈ Q, the net (xλ ) is frequently in A (for any λ0 , there exists
     some λ ≥ λ0 such that xλ ∈ A).
Let Q denote the collection of all admissible families and we partially order Q
by inclusion. Using Zorn’s lemma, we can show that Q has a maximal element
Qmax . You can show that if A ⊂ X, then either A ∈ Qmax or X \ A ∈ Qmax .
Now, we define a directed set Γ = {(λ, A) : λ ∈ Λ, A ∈ Qmax , s.t. xλ ∈ A} with
the order defined by (λ1 , A1 ) ≤ (λ2 , A2 ) if λ1 ≤ λ2 and A2 ⊆ A1 . Then, let
φ : Γ → Λ be defined by (λ, A) 7→ λ. This defines a subnet and you can check
that this subnet is indeed an ultranet.

edges.sourceExcerpt:
Proof. (⇒) Since each projection map πα : X = Xα → Xα is continuous, we
have that Xα = πα (X) is compact for each α.                              Q
     (⇐) Assume that Xα is compact for each α. Let {xλ } be a net in X = Xα .
Then, {xλ } has a subnet {xλµ } that is an ultranet. Then, for each α, the net
{πα (xλµ )} is an ultranet in Xα which has some cluster point yα ∈ Xα as Xα
is compact. Since {πα (xλµ )} is an ultranet, it converges to yα . Then, the net
{xλµ } converges to y = (yα ) ∈ X which is hence a cluster point of the original
net {xλ }. Therefore, by the characterization of compactness using nets, X is
compact.

Proof. (⇒) Let Y = X ⊔ {∞} with the topology τ defined as follows:
   • For any open set U in X, U ∈ τ ;
   • For any compact set K in X, the set Y \ K ∈ τ .
   To see that this is indeed a topology, note
   • ∅ and Y = Y \ ∅ are in τ ;
   • T
          S                        S               T
     U = Uα is open in X; and (Y \ Kβ ) = Y \ Kβ = Y \ C is in τ since
       Kβ is a closed
                    S subset
                           S of the compact set Kβ0 for some β0 and hence
     compact; and Uα ∪ (Y \ Kβ ) = U ∪ (Y \ C) = Y \ (C \ U ) is in τ since
     C \ U is a closed subset of the compact set C and hence compact.
   • U1 ∩ U2 is open in X; (Y \ C1 ) ∩ (Y \ C2 ) = Y \ (C1 ∪ C2 ) is in τ since
     C1 ∪ C2 is compact; and U ∩ (Y \ C) = U ∩ (X \ C) is open in X since C
     is closed in X.
    Note that the subspace topology on X induced from Y is the same as the
original topology on X (note Y \ C ∩ X is open in X).
    To see that Y is compact, note if U is an open cover of Y , then U must have
an element of the form ∞ ∈ Y \ K where K is a compact set in X. K is then
also compact in Y . Hence, there exists a finite subcover of U that covers K.
Together with the element Y \ K, we have a finite subcover of U that covers Y .
    To see that Y is Hausdorff, note for any x, x′ ∈ X, we just use the Hausdorff
property of X to separate them. For any x ∈ X and y = ∞, since X is locally
compact, there exists some open neighbourhood U of x and some compact set
K such that U ⊂ K. Then, U and Y \ K are disjoint open neighbourhoods of
x and ∞ respectively.
    (⇐) We still write the extra point in Y \ X as ∞. Note since Y is Hausdorff,
as a subspace, X is also Hausdorff. For any x ∈ X, since Y is Hausdorff, there
exist disjoint open neighbourhoods U of x and V of ∞. Then, K = Y \ V is
a compact in Y (and hence in X) since it is closed. Note that U ⊂ K ⊂ X.
Therefore, X is locally compact.
    It remains to show that Y is unique up to homeomorphism. Let Y ′ be
another compactification of X. Define the map f : Y → Y ′ as follows: h(∞) =
∞′ and h(x) = x for any x ∈ X. Then, I’ll leave it as an exercise to check that
h is a homeomorphism.

Proof. Assume that Y has a separation A, B. Pick a ∈ A and b ∈ B with a < b.
Then, [a, b] ⊂ Y . Let A0 = A ∩ [a, b] and B0 = B ∩ [a, b]. Then, A0 , B0 are open
in [a, b] w.r.t. the subspace topology which is the same as the order topology
on [a, b]. So A0 , B0 form a separation of [a, b].
     Let c = sup A0 . We show that c ∈    / A0 and c ∈  / B0 , contradicting that
[a, b] = A0 ∪ B0 .
     Suppose c ∈ B0 . Then, c ̸= a, so c = b or a < c < b. Since B0 is open, in
either case, there exists d such that (d, c] ⊂ B0 . If c = b, then d is an upper
bound of A0 less than c, contradicting that c = sup A0 . If a < c < b, then since
c is an upper bound, (c, b] ∩ A0 = ∅. Hence, (d, b] = (d, c] ∪ (c, b] ∩ A0 = ∅ which
makes d an upper bound of A0 less than c, again a contradiction. Thus, c ∈     / B0 .
     Now suppose c ∈ A0 . Then, c ̸= b, and so c = a or a < c < b. Since A0 is
open, in either case, there exists e such that [c, e) ⊂ A0 . But then any z such
that c < z < e is in A0 , contradicting that c = sup A0 (z exists because of (2)).
Thus, c ∈ / A0 .
   Now we can prove the intermediate value theorem.

Proof. Let X be an ultrametric space with ultrametric d. We need to show
that the components of X are singletons. Let x, y ∈ X be distinct points. Let
r = u(x, y) > 0. Then, Br (x) is an open neighborhood of x. I claim that
X \ Br (x) is an open neighborhood of y. Indeed, for any point z ∈ X \ Br (x),
we have u(x, z) ≥ r > 0. Pick r0 ∈ (0, r). Then, for any z ′ ∈ Br0 (z), we have
that u(x, z ′ ) = u(x, z) ≥ r. Hence z ′ ∈
                                         / Br (x) and thus Br0 (z) ⊆ X \ Br (x).
This shows that X \ Br (x) is open and hence an open neighborhood of y. This
implies that x and y lie in different components. Since x, y ∈ X are arbitrary,
we conclude that the components of X are singletons.

construct B = {(−x11 , x11 ) × (−x22 , x22 ) × · · · }. Then, 0 ∈ B but an ∈            / B for
all n ∈ N. So there exists a ball Br (0) ⊆ B for some r > 0 containing no point

metrizable.

Example 6.35 (Compact but not sequentially compact). Let X = {0, 1}[0,1]
with the product topology. By Tychonoff, X is compact. For each n ∈ N
define fn ∈ X by fn (r) = the n-th binary digit of r (choose the expansion not
ending in all 1’s). Take any subsequence (fnk ). If it converges, we know that for
any r ∈ [0, 1], the sequence (fnk (r)) must converge in [0, 1]. Choose r ∈ [0, 1]

fnk (r) = 0, 1, 0, 1, . . . does not converge. Therefore (fnk ) cannot converge in the
product topology. Hence no subsequence of (fn ) converges; X is not sequentially
compact.

a set U ⊆ X is open iff X \ U is countable or U = ∅.

{(a, −a)} = L ∩ [a, a + 1) × [−a, −a + 1) and hence {(a, −a)} is open in L. So L
has the discrete topology. So every subset of L is closed in subspace topology
and hence closed in Rℓ × Rℓ .
   Now let A = {(x, −x) : x ∈ Q} and B = L \ A. Both are closed in Rℓ × Rℓ .
One can check that there are no disjoint open sets separating A and B (see
Munkres Chapter 4 section 31 problem 9). So Rℓ × Rℓ is not normal.
   There is still a positive result about subspaces of normal spaces.

Example 6.35 (Compact but not sequentially compact). Let X = {0, 1}[0,1]
with the product topology. By Tychonoff, X is compact. For each n ∈ N
define fn ∈ X by fn (r) = the n-th binary digit of r (choose the expansion not
ending in all 1’s). Take any subsequence (fnk ). If it converges, we know that for
any r ∈ [0, 1], the sequence (fnk (r)) must converge in [0, 1]. Choose r ∈ [0, 1]
whose binary expansion has digit nk equal to 0 if k is odd and 1 if k is even
(this is possible since we prescribe digits only on the positions {nk }). Then
fnk (r) = 0, 1, 0, 1, . . . does not converge. Therefore (fnk ) cannot converge in the
product topology. Hence no subsequence of (fn ) converges; X is not sequentially
compact.

Example 6.36 (Sequentially compact but not compact). Let Y ⊂ {0, 1}[0,1]
be a subspace consisting of all functions f such that f (r) = 1 for at most
countably many r ∈ [0, 1]. We claim that Y is sequentially
                                                    S            compact but not
compact. Given any sequence (fn ) in Y , let A = n {r : fn (r) = 1}. Then, A
is countable. For each r ∈ A, the sequence (fn (r)) in {0, 1} has a convergent
subsequence. By a diagonal argument, we can find a subsequence (fnk ) such
that for each r ∈ A, the sequence (fnk (r)) converges in {0, 1}. For r ∈
                                                                       / A, define
f (r) = 0. Then, it is easy to see that f ∈ Y and fnk → f in the product
topology. Hence, Y is sequentially compact.
    To see that Y is not compact, we just need to show that Y is not closed.
Pick 1 ∈ X \ Y being the constant function with value 1. For any basic open
neighbourhood of 1 of the form

where πri : X → {0, 1} is the projection map, we can find f ∈ Y such that

any a′ ∈ [0A , a] satisfies f (a′ ) ∈ [0B , f (a)]. Thus, we get f ([0A , a]) ⊆ [0B , f (a)].

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let A = {Ai }i∈I be a family of nonempty sets. For each i ∈ I set

                              Bi := {(i, a) : a ∈ Ai }.

 Then the family {Bi }i∈I consists of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets. By the
 Axiom
 S         of Choice (the pairwise disjoint formulation) there exists a set C ⊆
   i∈I i such that C ∩ Bi contains exactly one element for every i ∈ I. For each
       B
iSwrite the unique element of C ∩ Bi as (i, ci ) with ci ∈ Ai , and defineS f :A→
   i∈I A i  by f (A i ) = ci . Equivalently, view f as a function f : I →  i∈I Ai with
f (i) = ci . In either view f (i) ∈ Ai for all i, so f is a choice function for A.
     The reason AC is debatable is that this doesn’t constructively provide a
way to choose elements from each set. If you have a finite collection of sets,
you can simply list the elements and choose one from each set. This idea may
still apply when you have a countable collection of sets. But when you have an
uncountable collection of sets, the Axiom of Choice becomes more controversial.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P1.50
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let A be a poset satisfying the assumptions of Zorn’s lemma. Let B ⊂ A
be a maximal chain. Let u be an upper bound of B in A. If u < v, then B∪{v} is
a chain containing B, contradicting the maximality of B. Thus, u is a maximal
element of A.

Proof. We’ve already S seen how 3 implies 2. Let’s see one more.
   4 ⇒ 1 Make U := Ai well ordered. Then, pick ai := min Ai since Ai ⊂ U .
Then, B = {ai }i∈I is a set such that B ∩ Ai is exactly one element for all i ∈ I.
Thus, the Axiom of Choice holds.
   2 ⇒ 1. Assume Zorn’s Lemma. Let {Ai }i∈I be a family of nonempty
(pairwise disjoint) sets. Consider the set

       F = {f | f is a function with domain J ⊆ I, f (j) ∈ Aj ∀j ∈ J},

      S ordered by extension (f ≤ g iff f ⊆ g). If C ⊆ F is a chain, then
partially
g := f ∈C f is an upper bound of C (the union is a function since members of
the chain agree on overlaps). By Zorn’s Lemma there exists a maximal element
f ∗ ∈ F. If dom f ∗ ̸= I pick i0 ∈ I \ dom f ∗ and choose a ∈ Ai0 (nonemptiness).
Then f ∗ ∪ {(i0 , a)} ∈ F strictly extends f ∗ , contradicting maximality. Hence
dom f ∗ = I, so f ∗ is a choice function.

Let g : A → {1, . . . , n} be a bijection (existence follows from finiteness). Then
the composite

is a bijection from the proper subset B to {1, . . . , n}, contradicting Theo-
rem 1.57. A commutative diagram summarising the argument:

                                                             B

                                                    g◦f −1

                              {1, . . . , n}

Hence such an f cannot exist.

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Consider the map f : N → N \ {1} defined by f (n) = n + 1. This is a
bijection onto the proper subset N \ {1}. If N were finite, this would contradict
Theorem 1.58. Hence N is not finite (i.e. infinite).

Proof. Define f : N → C inductively as follows: let f (1) = min C. If f (1), . . . , f (n)
have been defined, let f (n + 1) = min(C \ {f (1), . . . , f (n)}).
    f is injective: for m < n, f (n) ∈ C \ {f (1), . . . , f (n − 1)}, but f (m) is not
in the set. So, f (n) ̸= f (m).
    f is surjective: for any c ∈ C, there exists n ∈ N such that f (n) ≥ c. Let
m be the smallest integer with f (m) ≥ c. So for any i < m, f (i) < c. So
c ∈
  / {f (1), . . . , f (m − 1)} and hence f (m) ≤ c by its definition. This implies
that f (m) = c.
   The same proof can be used to prove the following result.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P1.66
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. We prove the implications as follows:
(1) ⇒ (2) If A is countably finite, then there exists a bijection and hence surjection
          f : N → A. If A is finite, then the composition is what we need: N →
          {1, . . . , n} → A.
(2) ⇒ (3) If there exists a surjection f : N → A, then we can define an injection
          g : A → N by g(a) = min{n ∈ N : f (n) = a} for all a ∈ A.
(3) ⇒ (1) If there exists an injection g : A → N, then we can decompose this as
          A → im(g) → N. If im(g) is finite, then A is finite. If im(g) is infinite,
          then by the lemma above, im(g) is countably infinite and hence so is A.

proofs.label: P1.71
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Define Φ : {0, 1}N → P(N) by
                                  
                        Φ (xn )n≥1 = { n ∈ N : xn = 1 }.

If (xn ) ̸= (yn ) pick k with xk ̸= yk ; then k belongs to exactly one of the two
images, so Φ(xn ) ̸= Φ(yn ). Thus Φ is injective. Conversely, for any A ⊆ N let
its characteristic sequence χA be given by χA (n) = 1 if n ∈ A, 0 otherwise.
Then Φ(χA ) = A, so Φ is surjective. Hence |P(N)| = |{0, 1}N |.
   In fact, this corollary is a special case of a more general result which we will
prove later.

with equality only if yk − xk = −1 for all k > n, i.e. xk = 1 and yk = 0 for

proofs.label: P1.74
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let G := F \ A. Then G is finite and disjoint from A. We need to show
that |A ∪ G| = |A|. Since A is infinite, we can choose a sequence of distinct
elements a1 , a2 , . . . in A. If G = ∅, the result is trivial. If G ̸= ∅, we write
G = {g1 , g2 , . . . , gn }, where n is finite. Define f : A → A ∪ G as follows:
   1. if a ∈
           / {a1 , . . .}, then set f (a) := a;
   2. if a = ai for some i ≤ n, then set f (a) := gi .
   3. If a = ai for some i > n, then set f (a) := ai−n .
Then, f is a bijection. Thus |A ∪ G| = |A|.
    For the second part, we let B := A\F . Then, |A\F | = |B| = |B ∪(A∩F )| =
|A|.
    Now, assume that F is countably infinite and A is uncountable. Let G :=
F \ A. Then, G is countable. WLOG, we assume G is infinite. We then can
write G = {g1 , g2 , . . .}. Still choose a sequence of distinct elements a1 , a2 , . . . in
A. Define f : A → A ∪ G as follows:
   1. if a ∈
           / {a1 , . . .}, then set f (a) := a;
   2. if a = a2n , then set f (a2n ) := gn ;
   3. if a = a2n−1 , then set f (a2n−1 ) := an .
Then, f is a bijection. Thus |A ∪ G| = |A|.

proofs.label: P1.78
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. WLOG, we assume that A and B are disjoint (otherwise replace B by a
disjoint copy). For each a ∈ A, we have the following sequence:
            f       g      f       g            f   g      f     g     f
        . . . 7→ b−3 7→ a−2 7→ b−1 7→ a0 = a 7→ b0 7→ a1 7→ b1 7→ a2 7→ . . .
There are only four possibilities for this sequence:
  1. (B-stopper) it stops at some b−k where k ≥ 1.
  2. (A-stopper) it stops at some a−k where k ≥ 0.
  3. (bi-infinite) it continues indefinitely in both directions.
  4. (cyclic) it is a cyclic sequence, i.e., ai = aj for some i < j.
   This also holds for any b ∈ B and hence these four possibilities give rise to
a partition of A ⊔ B.
   Now, we define h : A → B as follows:
                   
                   f (a),
                             if a is an A-stopper;
           h(a) = f (a),      if a is in a bi-infinite chain or a cycle;
                    −1
                   
                    g (a), if a is a B-stopper.
   This is a bijection.
   We proved this using Well-ordering theorem. We can also prove this using
Zorn’s lemma.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P1.79
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let M be the set of matchings between A and B:
M = {M ⊆ A×B | each a ∈ A appears in at most one pair of M, and each b ∈ B appears in at most one}.
We partially order M by inclusion. If {Mi }i∈I is a chain in M, then
                                       [
                                M=       Mi
                                          i∈I

is again a matching, since no element of A or B can be matched to more than
one partner within a chain. Thus every chain has an upper bound.
    By Zorn’s Lemma, M has a maximal element M ∗ .
    Suppose there exist a ∈ A and b ∈ B both unmatched in M ∗ . Then
                               M ′ = M ∗ ∪ {(a, b)}
is a matching strictly larger than M ∗ , contradicting maximality. Therefore, at
least one side is fully matched: either every a ∈ A is matched, or every b ∈ B is
matched.
   • If every a ∈ A is matched, define f : A → B by f (a) = b whenever
     (a, b) ∈ M ∗ . This f is injective, so |A| ≤ |B|.
   • Otherwise, every b ∈ B is matched. Define g : B → A by g(b) = a
     whenever (a, b) ∈ M ∗ . Then g is injective, so |B| ≤ |A|.

   Thus, for any sets A and B, either |A| ≤ |B| or |B| ≤ |A|.

proofs.label: P2.7
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let f : X → Y be Lipschitz continuous with constant L. Given ε > 0,
let δ = ε/L. Then, for any x ∈ X with dX (x, x0 ) < δ, we have
                                                               ε
                 dY (f (x), f (x0 )) ≤ L · dX (x, x0 ) < L ·     = ε.
                                                               L
Thus, f is continuous at x0 . Since x0 is arbitrary, f is continuous.
  If f is an isometric embedding, then for any x, x′ ∈ X, we have

                  dY (f (x), f (x′ )) = dX (x, x′ ) ≤ 1 · dX (x, x′ ).

Thus, f is Lipschitz continuous with constant L = 1.

Proof. Suppose first that f is continuous at x0 , and let (xn )n∈N be a sequence
converging to x0 . For any ε > 0, by continuity there exists δ > 0 such that

                   dX (x, x0 ) < δ     =⇒         dY (f (x), f (x0 )) < ε.

Since (xn ) converges to x0 , there exists an N ∈ N with dX (xn , x0 ) < δ for all
n ≥ N . Hence, for all n ≥ N , we have

                               dY (f (xn ), f (x0 )) < ε,

so (f (xn )) converges to f (x0 ).
    Conversely, suppose that for every sequence (xn ) converging to x0 , the se-
quence (f (xn )) converges to f (x0 ). Assume for contradiction that f is not
continuous at x0 . Then there exists ε0 > 0 such that for every δ > 0 there
exists some x ∈ X with

                dX (x, x0 ) < δ        but         dY (f (x), f (x0 )) ≥ ε0 .

For each n ∈ N, choosing δ = n1 , there exists xn ∈ X with

                                   1
                 dX (xn , x0 ) <       and    dY (f (xn ), f (x0 )) ≥ ε0 .
                                   n
Then (xn ) converges to x0 , yet (f (xn )) cannot converge to f (x0 ) since the
distance remains at least ε0 , which is a contradiction.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P2.20
proofs.sourceText:
Proof of Theorem 2.20. Suppose that f is continuous. Let x ∈ A. By the
lemma, there exists a sequence (xn ) in A converging to x. By continuity, (f (xn ))
converges to f (x). Since each f (xn ) ∈ f (A), by the lemma again, we have
f (x) ∈ f (A). Thus, f (A) ⊆ f (A).
    Conversely, suppose that f (A) ⊆ f (A) for every set A ⊆ X. Let x0 ∈ X
and let (xn ) be a sequence converging to x0 . Assume on the contrary that
(f (xn )) does not converge to f (x0 ). Then, there exists ε > 0 such that there is
a subsequence (f (xkn )) such that dY (f (xkn ), f (x0 )) ≥ ε for all n ∈ N.
    Now we let A = {xkn : n ∈ N}. Then, x0 ∈ A. Thus, f (x0 ) ∈ f (A) ⊆ f (A).
By the lemma, there exists a sequence (yn ) in f (A) converging to f (x0 ). But
this is not possible due to the ϵ constraint. Therefore, we conclude that (f (xn ))
must converge to f (x0 ).
    We now see that many intuitive properties of continuous real functions can
be generalized nicely to metric spaces. We will see that the open and closed
language still works well in the more general setting of topological spaces, while
the sequential language does not. In Willard’s book, a whole chapter is devoted
to the study of sequences in topological spaces.

metrizable since singletons are not closed.

Proof. By hypothesis, for any open U ∈ τ and any x ∈ U there exists B ∈ B
with x ∈ B ⊆ U .

verifying the first basis axiom.
    (2) If x ∈ B1 ∩ B2 with B1 , B2 ∈ B ⊆ τ , then U := B1 ∩ B2 ∈ τ . Applying
the hypothesis to U and x yields B3 ∈ B such that x ∈ B3 ⊆ B1 ∩ B2 , which is
the second basis axiom.
    Thus B is a basis. Let τB be the topology it generates. Since B ⊆ τ and τ
is closed under unions, τB ⊆ τ . Conversely, for any U ∈ τ ,

where each Bx ∈ B satisfies x ∈ Bx ⊆ U by the hypothesis. Hence U ∈ τB , so

Proof.    (i) Since X is open, ∅ is closed, so ∅ = ∅.
 (ii) A is contained in every closed superset, so A ⊂ A.
(iii) If D is closed and contains A, then taking closure again yields D itself.
(iv) For A, B ⊂ X: A∪B is closed and it contains A∪B. Hence, A ∪ B ⊆ A∪B.
     Since A ⊂ A ∪ B and B ⊂ A ∪ B, we conclude that A ∪ B = A ∪ B.
