proofs.label: P3.42
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Pick any U × V from the basis for the product topology. Now, for any
(x, y) ∈ U × V , we have that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Since B and B ′ are bases, there
exist Ux ∈ B and Vy ∈ B ′ such that x ∈ Ux ⊆ U and y ∈ Vy ⊆ V . Hence,
(x, y) ∈ Ux × Vy ⊆ U × V . This implies that the topology generated by B × B ′ is
finer than the product topology. On the other hand, since B × B ′ is a subset of
the basis for the product topology, the topology generated by B × B ′ is coarser
than the product topology. Therefore, they must be the same.

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let BX and BY be bases for X and Y respectively. Then, BX × BY :=
{U ×V : U ∈ BX , V ∈ BY } is a basis for the product topology on X ×Y . Hence,
the subspace topology of A × B has a basis

               BA×B = {(U × V ) ∩ (A × B) : U ∈ BX , V ∈ BY }.

Note that (U × V ) ∩ (A × B) = (U ∩ A) × (V ∩ B).
   Then,

         BA×B = {(U ∩ A) × (V ∩ B) : U ∈ BX , V ∈ BY } = BA × BB .

This finishes the proof.

A ⊆ Y , we have that

   (1) ⇒ (2): Let H be open in Y . If f −1 (H) = ∅, then done. Otherwise, for
any x ∈ f −1 (H), H is a neighborhood of f (x). Hence, there exists a neighbor-
hood V of x such that f (V ) ⊆ H. Thus, V ⊆ f −1 (H). Therefore, f −1 (H) is
open in X.
    (2) ⇒ (3): If C is closed in Y , then Y \ C is open in Y . By (2), f −1 (Y \ C)
is open in X. Then, f −1 (C) = X \ f −1 (Y \ C) is closed in X.
    (3) ⇒ (4): f −1 (f (A)) is closed by (2). Furthermore, A ⊆ f −1 (f (A)) (since
f (A) ⊆ f (A)). This implies that A ⊆ f −1 (f (A)) and hence f (A) ⊆ f (A).
    (4) ⇒ (1): Let x ∈ X and let V be a neighborhood of f (x) in Y . Set
E := f −1 (Y \ V ) = X \ f −1 (V ). Then, we have that f (E) ⊂ f (E) ⊆ Y \ V
(because Y \ V is a closed set containing f (E)).
    Now we have that x ∈ X \ E, which is a neighborhood of x. Then,
        f (X \ E) ⊂ f (X \ E) = f (X \ f −1 (Y \ V )) = f (f −1 (V )) ⊆ V.
This concludes the proof.

proofs.label: P3.65
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Suppose E is closed in A. Then A \ E is open in A, so there exists
      an open set U in X such that A \ E = U ∩ A. Let F = X \ U , which is
      closed in X. Then
                F ∩ A = (X \ U ) ∩ A = A \ (U ∩ A) = A \ (A \ E) = E.

      Conversely, if E = F ∩ A for some closed set F in X, then
                           A \ E = A \ (F ∩ A) = A ∩ (X \ F ),
      where X \ F is open in X. Hence, A \ E is open in A, so E is closed in
      A.

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Suppose there exists a homeomorphism f : [0, 1) → (0, 1). Pick any
x0 = 0 and consider the map g : (0, 1) → (0, 1)\{f (x0 )} defined by g(x) = f (x).
By the previous lemma, g is a homeomorphism. Note that (0, 1) \ {f (x0 )} is
not connected regardless the value of f (x0 ). However, (0, 1) = [0, 1) \ {x0 } is
connected. This is a contradiction.

open in Y and hence φ−1 is continuous.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P3.105
proofs.sourceText:
Proof that p is closed. Let F ⊂ [0, 2π] be closed. We show p(F ) is closed in S 1 .
Since S 1 ⊂ R2 is a metric space, it suffices to use sequences.
   Take any sequence (yn ) ⊂ p(F ) with yn → y ∈ S 1 . For each n choose tn ∈ F
such that p(tn ) = yn . The sequence (tn ) lies in the bounded interval [0, 2π],
so by Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence tnk → t ∈ [0, 2π].
Because F is closed and each tnk ∈ F , we have t ∈ F . By continuity of p,

                                  p(tnk ) −→ p(t).

But p(tnk ) = ynk → y, hence y = p(t) ∈ p(F ). Thus every limit of a convergent
sequence in p(F ) lies in p(F ); so p(F ) is closed in S 1 .
    Therefore p sends closed subsets of [0, 2π] to closed subsets of S 1 , i.e. p is a
closed map. Since p is surjective and continuous, it is a quotient map.
   In this way, we can identify S 1 with the quotient space obtained by attaching
end points of an interval [0, 2π]/(0 ∼ 2π).

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. (1) (⇒) Composition of continuous maps is continuous.
   (⇐) Suppose g is continuous. Let V ⊆ Z be open. Then

                       (f ◦ q)−1 (V ) = q −1 f −1 (V )
                                                       


is open in X. Since q is a quotient map, f −1 (V ) is open in Y ; hence f is
continuous.
    (2) (⇒) Suppose g is a quotient map. Let U ⊆ Z be such that f −1 (U ) is
open in Y . Then

                   q −1 (f −1 (U )) = (f ◦ q)−1 (U ) = g −1 (U )

is open in X. Since g is a quotient map, U is open in Z. Hence f is a quotient
map.
    (⇐) Suppose f is a quotient map. Let U ⊆ Z be such that g −1 (U ) is open
in X. Then
                    q −1 (f −1 (U )) = (f ◦ q)−1 (U ) = g −1 (U )
is open in X. Since q is a quotient map, f −1 (U ) is open in Y . Since f is a
quotient map, U is open in Z. Hence g is a quotient map. The same proof
shows that the composition of two quotient maps is a quotient map.

proofs.label: P3.115
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let H1 : X × I → Y be a homotopy f1 ≃ g1 and H2 : Y × I → Z a
homotopy f2 ≃ g2 . Then f2 ◦ H1 is a homotopy f2 ◦ f1 ≃ f2 ◦ g1 . Define
H(x, t) = H2 (g1 (x), t); this is continuous as a composite and gives a homotopy
f2 ◦ g1 ≃ g2 ◦ g1 . Transitivity yields f2 ◦ f1 ≃ g2 ◦ g1 .
   With the notion of homotopy between functions, we can define homotopy
equivalence between spaces.

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. If X is contractible pick x0 ∈ X and set Y = {x0 }. Let j : Y ,→ X be
inclusion and c : X → Y the constant map. Then c◦j = idY and j ◦c = c ≃ idX ,
so X ≃ Y .
    Conversely, suppose f : X → Y and g : Y → X exhibit a homotopy equiv-
alence where Y is a point. Then g ◦ f is constant and g ◦ f ≃ idX , giving a
homotopy from idX to a constant map, so X is contractible.

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Suppose on the contrary there is a homeomorphism f : R2 → R3 . Then
f restricts to a homeomorphism R2 \ {0} → R3 \ {f (0)}. But R2 \ {0} ≃ S 1 and
R3 \ {f (0)} ≃ S 2 . So S 1 ≃ S 2 . We will show this is not true.
   We will use the following lemmas.

   Now suppose S 1 ≃ S 2 via maps f : S 1 → S 2 and g : S 2 → S 1 . Then, we
know that f is homotopic to a constant map c : S 1 → S 2 . So g ◦ f : S 1 → S 1 is
homotopic to g ◦ c, which is a constant map. But g ◦ f ≃ idS 1 , which contradicts
the first lemma.

proofs.label: P3.134
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Assume F has no fixed point. For each x ∈ Dn draw the ray starting at
F (x) through x and let r(x) be the first intersection of that ray with S n−1 =
∂Dn . This gives a continuous map r : Dn → S n−1 which restricts to the identity
on S n−1 , hence a retraction. But S n−1 is not a retract (indeed not a deformation
retract) of Dn (proved earlier using homotopy ideas). Contradiction.

Homotopy equivalence = embedding + retraction
If there is one thing that you need to remember, that is homotopy equivalence
is basically embedding + retraction.
    First of all, we introduce the notion of embeddings.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P4.3
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. (⇒) Let (xn ) be a sequence in a metric space (X, d) converging to x ∈ X
in the metric sense. For every neighborhood U of x, there exists ϵ > 0 such
that Bϵ (x) ⊆ U . Then, there exists N such that d(xn , x) < ϵ for all n ≥ N . In
particular, xn ∈ Bϵ (x) ⊂ U for all n ≥ N . So we have xn → x in the topological
sense.
    (⇐) Let (xn ) be a sequence in a metric space (X, d) converging to x ∈ X in
the topological sense. For every ϵ > 0, the open ball Bϵ (x) is a neighbourhood
of x, so there exists N such that xn ∈ Bϵ (x) for all n ≥ N . This means that
d(xn , x) < ϵ for all n ≥ N . Hence, (xn ) converges to x in the metric sense.

Proof. If x ∈ E, then every neighbourhood U of x intersects E. Choose xU ∈
E ∩U for each neighbourhood U of x. Then the net (xU )U ∈Λ is a net converging
to x.
   Conversely, if there is a net (xλ )λ∈Λ in E such that xλ → x, then for every
neighbourhood U of x, there exists λ0 such that xλ ∈ U for all λ ≥ λ0 . In
particular, xλ0 ∈ E ∩U , so E ∩U ̸= ∅. Since U was arbitrary, we have x ∈ E.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P5.16
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let B = {Bn : n ∈ N} be a countable basis of X.
   • Let U be an open cover of X. For each Bn , choose Un ∈ U such that
     Bn ⊆ Un if such Un exists (when exists, there could be multiple such Un ,
     and we just choose one). Then {Un : n ∈ N, Bn ⊆ Un } is a countable
     collection. We claim that it covers X. For any x ∈ X, there exists U ∈ U
     such that x ∈ U . Since B is a basis, there exists some Bm such that
     x ∈ Bm ⊆ U . By construction, there exists Um ∈ U such that Bm ⊆ Um .
     Hence, x ∈ Um . This shows that {Un : n ∈ N, Bn ⊆ Un } covers X.
   • For each Bn , choose xn ∈ Bn . Then A = {xn : n ∈ N, xn is chosen from Bn }
     is a countable dense subset of X. To see this, pick any x ∈ X. Then, for
     any basis element Bn containing x, we have Bn ∩ A ̸= ∅. Hence x ∈ A.

proofs.label: P5.19
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let x ∈ X. To show that {x} is closed, we show that its complement
X \ {x} is open. For any y ∈ X \ {x}, since X is Hausdorff, there exist disjoint
open sets U and V such that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Then V ⊆ X \ {x}. Hence for
each point in X \ {x}, we can find an open neighbourhood contained in X \ {x}.
This shows that X \ {x} is open.

proofs.label: P5.24
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. When X is Hausdorff, suppose that a sequence (xn ) converges to both
x and y with x ̸= y. Since X is Hausdorff, there exist disjoint open sets U and
V such that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Since (xn ) → x, there exists N1 such that for all
n ≥ N1 , we have xn ∈ U . Similarly, since (xn ) → y, there exists N2 such that
for all n ≥ N2 , we have xn ∈ V . Let N = max{N1 , N2 }. Then, for all n ≥ N ,
we have xn ∈ U and xn ∈ V , contradicting the fact that U and V are disjoint.
Hence, the limit is unique.

proofs.label: P5.30
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. We prove the regular case. The normal case is similar.
   Suppose X is regular. Let U be a neighbourhood of x. Then, X \ U is closed
and disjoint from {x}. By regularity, there exist disjoint open sets V and W
such that x ∈ V and X \ U ⊆ W . Since V ∩ W = ∅, we have that V ⊂ X \ W
which is closed. Then, V ⊆ X \ W ⊆ U . Hence, we have found a neighbourhood
V of x such that x ∈ V ⊆ V ⊆ U .
   Conversely, let U = X \ B, where B is a closed set disjoint from {x}. By
assumption, there exists a neighbourhood V of x such that x ∈ V ⊆ V ⊆ U .
So x ∈ V and X \ V ⊃ X \ U = B are disjoint open sets separating x and B.
Hence, X is regular.
   Let me state some important results about these separation axioms.

proofs.label: P5.39
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let B = {Bn : n ∈ N} be a countable basis of X. Let S := {(Bn , Bm ) ∈
B × B : B n ⊆ Bm }. For each (Bn , Bm ) ∈ S, by Urysohn’s lemma, there exists a
continuous function fn,m : X → [0, 1] such that fn,m |B n ≡ 1 and fn,m |Bm
                                                                         c ≡ 0.

   Then, for any x ∈ X and any neighborhood U of x, there exists Bm ∈ B such
that x ∈ Bm ⊆ U . By regularity, there exists Bn ∈ B such that x ∈ B n ⊆ Bm .
Then, fn,m satisfies the requirement.

proofs.label: P5.38
proofs.sourceText:
Proof of Theorem 5.38. We reindex the functions in the lemma above as {fn :
n ∈ N}. Define a map F : X → [0, 1]N by F (x) = (f1 (x), f2 (x), . . .).
    Since each fn is continuous, F is continuous when [0, 1]N is equipped with
the product topology (cf. Theorem 3.91).
    We claim that F is an embedding. To see this, we first show that F is
injective. If x, y ∈ X with x ̸= y, then there exists a neighborhood U of x such
that y ∈/ U . By the lemma, there exists n such that fn (x) > 0 and fn |U c ≡ 0.
Hence, fn (y) = 0 ̸= fn (x), which shows that F (x) ̸= F (y).
    Next, we show that F is a homeomorphism onto its image. Since we already
showed that F is continuous and injective, it suffices to show that F (U ) is open
in F (X) for any open set U .
    Let x be any point in U and hence f (x) is an arbitrary point in F (U ). By
the construction of {fn }, there exists n such that fn (x) > 0 and fn |U c ≡ 0.
Let πn : [0, 1]N → [0, 1] be the projection onto the n-th coordinate. Then,
πn−1 ((fn (x)/2, 1]) ∩ F (X) is an open neighborhood of F (x) in F (X) and

   πn−1 ((fn (x)/2, 1]) ∩ F (X) = F ({y ∈ X : fn (y) > fn (x)/2 > 0}) ⊆ F (U ).

This shows that F (U ) is open in F (X).
   Now, we recall that [0, 1]N with the product topology is metrizable (Home-
work). Hence, F (X) is metrizable as a subspace of a metric space. Since F is
an embedding, X is metrizable.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P6.12
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. We will show that X \ Y is open. Given any fixed x ∈ X \ Y , for each
y ∈ Y choose disjoint open sets Uy and Vy such that x ∈ Uy and y ∈ Vy . Then,
{Vy : y ∈ Y } is an open cover of Y . By compactness
                                             Tn         of Y , there exists a finite
subcover {Vy1 , . . . , Vyn } of Y . Let U = i=1 Uyi . Then, U is disjoint from
Vy1 ∪ · · · ∪ Vyn and hence is an open neighbourhood of x disjoint from Y . Hence,
X \ Y is open.
   In fact, the proof above shows that for any x ∈ X \ Y , there exist disjoint
open sets U and V such that x ∈ U and Y ⊆ V .

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P6.24
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let U be an open cover of [a, b] where a < b. Define

        S = {x ∈ [a, b] : [a, x] can be covered by a finite subcover of U}.

It is clear that a ∈ S and if x ∈ S, then [a, x] ⊂ S. Since S is clearly upper-
bounded by b, we let c = sup S, i.e., the least upper bound of S. We will show
that c ∈ S and c = b.
     Clearly c ≤ b. If (a, c) is empty, then a = c ∈ S. Suppose (a, c) is nonempty.
Then, we have that [a, c) ⊂ S. Let Uc be an open set in U containing c. By the
definition of the order topology, there exists some (d, e) such that c ∈ (d, e) ⊆ Uc .
There must be some x ∈ (d, c) otherwise sup S ≤ d < c. Then, we know x ∈ S
and hence [a, x] can be covered by a finite subcover Ux of U. Note that Ux ∪{Uc }
is a finite subcover of [a, c]. This implies that c ∈ S.
     Suppose c < b. Now we consider the interval (c, b). Let T = {x ∈ [c, b] :
[c, x] = {c}} and let y = sup T . Note that y ≤ b. If y = c, then the open set
Uc containing c also contains some element z of (c, b), and hence [x, z] can be
covered by a finite subcover, which contradicts the definition of c. Therefore,
we must have y > c. But then the interval [a, y] can be covered by a finite
subcover of U by considering an open set around y, contradicting the definition
of c. Hence, we must have c = b.
     Therefore, we have shown that every open cover U of [a, b] has a finite sub-
cover. This completes the proof.


   As a corollary, we have the following result.

proofs.label: P6.26
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. (⇒) Assume K is compact. Then, K is closed since Rn is Hausdorff.
Then, consider the collection of open sets {Bm (0) : m ∈ N}, which is a cover of
Rn and hence K. There exists a finite subcover {Bm1 (0), Bm2 (0), . . . , Bmk (0)}
of K. Then, let M = max{m1 , m2 , . . . , mk }. It follows that K ⊆ BM (0),
showing that K is bounded.
   (⇐) Assume K is closed and bounded. Since K is bounded, it is contained in
some ball BR (0) for some radius R > 0. But then BR (0) ⊂ [−R, R]n . [−R, R]n
  1 This means any subset that is bounded above has a least upper bound. For example, we

know R satisfies this property as we can always take the supremum of a bounded set.
is compact as it is a finite product of compact sets (which we will prove later).
So K as a closed subset of a compact set is compact.
   In general metric spaces, we can’t expect closed and bounded subsets to be
compact as we have seen before. However, we do have the following important
characterizations of compactness in metric spaces.

proofs.label: P6.32
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Given ϵ > 0, for each x ∈ X, by continuity of f at x, there exists
δx > 0 such that for all y ∈ X, if dX (x, y) < δx , then dY (f (x), f (y)) < ϵ/2.
Then, {Bδx /2 (x) : x ∈ X} is an open cover of X. By compactness of X, there
exists a finite subcover {Bδxi /2 (xi ) : i = 1, 2, . . . , n}. Let δ = min{δxi /2 : i =
1, 2, . . . , n}. We will show that this δ works. Given any x1 , x2 ∈ X such that
dX (x1 , x2 ) < δ, there exists some i such that x1 ∈ Bδxi /2 (xi ). This implies
that dX (x1 , xi ) < δxi /2 and hence dX (x2 , xi ) ≤ dX (x2 , x1 ) + dX (x1 , xi ) <
δxi /2 + δxi /2 = δxi . Therefore, we have

   dY (f (x1 ), f (x2 )) ≤ dY (f (x1 ), f (xi )) + dY (f (xi ), f (x2 )) < ϵ/2 + ϵ/2 = ϵ.

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. (3) ⇒ (2): For completeness, let (xn ) be a Cauchy sequence in X. By
sequential compactness, there exists a convergent subsequence (xnk ) converging
to some x ∈ X. Since (xn ) is Cauchy, it must converge to the same limit x
(exercise). Hence, X is complete. For total boundedness, suppose not. Then,
there exists ϵ > 0 such that for any finite set F ⊂ X, there exists some x ∈ X
such that d(x, y) ≥ ϵ for all y ∈ F . In this way, we can construct a sequence (xn )
in X such that d(xn , xm ) ≥ ϵ for all n ̸= m. This sequence has no convergent
subsequence, contradicting the sequential compactness of X. Hence, X is totally
bounded.
    (2) ⇒ (1): Assume X is complete and totally bounded. Let {Uα }α∈I be an
open cover of X. Suppose there is no finite subcover.
    Using total boundedness, for each n ≥ 1 choose a finite 2−n -net Fn ⊂ X.
We build inductively a sequence (xn ) with (i) xn ∈ Fn , (ii) no finite subfamily
of {Uα } covers B2−n (xn ), and (iii) for n ≥ 2, B2−(n−1) (xn−1 ) ∩ B2−n (xn ) ̸= ∅.
    Base step: pick x1 ∈ F1 with (ii); such a choice exists because if every ball
{B2−1 (y) : y ∈ F1 } had a finite subcover, then, since F1 is finite, X would have
a finite subcover. Induction: having chosen xn−1 , consider those y ∈ Fn with
B2−(n−1) (xn−1 ) ∩ B2−n (y) ̸= ∅. If each such ball had a finite subcover, finitely
many of them would cover B2−(n−1) (xn−1 ), contradicting (ii) for xn−1 . Hence
choose xn with (ii)–(iii).
    From (iii), pick z ∈ B2−(n−1) (xn−1 )∩B2−n (xn ); then d(xn−1 , xn ) ≤ d(xn−1 , z)+
d(z, xn ) ≤ 2−(n−1) + 2−n ≤ 2−(n−2) . Thus for m < n,
                           n
                           X                         n
                                                     X
          d(xm , xn ) ≤           d(xk−1 , xk ) ≤           2−(k−2) ≤ 2−(m−2) ,
                          k=m+1                     k=m+1

so (xn ) is Cauchy and, by completeness, xn → a ∈ X.
    Choose α0 with a ∈ Uα0 and ε > 0 such that B(a, ε) ⊂ Uα0 . Pick n
with d(xn , a) < ε/2 and 2−n < ε/2. Then for any y ∈ B(xn , 2−n ), d(y, a) ≤
d(y, xn ) + d(xn , a) < ε; hence B(xn , 2−n ) ⊂ B(a, ε) ⊂ Uα0 , contradicting (ii).
Therefore the cover has a finite subcover, and X is compact.
    (1) ⇒ (3): Assume X is compact. Let (xn ) be any sequence in X. If
{xn : n ∈ N} is finite, then there exists some x ∈ X such that xn = x for
infinitely many n. Hence, the constant subsequence converges to x. Now assume
that {xn : n ∈ N} is infinite. Let A = {xn : n ∈ N}. Suppose that (xn ) has
no convergent subsequence. Then, for any x ∈ X \ A, there exists an open
neighbourhood Ux of x such that Ux ∩ A = ∅. This implies that A is closed
and hence compact. For any a ∈ A, since no subsequence of (xn ) converges to
a, there exists an open neighbourhood Va of a such that Va ∩ A = {a}. Then,
{Va } is an infinite open cover of A with no finite subcover, contradicting the
compactness of A. Therefore, (xn ) has a convergent subsequence.


   Neither does sequential compactness imply compactness nor vice versa in
general topological spaces.

proofs.sourceText:
Proof. (⇒) Assume x is a cluster point of the net (xα )α∈A . Define the directed
set
          Γ = {(α, U ) : α ∈ A, U is an open neighbourhood of xα }
with the order (α1 , U1 ) ≤ (α2 , U2 ) if and only if α1 ≤ α2 and U2 ⊆ U1 . Define
the map φ : Γ → A by (α, U ) 7→ α. Then, the subnet (xφ(γ) )γ∈Γ converges to
x. (Note that the map φ is not injective, so a subnet is quite different from a
subsequence.)
   (⇐) Assume there exists a subnet (xφ(γ) )γ∈Γ that converges to x. Given
any open neighbourhood U of x and any α0 ∈ A, by the definition of subnet,
there exists some γ0 ∈ Γ such that for all γ ≥ γ0 , we have φ(γ) ≥ α0 . Since the
subnet converges to x, there exists some γ1 ≥ γ0 such that for all γ ≥ γ1 , we have
xφ(γ) ∈ U . In particular, for this choice of γ1 , we have some β = φ(γ1 ) ≥ α0
such that xβ = xφ(γ1 ) ∈ U . Therefore, x is a cluster point of the net.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P6.44
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let {xλ } be an ultranet in X and let x ∈ X be a cluster point of the net.
Given any open neighbourhood U of x, since {xλ } is an ultranet, it is eventually
in U or eventually in X \ U . Since x is a cluster point, it cannot be eventually
in X \ U . Hence, it is eventually in U . Therefore, {xλ } converges to x.

proofs.title: Source sketch
proofs.label: P6.45
proofs.sourceText:
Sketch of proof. Let (xλ ) be a net in a set X. We call Q ⊂ P (X) a admissible
family if

   • for any A1 , A2 ∈ Q, we have ∅ ̸= A1 ∩ A2 ∈ Q;
   • for any A ∈ Q, the net (xλ ) is frequently in A (for any λ0 , there exists
     some λ ≥ λ0 such that xλ ∈ A).
Let Q denote the collection of all admissible families and we partially order Q
by inclusion. Using Zorn’s lemma, we can show that Q has a maximal element
Qmax . You can show that if A ⊂ X, then either A ∈ Qmax or X \ A ∈ Qmax .
Now, we define a directed set Γ = {(λ, A) : λ ∈ Λ, A ∈ Qmax , s.t. xλ ∈ A} with
the order defined by (λ1 , A1 ) ≤ (λ2 , A2 ) if λ1 ≤ λ2 and A2 ⊆ A1 . Then, let
φ : Γ → Λ be defined by (λ, A) 7→ λ. This defines a subnet and you can check
that this subnet is indeed an ultranet.

proofs.label: P6.47
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. (⇒) Since each projection map πα : X = Xα → Xα is continuous, we
have that Xα = πα (X) is compact for each α.                              Q
     (⇐) Assume that Xα is compact for each α. Let {xλ } be a net in X = Xα .
Then, {xλ } has a subnet {xλµ } that is an ultranet. Then, for each α, the net
{πα (xλµ )} is an ultranet in Xα which has some cluster point yα ∈ Xα as Xα
is compact. Since {πα (xλµ )} is an ultranet, it converges to yα . Then, the net
{xλµ } converges to y = (yα ) ∈ X which is hence a cluster point of the original
net {xλ }. Therefore, by the characterization of compactness using nets, X is
compact.

proofs.label: P6.64
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. 1⇒ 2: straightforward.
    2⇒ 3: Let V = ∪n Vn is a countably locally finite S
                                                      open refinement of U where
each Vn is locally finite. For each n, define Wn = Vn which is open. Then,
{W1 , . . .} covers X. Define An = Wn \ ∪i<n Wi . Then, {An } is a locally finite
refinement of {Wn } that covers X. Now, define

                        W = {V ∩ An : V ∈ Vn , n ∈ N}.

Then, W is a locally finite refinement of V and hence U that covers X.
    3 ⇒ 4: Let B be the collection of all open sets U such that U is contained
in some element of U (I just want something smaller so that I can take closure).
By regularity, B is an open cover of X. Then, it has a locally finite refinement
C that covers X by (3). Let D = {C|C ∈ C}. Then, D still covers X which
refines U . It is still locally finite which can be checked directly.
    4 ⇒ 1: Let V be a locally finite closed refinement of U that covers X. For
each x ∈ X, let Wx be a neighborhood of x meeting only finitely many elements
of V. Then, {Wx } is an open cover of X. Apply 4, there exists a locally finite
closed refinement A of {Wx } that covers X.
    For each V ∈ V, define
                                             [
                                 V∗ =X \          A ⊃ V.
                                       A∈A
                                      A∩V =∅

Then, V ∗ is open as it is the complement of a closed set. Furthermore, {V ∗ |V ∈
V} is an open cover of X. Now, we show that {V ∗ |V ∈ V} is locally finite. Given
any x ∈ X, there is a neighborhood U of x meeting finitely many A1 , . . . , An
(they also cover U ). But whenever U ∩ V ∗ ̸= ∅, there exists some Ai such that
Ai ∩ V ∗ ̸= ∅ which implies that Ai ∩ V ̸= ∅. Since each Ai meets only finitely
many V ’s due to the definition, we have that U meets only finitely many V ∗ ’s.
Therefore, {V ∗ |V ∈ V} is locally finite.
   Now, for each V ∈ V, pick U ∈ U such that V ⊂ U , and form W = V ∗ ∩ U .
Then, the collection of all such W ’s is an open refinement of U that covers X
and is locally finite.

contradicting that D is nonempty.

Proof. We prove the case of two spaces X, Y . Let (a, b) ∈ X × Y . For x ∈ X, let
Tx = (X × {b}) ∪ ({x} × Y ). Note that Tx is connected by the previous theorem
and the fact that the product of a space with a singleton is homeomorphic to
the space itself.
    Note that X × Y = ∪x∈X Tx is connected again by the previous theorem,
since all Tx contain the point (a, b).
    The general case follows by induction.

Proof. Assume that Y has a separation A, B. Pick a ∈ A and b ∈ B with a < b.
Then, [a, b] ⊂ Y . Let A0 = A ∩ [a, b] and B0 = B ∩ [a, b]. Then, A0 , B0 are open
in [a, b] w.r.t. the subspace topology which is the same as the order topology
on [a, b]. So A0 , B0 form a separation of [a, b].
     Let c = sup A0 . We show that c ∈    / A0 and c ∈  / B0 , contradicting that
[a, b] = A0 ∪ B0 .
     Suppose c ∈ B0 . Then, c ̸= a, so c = b or a < c < b. Since B0 is open, in
either case, there exists d such that (d, c] ⊂ B0 . If c = b, then d is an upper
bound of A0 less than c, contradicting that c = sup A0 . If a < c < b, then since
c is an upper bound, (c, b] ∩ A0 = ∅. Hence, (d, b] = (d, c] ∪ (c, b] ∩ A0 = ∅ which
makes d an upper bound of A0 less than c, again a contradiction. Thus, c ∈     / B0 .
     Now suppose c ∈ A0 . Then, c ̸= b, and so c = a or a < c < b. Since A0 is
open, in either case, there exists e such that [c, e) ⊂ A0 . But then any z such
that c < z < e is in A0 , contradicting that c = sup A0 (z exists because of (2)).
Thus, c ∈ / A0 .
   Now we can prove the intermediate value theorem.

that [f (a), f (b)] ⊆ f ([a, b]). Suppose not, then there exists r ∈ (f (a), f (b))
with r ∈/ f ([a, b]). Let U = (−∞, r) and V = (r, ∞). Then, U ∩ f ([a, b]) and
V ∩ f ([a, b]) separate f ([a, b]), contradicting connectedness of f ([a, b]).
   The interval [a, b] can be replaced by any connected space X.

Proof. Suppose U, V separates X. Let f : [a, b] → X be a path from x ∈ U to
y ∈ V . Since [a, b] is connected, f ([a, b]) is connected. So by a theorem we proved
previously, f ([a, b]) is contained in U or V , contradicting that f (a) = x ∈ U
and f (b) = y ∈ V .

point x0 in common.

V ⊆ P since P is a path component. Thus, P is open.

containing x is an open path connected neighborhood of x contained in U .

theorem above, we know C is open. Then, by the theorem again, P and Q are
open in C and hence separate C, contradicting connectedness of C.

proofs.title: Source argument
proofs.label: P7.44
proofs.sourceText:
Proof. Let X be an ultrametric space with ultrametric d. We need to show
that the components of X are singletons. Let x, y ∈ X be distinct points. Let
r = u(x, y) > 0. Then, Br (x) is an open neighborhood of x. I claim that
X \ Br (x) is an open neighborhood of y. Indeed, for any point z ∈ X \ Br (x),
we have u(x, z) ≥ r > 0. Pick r0 ∈ (0, r). Then, for any z ′ ∈ Br0 (z), we have
that u(x, z ′ ) = u(x, z) ≥ r. Hence z ′ ∈
                                         / Br (x) and thus Br0 (z) ⊆ X \ Br (x).
This shows that X \ Br (x) is open and hence an open neighborhood of y. This
implies that x and y lie in different components. Since x, y ∈ X are arbitrary,
we conclude that the components of X are singletons.
